title: The intake brake summons the development manager at once and releases itself: no hold waits on a person unless she has escalated it
description: Label: reliability. Operator decision, Mason, 2026-09-19, via his assistant, recorded as a directive the same day. His words: 'I'm ok with it so long as the DM will always be immediately invoked to figure it out and get things moving again -- no waiting.' CONTEXT: the brake tripped on Sep 2, 5, 13, 17, and 19; each time it stayed held until a person released it, today for about two hours unnoticed with a free developer slot idle. SCOPE: (1) the moment the brake trips, the harness invokes the development manager's sweep at once rather than at her next scheduled pass, with the three blocked runs and the reason each blocked in front of her (353's delivery machinery is the vehicle; the entries ride the wake, not the opening briefing); (2) she decides what happens: release intake, re-run or repair the runs, or keep the hold and escalate to the operator; (3) the brake is SELF-RELEASING: after her decision, or after a configured cooldown if she has not decided, one probe run starts; a landed probe reopens intake, a blocked probe keeps the hold and tells the operator once (383 owns the telling); (4) a hold never waits on a person unless the development manager has escalated it. Environmental stops (394's classes; 377's provider outages) do not count toward the trip, per 383's note. Done means: the 2026-09-19T17:56Z shape replayed produces a development manager turn within one poll with the three entries delivered, a recorded decision, and either a reopened intake or a probe within the cooldown; yoyo status names the hold, who is deciding, and the probe; the sweep record shows the summoned pass; and docs/operations.md's intake-hold section says a person is asked only on escalation.
notes:
Admitted to the backlog by the product manager in conversation chat-91253e0e070c17b0663651cc48602122, after turn 655.

Reason: Operator decision: a brake that waits on a person is a stall the harness inflicts on itself; five trips in seventeen days, each waiting on a person, and he named it as blocking reliable execution.

title: The reviewer's bounded patch orders code before test data and generated files, so the bound never cuts the Go that matters
description: Successor to 387 (closed 2026-09-19) for three reviewer reports on 141.3 filed after it closed: the reviewed patch is cut alphabetically at the size bound, so a change whose committed fixtures sort before its code (5,500 lines of internal/dashboard/testdata/renders ahead of ~850 lines of internal/readmodel, the throughput derivation the page depends on) leaves the code unreviewable; the read-model went to review unseen and it cost 141.3 two rounds. Done means: within the existing size bound the patch presents source files first, then tests, then testdata and generated or golden files, with the cut falling at the tail; a file the bound cuts is listed by name and size so the reviewer knows what she did not see; large fixtures can be delivered as openable evidence outside the diff body; and the 141.3 diff replayed through the bound presents internal/readmodel whole.

title: A check stage cannot take hours: the race suite runs once per landing on main or narrowed to the touched packages, and the per-run check stage has a declared time bound the operator sees
description: Operator order, Mason, 2026-09-19, at priority 0 ahead of the dashboard children. EVIDENCE: on 2026-09-19 a run on 389 sat in its checks for over two hours under load (make race alone 1h33m and counting), which held the watch session's drain for the same two hours (398) and starved the second seat; 21 timing-flake reports this fortnight are the same suite failing under the load it creates. WANTED: (1) the full race suite runs ONCE PER LANDING on main - after integration, over the integrated commit, with a failure reported as a red landing that files its own item and never blocks the developer run that landed it - or, where the harness can compute it, narrowed to the packages the change touches for the per-run gate; (2) the per-run check stage has a DECLARED TIME BOUND, configuration beside docs/configuration.md#how-long-a-check-may-take with a default in minutes, that yoyo status shows while checks run ('checks: 14m of 30m') and that ends the stage as a stoppage naming the bound and the check when reached, rather than running on; (3) the bound is visible in the sweep record and the Slack line for the run. The declared checks list in .yoyodyne/config.yaml is the operator's paste and this item does not touch it; the item says what the line should read. If the architect reads a narrowed per-run gate as a change to developer-verifies-before-submitting or integration-requires-revision-bound-evidence, she rules on it through the governed path and the run builds to the ruling. Done means: the 389 shape replayed (a two-hour race suite under load) ends the check stage at the bound with the reason named; a landing on main runs the full suite once and reports its result; a run over a change to one package runs that package's race tests in the gate; and docs/operations.md and docs/configuration.md say what a check may cost and where the full suite runs.

title: A draining watch session keeps pulling and running recurring tasks until it restarts, and the drain is bounded
description: Operator's assistant, 2026-09-19, under the reliability directive. WHAT HAPPENED: at 07:35Z the watch session logged 'stopped pulling: a build was deployed over the one this session was started from, and the session is restarting into it', then did nothing for over two hours - no pull, no recurring task - because the self-redeploy (288) waits out the runs it hosts before restarting, and the one run it hosted (389) had been in its checks under load for over two hours (make race alone 1h33m and counting). Seen by the operator: no tokens spent for two hours, the development manager's hourly sweep silently missed two passes (last 07:35Z), the second seat stayed empty. WANTED: (a) a draining session keeps running its recurring tasks and keeps pulling into free seats until the moment it actually restarts - draining is about the runs it hosts, not the scheduler's other duties; a task or pull that must be skipped for the drain says so in the sweep record and yoyo status (372's rule). (b) the drain is BOUNDED: past a declared limit (configuration, with a default measured in minutes, not hours) the session restarts anyway and the hosted run is preserved and re-adopted by the new session; failing adoption, the run is recorded as cancelled with its branch and worktree preserved and its reason naming the redeploy, never silently held. title: An operator-action finding reaches the operator when it is recorded: one direct message, and a named line in Needs-a-human
description: Operator's assistant, 2026-09-18, under the reliability directive. EVIDENCE: six developer reports asking for a change only a person could make sat in the report pile from 2026-08-17 until the 2026-09-14 sweep reached them, and the resulting operator-action finding landed on the product manager's checklist, which the operator sees only when he asks. He asked why it took a month to reach him. WANTED: (a) when a finding that needs the operator's hand is recorded - by the product manager handling a report, by a role filing one at a severity that means action, or by a run stopping on a condition only a person can clear - the operator is sent one Slack direct message, tagged by member id per the communication rule, saying what is needed and where it is recorded; one message per finding, never repeated on later passes; (b) yoyo status lists each such finding by name under Needs-a-human, ahead of undecided amendments and never folded into 'and N things not named here'. Done means: the CLAUDE.md case replayed sends the message the moment the finding is recorded and shows it by name in status; a second pass sends nothing more; and docs/operations.md says where such findings go.

title: An undecided stoppage is re-offered until it has a decision
description:
Operator-directed at p1, 2026-09-07, widened 2026-09-14 by the operator's assistant's finding into the fuller shape - the sweep is BLIND to the docket. The path that puts a stopped run to the development manager fires only when a run NEWLY stops (last at 01:21Z on 09-07); her hourly sweep records 'no stoppage, dead claim, or docket entry reached this desk' and 'a survey shows open items and not running ones' while yoyo status counts THIRTY stopped runs with preserved work awaiting her decision - 192 and 187 since 2026-08-30, most from the 2026-09-04..07 forge-divergence window - plus FOUR recorded decisions nobody carried out (117.1, 349, 346, 330.2). The sweep's prompt asks her to sweep for undecided stoppages, and the harness gives her no docket read, so the pile is invisible to the one role whose job is deciding it; the operator's assistant relays it by hand, which is the courier role 142 existed to end.

SCOPE: (1) the sweep pass is HANDED THE DOCKET as part of its wakeup - every undecided stoppage with its run id and blocker, and every recorded-but-uncarried decision with what it decided - so 'the queue is quiet' can never again mean 'thirty items wait where I cannot see them'; (2) the wakeup covers a docket entry's CREATION per the management-and-supervision design, so a new stoppage reaches her within the hour rather than only when a run newly stops; (3) a stoppage with no decision standing is RE-OFFERED on a schedule until it has one - idempotent, not a one-shot event; (4) the count of undecided stoppages and uncarried decisions is on the surfaces her sweep and the operator read. Composes with 346 (a recorded decision carries itself out): this gets decisions made, 346 gets them executed. FOR THE RECORD, from the operator: the twelve stoppages the scheduler log says could not be put to the DM are from 2026-09-03, not from any current stall - they still need a person and are not evidence of a live failure.

Done means the sweep's wakeup carries the docket, a new entry wakes her, an undecided entry reappears until decided, the counts are visible, and today's shape replayed - thirty stoppages, four uncarried decisions, a sweep reporting calm - is impossible.

title: Action and capability registries wrapping the existing pipeline steps
description: Second runtime child of 209. The registry of named actions - each wrapping an existing trusted pipeline step (claim, develop, publish, check, review, promote, clean up) - with the capabilities each requires declared in code. Configuration will choose sequence from these names; it can never mint one, which is the epic's capability-stays-trusted-code law. No caller changes: the existing hard-coded pipeline keeps calling its steps directly; the registry is a second door onto the same functions. Done means: every step the delivery pipeline executes today has a registered action naming its capability requirements; the registry refuses duplicate names and unknown capabilities at construction, tested; a repository test asserts the registry's coverage against the pipeline's actual step set so a later step cannot be added unregistered silently; existing behavior is byte-for-byte unchanged (the 211 golden traces still pass unmodified); the diff is shown whole to review. Dispatch waits on the hardening freeze.

title: Workflow definition schema: versioned, digest-pinned, validated
description: First runtime child of the configurable-workflows epic (209), per the landed design's conversion order. The declarative workflow-definition format: versioned schema for states, transitions, and action references; a content digest computed over the definition so instances can pin to it; validation types that make an ill-formed definition unrepresentable rather than checked later. title: The four-line status: running, working, not-startable-with-reasons, needs-a-human
description:
Operator directive, 2026-08-30, admitted at the queue front - his third ask for clear running-state in two days, with each stall's confusion tracing to its absence. The rendering surface for the certainty contract (139), in the ratified four-line format whose quoted example is the canonical fixture:

Running (N developer runs) - each with item, phase, elapsed, spend.
Working (N conversations) - the persona turns in flight, which no surface counts today.
Not startable - each ready-but-unstarted item with its named reason taken from the real refusal, never session memory.
Needs a human - always present: 'nothing' or the explicit list with whose-move.

A state that cannot render into these four lines is a bug in the state. Lands first on the CLI (yoyo status or the builder's naming) per the contract's CLI-first sequencing, serving from the read model's query where it exists and from the truest available sources meanwhile - the format must not wait for 139's full machinery to say what is already knowable, but must converge on the one query as it lands. The heartbeat adopts the same four lines. Done means the operator's example renders from live state, all four lines always print, the working line counts conversation turns for the first time, and no residual category exists anywhere in the output.

The acceptance clauses are met and tested: all four lines always render (TestQuietHarnessPrintsAllFourLines pins the exact text), the operator's quoted example renders from live state (TestTheOperatorsExampleRendersFromState), the working line counts conversation turns from the lease for the first time (TestWorkingCountsOnlyHeldConversations), and the absence of a residual bucket is asserted at the CLI level. The unreadable-versus-empty discipline is held consistently — an unreadable source, an unreadable switch, an unwired source, and an unpriceable run each have a test proving they are never reported as nothing or as free — and the heartbeat states the absence of the lines rather than omitting them. No delivered invariant is violated: nothing here writes to the repository, invokes a role, touches a promotion lease, claims work, or stores durable state in a provider session. docs/operations.md and docs/reporting.md were updated alongside, and I found no document in the patch left asserting something the change made false, beyond the one example-line discrepancy below. All four checks pass and they exercise the new behaviour rather than merely compiling it. The observations below are minor and do not block.
Finding [minor] (docs/operations.md:600): The documented canonical example cannot be produced by the renderer. readNeedsHuman formats attention as `fmt.Sprintf("directive %s is unresolved: %s", paused.ID, ...)`, which yields `directive <ID> is unresolved`, but the example line reads `directive-4f2c… is unresolved` with a hyphen and no space. Either the example has a typo, or directive IDs carry a `directive-` prefix (as run-… and chat-… IDs here do) and the rendered line stutters as `directive directive-4f2c… is unresolved`. Reconcile the two, and check `run %s of %s ended still owing a step` for the same stutter against `run-…` IDs.
Finding [minor] (internal/readmodel/standing.go:330): readWorking answers "is a turn in flight" by acquiring and immediately releasing each recorded conversation's exclusive advisory lease. That probe previously ran only under `yoyo agent`, an explicit inspection verb; it now runs on every `yoyo status` and on the Slack heartbeat, which is a long-lived background process. A conversation that tries to start inside the probe's window sees ErrConversationHeld and may report itself as somebody else's conversation. The window is tiny, but consider whether a shared/read probe or a retry on the acquiring side is warranted now that a background process takes these locks periodically.
Finding [minor] (internal/cli/status.go:270): standingSources silently drops the error from every store constructor except the tracker, leaving the source nil, so the line then reports "nothing was wired to read …" when what actually happened is that the state directory would not open. The comment on unreadableTracker states the right rule — "so the line says what actually went wrong instead of reporting a wiring gap" — and applies it only to the tracker. Carrying the construction error the same way for the run, conversation, hold, and session stores would make the four lines say the real cause to an operator debugging a broken state root.
Finding [minor] (internal/cli/status.go:162): The item's done clause reads "all four lines always print", and the change omits them entirely when an item is named. The rationale is coherent and is documented in operations.md, the usage text, and a test, so I am not treating it as incomplete — but it is a product decision beyond the literal clause and the operator may want it confirmed, since `yoyo status <id>` is a common invocation that now answers a strictly narrower question than the directive described.

The item's done-criteria are met by this change as far as a diff can meet them (the DM tier is live and the inbound path is tested; closing 68.20 and 68.22 is a tracker act at landing), but the change is not yet complete against its own documentation: by subscribing message.im and reading every conversation, it made the sink able to see direct messages, and a message that @-mentions the app in a DM now gets silence (or the 'nothing was recorded' text) while docs/reporting.md and docs/slack/setup.md still promise that an @-mention is always answered wherever the sink can see one. Finding [major] (internal/slack/inbound.go:208): docs/reporting.md (the patched paragraph 'Outside those threads the sink is silent, with two exceptions… a message that @-mentions the app is always answered, wherever it can see one') and docs/slack/setup.md ('Asking the app directly: @-mention the app and you always get an answer. Anywhere the sink can see…') now assert something this change made false. Before it, readInbound refused every conversation but the reporting channel and the manifest had no message.im, so a DM was never seen; now every DM is read and routed by handle straight into decideThread before the mention check, so an operator who @-mentions the app at the top of a DM the sink never asked in gets no answer at all (Latest returns not-found and decideThread returns silently), and one in a conversation with a prior ask gets the misplaced-reply text rather than the four lines. Silence after a person addresses the app is the failure class this package's own documentation rules out. Resolve it one way or the other: in decideThread, when threadTS is empty and the text mentions the app, answer as mention.go does (and let the misplaced-reply text cover only un-mentioning top-level messages), with a test that a DM @-mention is answered — or narrow both documents to say the always-answered promise holds in the reporting channel only and that a direct message outside an ask's thread is answered only when it is a decision typed in the wrong place.
Finding [minor] (docs/slack/manifest.yaml:32): The patched im:write comment in docs/slack/manifest.yaml still opens 'It is used for one class of message and only that one: the harness itself being degraded', and then enumerates two degraded states, while docs/slack/setup.md and docs/reporting.md in this same change describe two classes (degraded and advisory-once) and four degraded states. The sentence was already imprecise before this change, but the paragraph was rewritten here and the 'one class … only that one' claim was kept; align it with setup.md's wording.
Finding [minor] (internal/slack/decision.go:150): standingMark returns "" when the heartbeat cursor cannot be read, and misplaced then tells the operator their last ask 'has since cleared, so nothing is waiting on a decision from you now' — a positive claim the sink cannot vouch for when the read failed, and one that could send somebody away from a line that is still stopped. Distinguish 'could not tell' from 'cleared': on a cursor read error, say that whether the ask still stands could not be read and point at the thread anyway, or say only that nothing was recorded and where a decision is recorded.

Two minor observations are below. The README invokes it as `bash bin/yoyo-account`, which works, but the script's own usage header shows `yoyo-account` and `yoyo-account --alias personal`, and the sibling bin/yoyo-status is documented as `./bin/yoyo-status`. Add the executable bit so both spellings work.
Finding [minor] (internal/orchestrator/pipeline.go:843): In resumeRun, a record whose AccountAlias is empty (one written before the field was carried) now only gets an alias if chooseAccount succeeds; under a pool with every budget spent it stays empty, and activeRun.account() then resolves an empty alias to an empty directory — so the resumed invocations run in the machine's own provider home (the `default` account's login under a pool) and are recorded pinned to no account at all. title: Worktree cleanup keeps the sandbox viable: prune stale registrations, bound the deny list
description: Critical report from the developer on 82.2's run, 2026-08-23: every Bash command in that worktree fails at spawn with E2BIG - the sandbox profile adds 335 filesystem deny paths per command, 168 of them for registered git worktrees, and the list grows without bound as the harness creates worktrees. That run was documentation-only and cost nothing; the next code change in that environment cannot run make check, go test, or bd at all. Immediate remedy per the report: git worktree prune and stale-worktree removal on the machine. The durable fix: the harness cleans up its per-item worktrees - many run records this month carry 'worktree (cleanup pending)' - so registrations do not accumulate into the deny list until command spawning breaks. Done means the machine's registered-worktree count reflects live runs plus a bounded tail, cleanup runs as part of settle or reconcile rather than by hand, and a command in a fresh worktree spawns with a deny list that does not scale with harness history.

title: The release gate commits the tracker's derived exports instead of refusing on them
description:
Operator-directed from v0.3.0's first cut, 2026-08-23, deadline: before the product manager's first delegated release tomorrow. The cut refused because .beads/interactions.jsonl and .beads/issues.jsonl were dirty - derived exports that mutate whenever anything touches the tracker, including the walkthrough the gate itself runs, which is why the stash-pop after the successful cut also conflicted. They affect nothing a release ships, but under the delegated daily cadence the refusal means most days stall with nobody standing there to stash.

Fix shape, the operator preferring the second: the cleanliness check ignores the tracker's derived exports, or the cut commits them first as their own housekeeping commit so the tag still names a fully-clean tree. The housekeeping commit is stronger - it keeps the archives-match-commit property literal rather than excepted; the builder confirms or argues. Everything else about the refusal was the gate working: it stopped before writing anything and named its reason - preserve that.

Done means a cut on a tree dirty only in the tracker's derived exports proceeds - exports committed as housekeeping, tag naming a clean tree - a tree dirty in anything else still refuses by name, and the stash-pop conflict cannot recur because nothing is stashed.
notes:
Admitted to the backlog by the product manager in conversation chat-91253e0e070c17b0663651cc48602122, after turn 208.

Reason: Tomorrow's first delegated cut stalls without it - the gate refuses on files the gate itself dirties, most days, with nobody standing there. Priority 0 alone at the front so tonight's selection takes it ahead of everything; displacement is the whole p1 tier waiting one pull, accepted against the deadline the operator named.

Review summary: The change does what the work item asked and does it in the shape the operator preferred: the cleanliness gate excludes the two tracker exports via `:(exclude)` pathspecs while still naming any other dirt by file, the exports are committed as their own housekeeping commit placed after the last gate and before the tag so the tag names a tree with nothing uncommitted, the index is put back if that commit fails, and the publishing line becomes `git push --atomic origin <branch> <tag>` only on a day the commit was made. The shell suite genuinely exercises all three acceptance criteria — dirty-only-in-exports proceeds, dirty-in-anything-else refuses by name and leaves no tag, and nothing is stashed — plus the two cases the item did not mention but that decide whether the fix holds: the walkthrough dirtying the exports on its own way through, and the tracker's post-commit export hook, with a self-check proving that fixture's hook actually fires. README.md and docs/developing-yoyo.md are both brought in line with the new behavior, and wiring the suite into `make test` from Go is a reasonable way to make that evidence run in the ordinary loop. One thing blocks approval: the script's own stated prerequisite line, rewritten by this change, names a git floor its new code exceeds, and the gap silently defeats the hooks-off guarantee the housekeeping commit depends on. Note that only a selected subset of invariants was before me, so this is not a statement that the invariants as a whole are satisfied, and documents this change does not touch were not visible to me.
Finding [major] (scripts/cut-release.sh:29): The header now states "Requires git (1.9 or newer, for the `:(exclude)` pathspec the cleanliness check uses)", but the housekeeping commit this same change adds runs `git -c core.hooksPath=/dev/null commit`, and `core.hooksPath` is only honoured from git 2.9. On git 1.9-2.8 the option is unknown config and is silently ignored: the tracker's post-commit export hook runs, `.beads/*.jsonl` are dirty again immediately after the commit that exists to clean them, and the tag names a dirty tree with nothing downstream detecting it — the exact property the change is built to preserve, lost without a message. The printed `git push --atomic ...` likewise needs git 2.4 on the operator's side. Raise the stated floor to 2.9 and name `core.hooksPath` as the reason alongside `:(exclude)`, or suppress the hook in a way the stated floor actually supports.
Finding [minor] (internal/cli/release_repository_test.go:71): TestTheReleaseVerbHousekeepsTheExportsARunAllows asserts the two lists are strictly equal, and the new docs/developing-yoyo.md row instructs "Add the path to both." The lists coincide today but answer different questions — what a run may tolerate the primary checkout acquiring, versus what a release cut may commit on the operator's behalf — so a path legitimately added to `AllowedPrimaryChanges` alone will fail this check and the documented remedy will push someone to make the cut commit a file it should not. Consider asserting containment in the direction that is actually implied, or stating in the row that a deliberate divergence means changing the check rather than the lists.

title: The architect settles the publish shape for approved artifact writes
description: Carved from yoyodyne-ifd.100's rescope as the gate its publish child cites: the architect's design answer on how a typed artifact write's commit and pull request work - how the commit relates to the primary checkout, given a run refuses to start over uncommitted changes; whether the write publishes through a branch and pull request like a run or commits directly under the harness identity; and how the operator's recorded approval relates to the publication. Argued in the architect's conversation, recorded by the operator into the governed designs. Done means the shape is recorded in an architect-owned design or decision record, and yoyodyne-ifd.100.1 can be implemented against it without inventing anything.
notes:
Created under yoyodyne-ifd.100, decomposing it by the development manager in conversation chat-419cedb4a013b063f477e322a2a60466, after turn 45.

Reason: 100.1 was gated on an answer that existed as no item, so nothing stopped the scheduler pulling it and having a developer invent the shape the reviewer refused; this makes the gate real and marks it for the conversation that owns it.

Goal served: A newcomer can go from the documented install to a working first run on their own repository using the readme alone.
Noted by the product manager in conversation chat-91253e0e070c17b0663651cc48602122, after turn 237.

Reason: The architect's pending answer is the closer for a recurring operator friction; the evidence lands on the item that carries the question so the decision weighs the operational cost, not only the governance shape.

Operational evidence for the publish-shape answer, from three developer reports on ifd.100's run, 2026-08-23: a document approved from a conversation is written into the primary checkout and left uncommitted, and gitworktree.ValidateReady refuses to start any run while the primary checkout is dirty - so an operator who writes their goals from chat and then asks for work sees 'primary repository has uncommitted changes: docs/product/v1-goals.md' until they commit by hand. The friction is documented and announced on every write, but it is exactly the gap the unimplemented publish step closes, and it makes the shape question concrete: whether the harness commits, opens a pull request, or leaves the file is not just governance - it decides whether writing a document from chat stalls the work loop. The filed amendment on the publish shape should be decided with this in view.
Architect ruling, 2026-08-31, stated whole: the typed artifact-write's output stops at the operator's working tree. Authorize records approval in frontmatter against the revision produced; publication is the operator's own commit under their own identity; until they commit, the document is an uncommitted change and runs refuse to start over it - and the surface that performed the write says so at the moment of writing. Added reason: no path into the target branch exists except a reviewed promotion or the operator's hand - a harness-made commit would be a promotion by another name sweeping in unapproved tree state - and the working-tree stop keeps the artifact read model two-valued: committed state, or operator-pending edit visibly blocking runs. No committed-but-never-operator-touched third state.

Store writes go through repowrite with the supervision directory as the declared root, and the planted-symlink test asserts an EscapeError rather than a write landing outside, which is what repository-writes-are-physically-confined asks for. One minor observation about the CLI wiring accompanies the approval.

Review summary: The replay onto the landed exchange machinery is the right shape: the durable contract keeps a round on disk with its holder before the answering voice is reached, Interrupted() reads the crash window off the record, the per-exchange lease is what tells a dead carrier from a live one, Survey returns a plan rather than acting (so the harness stays the only invoker), staleness is derived from recorded references and reports rather than gates, and the docs touched — reconcile's usage text, docs/operations.md, docs/conversation.md, and the authority inventory's new Leases row — describe what the code now does, including the honest admissions that the in-flight bound is derived-but-unenforced and that no current revisions are fed in yet. Checks pass and the orchestrator tests run over the real store and real OS leases, which is the right evidence for these claims. One real defect stops approval: SupervisionLoop.Run surveys and acts on the snapshot it read from List() before it took any lease, so an exchange whose live carrier finishes and releases in the window between List() and Hold() is reclaimed against a stale copy — overwriting a recorded answer (and its cost) with 'the process carrying it is gone'. That is exactly the double-write the lease is claimed to prevent, and Conductor.Reclaim's own comment asserts the guarantee this path does not deliver. Two minor observations accompany it. Note that I can see only the patch and the work item, so this is not a statement about the repository's other documents, and the invariants I was shown are a selected set.
Finding [major] (internal/orchestrator/supervision.go:0): Run() takes each lease *after* reading the records, then surveys and acts on the pre-lease snapshot. If a live process finishes its round and releases the lease in the window between Store.List() and Store.Hold(id), Hold succeeds, the stale copy still shows the round unanswered, Survey plans a Reclaim, and Conductor.Reclaim is handed the stale Exchange — writing back a record that destroys the answer and the cost the provider was just paid for and replaces it with 'was carrying it and is gone; nothing came back'. Reclaim's own doc comment claims the lease prevents exactly this, and Conductor.Put avoids it by loading the record after taking the lease; this path does not. Re-load each exchange from the store once its lease is held and survey/act on that copy (or refuse to act when UpdatedAt has moved since the listing), and add a case that interleaves a completing round with the sweep's discovery.
Finding [minor] (internal/orchestrator/supervision.go:0): The sweep still holds a lease on every open exchange it could take for the span between the discovery loop and the early release after Survey, and a conductor meeting a held exchange refuses the ask outright rather than waiting. TestASweepHoldsOnlyTheThreadsItIsActingOn only proves the idle thread is free during the acting phase, so the discovery window is untested and unmentioned; the comment above the early release reads as though the collision had been eliminated rather than narrowed. Worth either narrowing further (hold, decide, and release per exchange) or saying plainly in the comment that the window remains.
Finding [minor] (internal/cli/reconcile.go:0): The CLI wiring is still the one path with no test behind it: reconcileRuns/sweepSupervision/supervisionLoopFrom are never exercised with a real configuration, and supervisionErr is joined into the result so a supervision problem makes `yoyo reconcile` exit 1 even when every run reconciled cleanly. The added tests build the loop by hand and call reportReconcileResult directly. A case running the reconcile path over an empty supervision store would cover the wiring and the exit status.

First, severity: the park posts at note, the same weight as checks-passed, when an exhausted usage limit is the single highest-value message the channel can carry while nobody is watching - it means nothing will happen for hours. It posts at warning.

title: A subagent's result is not the run's terminal result
description:
Run run-841f5ee1866addb533c02a30e67f001a for yoyodyne-ifd.60 died on the second-terminal-result guard while its developer was mid-sentence resolving the last review findings. The developer had spawned Claude Code subagents (system task_started/task_notification events precede it), and a subagent's completion arrives in the parent stream as another type:result envelope -- event 1185 in the recorded stream: empty result text, empty terminal_reason, is_error false -- which the guard from the earlier parser fix reads as a forbidden second terminal result.

The guard was built when no harness developer used subagents; the first one that did lost its run at the finish line, after two repair attempts, with the third attempt's work complete in the worktree.

description:
Operator decision, 2026-08-18, after reviewing candidate openings: direction B, problem-first. The approved opening, verbatim, is the constraint:

'Writing code was never the hard part. Yoyo is that structure, built to run without you driving each turn: goals in, merged software out, a conversation to steer it.'

And the product is referred to as yoyo in the README's prose, matching the command people actually type. title: Give the backlog owner a live survey, and say when a tracker action touches a closed item
description:
The product manager ordered the backlog from a stale picture. Turn 19 of the 2026-08-18 conversation moved yoyodyne-ifd.23 down-tier citing yoyodyne-ifd.41 as in progress -- both had been closed for hours. Its per-item reads are live, but the open-items survey it reasons from is the one gathered when the conversation opened, external changes never reach a running conversation, and the role that owns backlog ordering is exactly the role that cannot afford a stale list. The harness also applied the priority change to the closed item without a word.

Two fixes. First, a survey tracker action, so the product manager can ask for the current open list mid-conversation the way it already reads single items -- ordering decisions then start from a fresh list as a matter of discipline stated in the persona. Second, act-time honesty: a tracker action whose target's status changed since the conversation's picture of it -- above all one targeting a closed item -- is applied only if still meaningful and its result says plainly what the target's current status is, so reasoning built on a stale premise is corrected at the moment it acts rather than never.
acceptance_criteria: The product manager can request a current backlog survey mid-conversation as a tracker action; the persona directs ordering decisions to start from one; a tracker action on a closed or changed item reports the item's current status in its applied summary; a priority change on a closed item is either refused or applied with the closure stated, never silent; a test replays the ifd.23 case and the reply visibly learns the item is closed.

title: Give product and design artifacts stable identity and metadata
description:
Product and design artifacts have no stable identity. docs/product/brief.md, the goals, the non-goals, docs/designs/, and docs/decisions/ are ordinary Markdown; nothing can reference one durably, so no relationship between them can be validated. Define the identity and metadata schema those artifacts carry: a stable id, an artifact kind, a lifecycle status, and the references the artifact makes upstream.

CONSTRAINT: follow the model yoyodyne-ifd.17 already shipped for invariants rather than inventing a second scheme - the filename is the id, a frontmatter id that disagrees is refused, status is explicit, and changes append to a revision log. Two identity schemes in one repository is the failure to design against. Do not reword any document's prose; this adds identity to what exists. The brief and goals are the product manager's and the operator writes them, so a change to their content is out of scope here even where the metadata sits in the same file.

DONE: an artifact in docs/product, docs/designs, or docs/decisions carries a stable id and metadata validated on load; a malformed or duplicate id is refused with a message naming the file; docs/configuration.md documents the schema.

DECOMPOSITION NOTE: created by the product manager under operator authorization 2026-08-17, because no development manager exists yet - the role arrives with yoyodyne-ifd.4, which yoyodyne-ifd.1 gates. Decomposition belongs to the development manager; this shape should be re-derived or ratified when the role runs.
notes:
Shape check the product manager's warning asked for, done 2026-08-17 by the operator's agent, which can read the design document: the nine children were compared against Milestone 2 verbatim. All seven enumerated capabilities map to a child (IDs 1.1, relationship validation 1.2, role ownership 1.4, change proposals 1.5, staleness 1.6, directive reconciliation 1.7, approvals 1.8), seeding maps to 1.9, and 1.3 is a justified addition from the backlog audit. Two nuances, not gaps: 1.8 covers the durable approval record because the configurable half of approvals already shipped; and Milestone 2 seeds 'brief, goals, and designs' while 1.9 names product and decision artifacts -- the designs home does not exist yet, so whoever builds 1.9 should either create docs/designs/ under the settled ownership or state why seeding defers it.

title: Fix the worktree test that fails its own cleanup
description:
TestManagerIntegrateRefusesNonFastForwardAndKeepsHarnessCommit fails intermittently in CI during teardown, not assertion: 'TempDir RemoveAll cleanup: unlinkat .../repository/.git: directory not empty'. Its checks pass; Go's t.TempDir cleanup then races something still holding or repopulating the repository directory, most likely a git worktree registration or a background git process that has not exited.

Observed on pull request 13 (run 31992104553) for yoyodyne-ifd.21, where it blocked the merge. The same commit passed the harness's own make test, make race and make vet, so this reproduces in CI and not locally.

P0 because build is a required status check on a protected main: a test that fails intermittently in teardown blocks every publication, and the harness cannot merge past it. It also teaches the wrong lesson -- a red required check that is usually spurious is one people stop reading.
design:
Make the test responsible for what it created rather than leaving it to TempDir. A worktree the test registered should be removed by the test before cleanup runs, and any git invocation it started should be waited for, so the directory is genuinely idle when Go tries to delete it.

Prefer fixing the leak to retrying the deletion. A cleanup that retries until the directory goes quiet hides whichever handle is still open, and that handle is the interesting thing: if a git process outlives the call that started it, the harness has the same problem outside tests.

Check the sibling tests in internal/gitworktree for the same shape before assuming this one is unique. The failure is timing-dependent, so the one that fails is not necessarily the only one that can.
acceptance_criteria: The test cleans up the worktrees and processes it creates so TempDir removal has nothing to race; it passes repeatedly under CI conditions, including with -count high enough to expose the race; no cleanup step retries deletion to paper over a held handle; sibling tests with the same pattern are corrected too.
notes:
Found 2026-08-16 when it blocked pull request 13 and stalled the queue. Rerunning the job cleared it, which is the symptom of a flake rather than a fix.

title: Queue the merge with --auto so required checks are waited for
description:
Publishing merges the moment the reviewer approves, but a protected branch will not accept a merge until its required checks have passed. CI takes about forty seconds and the harness asks within seconds of approving, so the merge is refused on essentially every run.

Observed on the first published run, run-ab96b7a966d3b718dc9287d9f5846725 for yoyodyne-ifd.20.1. The run succeeded, the reviewer approved, the work integrated locally and pull request 5 opened, and the merge was refused: 'the base branch's protection rules are not satisfied (BLOCKED) ... the base branch policy prohibits the merge.' GitHub's own message names the remedy: add --auto to have the pull request merged once the requirements are met.

Nothing is lost when this happens -- the outcome is reported as 'the change is integrated locally; the pull request still needs to be reconciled by hand' -- but it leaves an open pull request and an unpushed local branch after every run, which is precisely the manual reconciliation that publishing exists to remove.
design:
Ask GitHub to merge when the requirements are met rather than asking it to merge now. gh pr merge --auto queues the merge and lets the forge complete it once required checks pass, which is what a protected branch is asking for.

Auto-merge is a repository setting, so it can be unavailable. Detect that and say so plainly rather than failing obscurely: a repository with auto-merge disabled and required checks configured cannot be published to this way, and the operator should be told which setting to change.

Do not reach for --admin. Merging with administrator privileges bypasses the very checks the protection expresses, and a harness that routinely overrides branch protection has removed the gate rather than satisfied it.

The confirmation loop needs rethinking alongside this. It currently asks three times over seven seconds whether the merge landed, which suited an immediate merge and cannot suit a queued one. A queued merge completes minutes later, so the run should record the pull request as queued and finish, rather than waiting for something that will not happen while it watches. What reconciliation does about a queued merge that later fails is the open question worth answering here.
acceptance_criteria: A merge into a protected branch with required checks succeeds without manual reconciliation; the harness queues the merge rather than demanding it immediately; a repository that cannot auto-merge is reported with the setting that needs changing rather than a generic refusal; administrator override is never used to bypass protection; a run whose merge is queued finishes and reports the pull request as queued rather than blocking on a confirmation that cannot arrive; reconciliation defines what happens to a queued merge that later fails.
notes:
Found 2026-08-16 on the first run after enabling branch protection and approvals.publishing. P0 because it affects every published run and reintroduces the manual step publishing was meant to remove.

title: Do not discard a completed run over provider output after the terminal result
description:
internal/backend/claudecode/parser.go rejects any line arriving after the provider's terminal result envelope: ParseLine returns 'provider event received after terminal result' as a fatal error. The Claude Code CLI does emit trailing events after its result, so a run whose developer finished successfully is thrown away.

Observed on run-44a559a57d3710e6cd99125efd29ee2d for yoyodyne-ifd.12. The developer completed and emitted its final summary at sequence 586; the run then failed with that parse error, discarding 975 insertions of finished work that never reached checks or review. The error repeated three times in the output, so more than one trailing event arrived.

This is a reliability defect affecting every run, not a problem specific to that work item, which is why it is P0: any run can complete its work and then be discarded for output the provider legitimately emits. It also interacts with yoyodyne-ifd.12, since a rate-limit notice is one of the things plausibly arriving late.
design:
A terminal result means the run's outcome is decided; it does not mean the provider stops writing. Record events that arrive after it rather than failing on them, and keep the already-decided result. Guard the actual invariant, which is that a second terminal result must not silently replace the first, rather than treating all trailing output as corruption.

Preserve what the trailing events carry instead of discarding it. They are exactly where a late rate-limit notice would appear, and yoyodyne-ifd.12 needs that payload. Do not let a post-terminal event mutate the recorded result, session identifier, resolved model, usage, or cost, since those belong to the terminal envelope; append them to the event stream so they remain diagnosable.
acceptance_criteria: A provider event arriving after the terminal result no longer fails the run; the terminal result, session identifier, resolved model, usage, and cost are unchanged by anything arriving after it; trailing events appear in the recorded event stream; a second terminal result is still rejected rather than replacing the first; a test replays a stream with events after the result and asserts the run succeeds with the original outcome intact.
notes:
Found 2026-08-16 when ifd.12 was discarded after its developer had already finished. The work is preserved unreviewed at branch yoyodyne/yoyodyne-ifd-12/44a559a5, commit e4ba361, for reference only.
Yoyodyne run passed checks, was approved by an independent reviewer, and was integrated automatically.

Review summary: The change replaces the blanket post-terminal rejection with the narrower invariant the design asked for: trailing lines are parsed and emitted normally, while a second envelope of type "result" is rejected before it can reach parseResult, so the recorded result text, is_error, stop reason, usage, and cost of the first terminal envelope are structurally unreachable by later lines. Session ID, resolved model, and assistant FinalText are each individually guarded with !p.sawResult, covering the three fields that non-result envelopes could otherwise have mutated. The new test replays a realistic stream (result, then rate-limit event, assistant text, and a late init carrying a different session and model) and asserts both that the run succeeds with the original outcome intact and that all five events, including the trailing three, reach the sink with the sequence checkpoint advanced — it would fail on the pre-change parser. The rewritten negative case now pins the retained invariant. Checks pass and do exercise the new path.
Finding [minor] (internal/backend/claudecode/parser.go:118): A trailing system/init still emits EventRunStarted a second time (the new test's fifth line does exactly this). The model and session it carries are correctly ignored, but consumers that treat EventRunStarted as the beginning of a run now see two for one run. Worth considering whether post-terminal init should be emitted under a neutral event type or marked as post-result, so the event stream stays self-describing.

title: Landings serialize on a lease and share a build cache, so two full race suites never run at once beside the per-run gates
description: Label: reliability. Three reviewer reports on 401 (2026-09-19): landing checks run in the landing run's own process with no concurrency bound and a cold Go build cache per checkout, so with two seats two back-to-back landings run two whole race suites at once in two landing checkouts beside the next developer runs' gates - which is the load this fortnight's twenty-one flake reports came from - and a flaky red landing now files a priority-0 bug. Done means: landings queue on one lease per target branch so at most one landing suite runs at a time; the landing checkout uses the shared build cache (the repository's configured GOCACHE) rather than a cold one; a landing that would start while another runs waits with the wait named in yoyo status and the sweep record; a test drives two landings and asserts serialization; and docs/operations.md's landing-checks section says so. Whoever pastes landing_checks into this project's configuration watches the first few landings for a red one; a flake there is 389's list, not a new item.

The dashboard child's adoption is 4 of 4; here it is started only if 4 has landed, else reported as not yet a child.

title: Agent invocations run with an explicit environment: no Slack token ever reaches a run's subprocess tree
description: Developer on 68.3, 2026-08-19, never admitted: the Slack design's decision 2 states that no run process, and therefore no agent's subprocess tree, ever has a Slack token in its environment, and nothing enforces it - agent invocations leave Command.Env nil (internal/execution/process.go), so the backend subprocess inherits the harness's whole environment. An operator who exports SLACK_BOT_TOKEN or SLACK_APP_TOKEN in a shell profile hands both to every agent the harness starts. The setup and configuration documents warn against it; the claim is stated as structural. OPERATOR CONSTRAINT this serves: the sink is the only credential holder and tokens never reach an agent process. description: Label: reliability. What keeps it from closing is one defect in the recovery's own crash-safety: recoverPublication saves the request onto the record before arming and its comment says a process that dies between the two is picked up by the next sweep, but the selection predicate requires PullRequest to be nil, so a lease timeout, a process death, or the defensive verdict refusal between that save and the merge leaves a record that carries the request and still says it holds none, is never selected again, and is presented on the docket and the status line as a request nothing asked the forge to merge — the operator's, which is the hand merge the item forbids. That is the same self-contradicting-record class the last round was sent back for and it needs one bounded fix plus a test. Two minor observations accompany it.
Finding [major] (internal/orchestrator/publication.go:204): recoverPublication writes state.PullRequest and saves before armRecoveredMerge runs, and its comment claims that a process dying between the save and the merge leaves 'the same record with the same account' for the next sweep to arm. It does not: lostPublicationRecord is State.PublicationUnrecorded, which requires PullRequest == nil, so once the first Save lands the run is never selected again. Every path out of armRecoveredMerge that does not itself save — LeasePromotion failing (the promotion queue is bounded at fifteen minutes and times out during a long forge wait), a process death, the defensive ReviewDecision refusal — therefore leaves a durable record holding the request while its PublishFailure still says 'its record holds no pull request for branch … so nothing was asked of the forge', and that record is docketed and named on the attention line as the existing 'nothing ever asked the forge to merge — the operator's' case, which no sweep re-arms and `yoyo triage rearm` will not touch (no MergeDrop). That is a hand merge by another route and a record contradicting itself, the class the previous round was sent back for. Fix either by deferring the first Save until the arming outcome is decided (the Merged/MergeQueued cases and the drop and success paths already save, so a crash then leaves the untouched lost account and the next sweep retries as the comment says), or by selecting for recovery on the lost account regardless of PullRequest and skipping the forge lookup when the request is already on the record. Add a test that a recovery interrupted after the request is written — e.g. with the target's promotion lease held so LeasePromotion refuses — is armed by the next sweep and never leaves the lost-account sentence beside a recorded request.
Finding [minor] (docs/operations.md:0): docs/operations.md's 'Needs a human' bullet in the four-lines section still enumerates three movers for unpublished promotions ('the forge's … the development manager's … the operator's … All three leave the line…') while this change adds a fourth, the harness's, for a promotion whose record holds no request; the read-model comment was updated to four but the operator-facing enumeration was not. Add the fourth case there so the status section and the recovery paragraph agree.
Finding [minor] (internal/triage/triage.go:1770): The item's done-means asks that a docket entry for a run with an open publication name the request's state (open, mergeable, checks) and whether the merge is armed. Artifacts now carry number, URL and merged, and the non-publication render says 'open on the forge, unmerged' or 'merged', but not whether auto-merge is armed (MergeQueued) nor mergeability or checks; the docket by design asks the forge nothing when it builds, so the last two are out of reach, but MergeQueued is on the record and could be carried and rendered so an escalation or death entry says whether a merge is already queued for the request it names.

title: The cap counts only rounds that ended in a verdict requiring repair: 279's completion, with 349 and 309 as regression cases
description: Operator's assistant, 2026-09-18, under the reliability directive; paired with 309 (the development manager may cross a cap himself) by the operator's decision the same day. 279 landed on 2026-09-05 that an approving round, or one whose only residue is a single minor finding, spends no retry budget. The record says it is not holding, and the rule is restated here as 279's completion: THE CAP COUNTS ONLY ROUNDS THAT ENDED IN A VERDICT REQUIRING REPAIR. An approving round spends nothing; a granted round that never executed spends nothing; an empty-diff verdict against a run with no change present spends nothing. REGRESSION CASES, both of which cost an operator override: (1) 349, 2026-09-15: its repair round ended with an approve-as-implementation verdict, then stopped at a replay conflict, and the development manager's rerun was refused at 4 of 4 review rounds - the approving round was counted; (2) 309, 2026-09-18: a repair recorded this hour reserved the cap's last round, the harness then found the worktree retired and refused to continue, and the rerun that replaced it was refused at 6 of 6 - a round that never ran was counted. Also in scope, from the development manager's 09-14 reports: rounds spent reviewing an empty diff from a mis-selected or stale-worktree run count identically to real repair rounds. Done means: the counter is charged at verdict time and only by a verdict requiring repair against a change that was present; a reservation taken for a round that does not execute is released, not spent; a replay conflict after approval charges nothing and re-enters through the conflict path with the approval standing; tests replay the 349 and 309 shapes and both reach their rerun without an override; the four 279 escalation shapes still pass; and docs/configuration.md's cap section says what spends a round and what does not, citing 279 and this item.

title: Work items carry labels, and a developer slot can prefer a label: it pulls work with that label first and the rest only when none is ready
description: Operator direction, Mason, 2026-09-19, recorded as a directive, re-scoping this item; reworded the same day in the harness's own words (developer slot, label). His words: 'I want to be able to assign tags to work items, tell one or more seats to work on specific tags. They should only work on other beads when they have exhausted all items with their assigned tag.' THREE CHANGES from the item as admitted: (1) LABELS on work items are the unit, not an epic id - the tracker's labels, settable by the product manager and development manager (419 gives the product manager the action); the dashboard children would have carried one. (2) A developer slot that prefers a label PULLS THAT LABEL'S READY WORK FIRST and, only when none is ready, pulls from the rest of the backlog - it never idles on an empty label. (3) One or more slots may prefer the same label, and a slot may prefer more than one. KEPT: slots with no preference skip labelled work while a preferring slot is free to take it; yoyo status names the preferred label beside each slot; the schedule report names an item passed over as labelled-for-another-slot rather than deferred; docs/configuration.md documents the block, using developer slot and label, with the dashboard as the example; a replay test shows the pull order for two slots, one preferring a label, over a backlog with labelled and unlabelled ready items, including the fallback once the label's work is exhausted. Configuration selects what a slot pulls and never widens what it may do (configuration-never-grants-authority). The architect proposes any amendment the workflow-participation shape in the configurable-workflows design needs; the run builds to the shape as ratified. The project's own .yoyodyne/config.yaml is the operator's paste and the item states the block. No new term enters docs/terms.md.

title: A reviewer on a continued run sees the whole branch diff against its base, not the tail above earlier commits
description: Seven reports (reviewers on 121.5, 274, 297; 2026-09-04/05, all after 236's diagnosis landed): when a run continues on a branch that already carries earlier attempts' commits, the review evidence is the uncommitted worktree diff or the delta above those commits, so the change the item is about - a 3,000-line README reduction, a gate implementation, a converge fix - is never in front of the reviewer, who infers it from passing tests and approves. 121.5 named 'the diff is shown whole to review' as an acceptance criterion and it was not met by the handoff. Done means: for every review of a run whose branch carries commits since its recorded base, the evidence presented is the branch's full diff against that base, within the existing size bounds and clipped whole rather than tail-first; the review record names the base and tip it was judged against; the 121.5 handoff replayed presents the README reduction; and docs/work.md says what a reviewer is shown for a continued run.

title: A manager conversation with a stale picture re-reads before advising the operator, or says how old its picture is
description: Operator's assistant, 2026-09-18, under the reliability directive. EVIDENCE: the product manager advised the operator to edit CLAUDE.md to say developer runs never use the tracker. CLAUDE.md at HEAD already opened with a section saying exactly that; the six reports the advice cited were from 2026-08-17/18, before the section existed; the product manager's repository picture was taken 2026-08-17 and roughly 500 commits had landed since. Advice built on a month-old picture cost the operator a false action item and two wrong claims about who could edit the file. WANTED: a manager conversation (product manager, development manager, architect) knows how old its repository picture is, measured in landings on the target branch since it was taken, not wall clock. When that count exceeds a configured threshold and the reply advises the operator about the repository, the conversation either re-reads the documents the advice rests on before replying, or the advice states plainly how many landings old its picture is. Done means: the conversation record shows the picture's age at each reply; a reply that advises the operator over a stale picture without re-reading carries the age in its own text; the threshold is configuration that cannot disable the statement; and the CLAUDE.md case replayed produces either a correct reading or a reply that says its picture is 500 landings old.
notes:
Admitted to the backlog by the product manager in conversation chat-91253e0e070c17b0663651cc48602122, after turn 560.

Reason: The operator's routine interface advised him from a month-old picture and was wrong; the harness knows how old the picture is and the conversation did not.

Reason: Carries the architect's ruling into the item's scope so the run builds a refresh, not a disclaimer.

Architect's companion ruling, 2026-09-18 (chat-11558d325e9a214ebfd00bb4a0012750): a per-turn read does not make freshness moot - reads sample what a role thinks to read; staleness is what it does not know it does not know. So this item is MECHANICAL, not advisory: a picture older than N landings on the target branch is refreshed by the harness before the next turn is answered, with the shipped freshness line as the trigger. The 'or says how old its picture is' branch in the title stands only for the case where a refresh is impossible in the turn (store outage), and then the reply carries the age. Depends on the repository-read capability admitted the same day.

title: An unauthenticated or unreachable provider is a named wait: the operator is told, the brake does not trip
description:
Operator's assistant, 2026-09-18, under the reliability directive, admitted at p1. WHAT HAPPENED: the Claude Code login expired. From 2026-09-17 18:17 local every provider invocation failed ('the claude-code backend is not authenticated for account default'); earlier runs died with 'the provider kept ending its invocations without judging the work' and 'API Error: Can't reach the API'. Three runs blocked in a row with nothing landing, so the intake brake tripped at 2026-09-17T19:15Z and held; every recurring sweep pass since recorded 0 turns; the operator's maintenance job force-restarted the watch 158 times, uselessly. The operator learned by asking, re-authenticated, and the assistant lifted the brake by hand.

(a) A provider that is NOT AUTHENTICATED or UNREACHABLE is a NAMED capacity-class wait, distinct from 355's capacity window (which has a reset; this has none): yoyo status's needs-a-human line says 'the provider is not authenticated; the operator must log in' (or 'the provider cannot be reached'), the sweep passes record THAT reason instead of 0 turns, and the intake brake does NOT trip on it - no run can fix it and the brake's remedy (yoyo release) is the wrong one, so tripping converts one hand step into two. (b) THE OPERATOR IS TOLD ONCE, in Slack, the moment authentication fails - tagged by member id per the communication rule, since it is both important and his to act on - and once more when it is restored. Done means the 2026-09-17 shape replayed produces the Slack message within one poll, the status line names the login, the sweep records the reason, the brake stays untripped, and re-authentication resumes the line without a release.

Admitted to the backlog by the product manager in conversation chat-91253e0e070c17b0663651cc48602122, after turn 542.

Reason: Three days stalled on a condition only the operator can fix and nothing told him - the five-day capacity silence again, one layer over, with the brake making it worse by prescribing the wrong remedy.

Reason: Operator directive of 2026-09-18 carried into the item that answers it: the auth-and-network wait must cost the run nothing, not merely be named.

OPERATOR DIRECTIVE, Mason, 2026-09-18, verbatim: 'I don't want a run killed just because the network is flaky, the laptop is asleep, or I need to re-auth a session.' Folded into this item's scope; p1 stands. What it adds beyond the status line and the brake: today a run whose provider invocation fails on a network error or an expired login spends its relaunch budget ('the provider kept ending its invocations without judging the work, relaunches 2 of 2 permitted'; 'API Error: Can't reach the API server') and is recorded FAILED - the harness killing the run - which happened to at least two runs in the 09-15..09-18 outage. Under the rule: a provider failure classified as unreachable-or-unauthenticated (342's refusal-classification suite is the natural place to classify it) puts the run into a wait that spends NOTHING - no relaunch, no repair attempt, no stoppage on the docket - with its claim, branch, and worktree kept, and the run resumes when the provider answers again. The same for a recurring task's turn. Done additionally means: a run interrupted by an unreachable or unauthenticated provider finishes with its relaunch and repair counters untouched once the provider returns. Environment note: the operator's maintenance job now itself refuses to restart anything while the provider is unreachable or unauthenticated, so the harness must not depend on a restart to recover.

title: The architect rules whether the harness may cut a release the product manager has decided
description: Coherence finding from the 2026-09-15 sweep. The operator delegated the release cadence to the product manager (2026-09-13) so he would not be asked to approve releases, and the first release item under that cadence (361) landed its classified notes and then parked: a developer run pushes no tags (the 152 ruling: agents push no tags) and cut-release.sh refuses off main, so the tag, its push, and the publication are the operator's or the release workflow's. Every release item will park at the same point, which puts the delegated decision back in his hands one step later. THE RULING ASKED: whether the harness - a trusted Go process, not an agent - may perform the cut (re-derive notes on origin/main, make release, push the tag) for a release the product manager has decided under the delegated cadence, and under what gates (the adoption walkthrough and make check green, the notes re-derived at the tag base, the intake hold and spending pause read); or whether the tag push stays a human act by design, in which case the release item's done condition and the sweep's release job should say so and stop implying otherwise. Adjacent to 348 (the capability change for broad DM and PM authority): a release cut is the product manager acting rather than recording, and the same boundaries apply - visible, reported, never self-approving. Done means the ruling is recorded where the release machinery and the sweep's release job can cite it, and 361's successor release items are admitted against it.

title: A recurring task that skips says why, and resumes on its own
description: Operator-directed at p1, 2026-09-14, under the standing directive that anything blocking reliable execution is fixed ahead of feature work. The development manager's hourly recurring task silently did not fire for twenty hours inside a live watch session: no pass recorded between 2026-09-13T18:31Z and 2026-09-14T14:35Z, while the session ran the whole time - yoyo sweeps is the evidence. The operator's maintenance job alarmed correctly; the harness said nothing. Whether a capacity wait held it (the provider window closing on the role's model, with failover only enabled that day), or the scheduler dropped the cadence, is what the run and sweep records must show. Done means: a recurring task that misses its cadence records WHY in the sweep log (capacity wait with the reset, a held lease, a scheduler fault), the miss is reported per the communication rule as important breakage rather than silently absorbed, and the task RESUMES on its own once the cause clears rather than waiting for the session to restart; the twenty-hour gap replayed produces a recorded reason at the first missed fire and a resumed cadence when the cause lifts. Composes with 355 (a capacity wait holding every role is reported) if capacity was the cause.
notes:
Admitted to the backlog by the product manager in conversation chat-91253e0e070c17b0663651cc48602122, after turn 531.

Reason: Operator-directed: the recurring loops are the harness's standing hands, and a cadence that stops without a word is the five-day capacity silence at a smaller scale - the operator's own job caught it, which is the courier role again.

title: A reply carrying more than one sweep block records the last, not nothing
description: From the operator's assistant, 2026-09-14: the product manager's twice-daily sweep result could not be recorded twice today - 'the product-manager answered with a sweep block the harness cannot read: a reply carries at most one sweep block' - because a reply carried two JSON blocks (a 'more' and then a 'complete'). Done means the two-block shape replayed records the final block and a warning, and a single-block reply is unchanged.

title: A red configured check cannot integrate: how 347 landed locally with make test failing
description:
Operator's assistant, 2026-09-13, routed by the product manager to the development manager and the builders. WHAT HAPPENED: yoyodyne-ifd.347's Codex cache test (TestAnInvocationIsMadeUnderTheAccountItWasGiven) asserted a GOCACHE redirect while handing the backend a working directory in no repository, which the redirect correctly leaves alone - so make test was red on that branch. 347 integrated into local main anyway on 2026-09-07, and four later landings carried the same red test. On the forge, every pull request since (487 through 495, ten items) sat BLOCKED because the required 'build' check failed on all of them; local main integrated twelve landings meanwhile and origin/main did not move for six days, until the assistant found it. The test fix (build a real temporary worktree, as the Claude backend's twin test does) plus an adoption-job fix are PR 497, auto-merging with the twelve held landings.

THE QUESTION, his: how did 347 integrate locally with a test that fails under make test, a configured check? Either the check did not run on that branch, or its verdict was not what gated integration - and the same applies to the four later landings that carried the red test. Establish which from the run records (check results, exit codes, the check phase's recorded verdict for run-5f8eb416 and the four after it), then close the gap so that a configured check's failure cannot be followed by integration - the developer-verifies and integration-requires-revision-bound-evidence invariants are what this bears on.

THE SECOND HALF: nothing reported that the forge's required check was failing on every pull request for six days - ten queued merges blocked and local/origin diverging by twelve landings, invisible to every surface. 357 (a publication awaiting the forge settles) owns the per-publication case; this item establishes why a forge-wide required-check failure produced no message and adds that condition to what the reconcile sweep reports. Done means the integration path is shown to refuse a red configured check with a test proving it, the five landings are explained in a diagnosis, and a required-check failure across queued merges reaches the operator within a sweep rather than six days.
notes:
Admitted to the backlog by the product manager in conversation chat-91253e0e070c17b0663651cc48602122, after turn 515.

Reason: The check gate is the one thing that makes autonomous integration safe, and five landings passed it red while the forge stalled six days unnoticed; the operator's assistant asked for the item and it is the costliest unexplained event on record.

title: A half-written worktree registration is cleared, and every registration-walking Git command tolerates one
description: Coherence finding from the 2026-09-13 sweep, from reports on 332 and 275. 332 landed narrowly: it keeps 'git worktree list' working across another run's half-written registration. Two things it left: (1) a registration left half-written by a killed 'git worktree add' is not cleared by 'git worktree prune' and blocks EVERY new worktree creation in the repository with exit 128 - verified on git 2.50.1 - and nothing detects or clears it; remediation today is a hand 'rm -r .git/worktrees/<entry>' documented in docs/operations.md, which an operator learns of only when every new run fails at creation; (2) every other Git command that walks the registrations - rebase among them, seen failing a concurrent-runs test with 'failed to read .git/worktrees/<other>/commondir' - is unprotected, since the retry lives only around the listing. Done means the convergence sweep (or worktree creation itself) detects a registration with no index and no live creation lease and clears it with a recorded note; the tolerance moves below the listing so any registration-walking command survives a concurrent creation; and the killed-add shape replayed leaves the next run able to create its worktree. Coordinate with 292 (watch lease) and 334 (Git fence) so the three concurrency guards agree.

title: A publication awaiting the forge settles: the hold lifts, the count clears, status agrees
description: Coherence finding from the 2026-09-13 sweep, from reports on 68.14 and 301. Three surfaces disagree about a promotion the forge has not merged. (1) The Slack heartbeat counts promotions awaiting the forge; yoyo status's four lines do not - readmodel.readNeedsHuman derives from runstate.Store.Outstanding(), and a run settled after a dropped merge is not outstanding, so its unpublished promotion shows in no line at a terminal (internal/readmodel/standing.go:691, runstate.State.AwaitingForge()). (2) The heartbeat's count is driven by PullRequest.Merged being false on a terminal run, and nothing writes that flag back - not a reconcile sweep, not a person merging by hand on the forge - so once a merge is dropped the hourly 'N promotions awaiting the forge' line stops only if a rearm settles it. (3) 301's publication hold keeps such an item out of the pull, and holds are never released automatically; docs/work.md asserts a hold lifts 'by the publication being settled' with no lever behind the sentence. Done means one derivation answers 'what is awaiting the forge' for status and the heartbeat alike; a reconcile sweep re-asks the forge about a dropped merge and records a hand-merge as merged; settling clears the hold, the count, and the 'Publication outstanding' line on the item (run-82472041's stale line after PR #401 merged is the worked example); and the dropped-merge shape replayed leaves no surface disagreeing with another.

title: An attempt that dies before its run record still records what happened
description:
Operator-directed at p1, 2026-09-13, the second defect behind the five-day stoppage - and the reason the line was still stopped four hours after capacity returned. At 06:25Z the watch session pulled work and tried yoyodyne-ifd.353 and yoyodyne-ifd.354. NEITHER PRODUCED A RUN RECORD: the runs directory has written nothing since 09-08T05:48. Both were then marked 'already tried this session' and skipped, and the session went idle over 74 items. The operator could not find out why those two failed, because the failure is not recorded anywhere - which is the defect.

FIX SHAPE, his: (1) an attempt that dies BEFORE its run record is written still records what was attempted and why it failed - somewhere durable that a sweep can read; (2) 'already tried this session' CARRIES THE REASON rather than being a bare exclusion, so an item skipped for the rest of a session says what excluded it.

This is one layer earlier than yoyodyne-ifd.338 (a run that dies before claiming gets a docket entry): 338 covers a run that exists and cannot claim; this covers an attempt that never became a run at all. The combination that cost the recovery - silent failure plus session-scoped exclusion - is what turned a returned capacity window into a still-idle queue over 74 items.

Done means the 06:25Z shape replayed leaves a durable record of both attempts and their failures, the session's exclusion list names its reasons, and a sweep can see that two items were tried and failed rather than seeing nothing at all.
notes:
Admitted to the backlog by the product manager in conversation chat-91253e0e070c17b0663651cc48602122, after turn 509.

Reason: Operator-directed: an attempt that fails into no record at all defeats every surface built this fortnight to end silence, and pairing it with a session-long exclusion means one invisible failure idles the queue until a person notices.
