title: A capacity wait that holds every role is reported, and a single-model project is warned
description:
Operator-directed at p1, 2026-09-13, the first of two defects behind the five-day stoppage. WHAT HAPPENED: nothing landed between 2026-09-08T04:55Z and 2026-09-13. All five roles ran on opus; opus's seven-day capacity ran out on 09-08 with a reset of 2026-09-13T03:00Z. Across those five days the harness recorded 131 capacity waits and fired the development manager's sweep 18-23 times a day, each refused for want of capacity. It waited out the whole window. The operator learned of it from his assistant, five days later.

TWO PARTS. (1) NOTHING REPORTS A CAPACITY WAIT THAT IS HOLDING EVERY ROLE. The harness knew this durably, 131 times. A capacity wait that blocks every role is reported with the reset time and repeated while it stands - the same escalating shape 354 gives a stopped line, and distinct from it: 354 is the stall alarm going quiet, this is the capacity half, and a line stopped on a known reset is a different message from a line stopped for unknown reasons. (2) NOTHING WARNS THAT A PROJECT HAS EVERY AGENT ON ONE MODEL WITH NO ALTERNATE CONFIGURED. That is a condition yoyo doctor can state in one line, and it is the condition that made this five days instead of one turn.

CONTEXT THE FIX SHOULD CARRY: model failover (331) shipped, merged and working, deliberately off by default so the operator could choose it per agent - and this project never turned it on, so no alternate was attempted for five days. Account failover (306) is still with the architect and the second account was never configured, so that path was absent too. The operator has now enabled failover on all five agents with sonnet as the alternate. Done means a capacity wait holding every role produces a message naming the reset, repeated as it stands; doctor names a single-model-no-alternate configuration; and the 09-08 shape replayed reaches the operator within minutes rather than five days.
notes:
Admitted to the backlog by the product manager in conversation chat-91253e0e070c17b0663651cc48602122, after turn 509.

Reason: Operator-directed: five days of stopped line while the harness held the answer durably 131 times is the most expensive silence this system has produced, and the doctor warning is one line that would have made the whole window impossible.

Goal served: The harness's surfaces read clearly: boundaries between topics and speakers are visible, important findings stand out, every distinction survives a terminal that cannot render emphasis, and user-facing language chooses the ordinary, literal word over metaphor, coinage, or term of art.

title: A stopped line gets louder as it stands, and tags the operator
description:
Operator-directed at p1, 2026-09-07, the second defect behind last night's stop: the stall alarm speaks ONCE and then goes quiet. It fired at 02:48Z and by design says nothing more while the stall stands - the code comment states that intent explicitly. So a line fully stopped for over four hours produced one message, four hours ago, and nothing since.

HIS DIRECTION, inverting that design: a line that is COMPLETELY STOPPED is the most serious thing the system can report, and it should get LOUDER RATHER THAN QUIETER. (1) REPEAT while the stall stands, on a cadence rather than once; (2) RAISE THE SEVERITY AS IT AGES - a four-hour stop is not the same message as a twenty-minute one; (3) TAG HIM BY HIS SLACK MEMBER ID, resolved from the operators config, so it arrives as a real notification - he has asked for that behaviour before for urgent items and it belongs here above all.

Composes with 324 (the alarm reads the shared cause derivation rather than deriving its own) and 345 (awaiting-a-decision and awaiting-execution named separately): the repetition carries the cause and the next mover, so a louder message is also a more useful one rather than only a more frequent one - and under the communication rule, this is the case where repetition is warranted precisely because it is important and unresolved.

Done means a standing stall produces escalating messages until it clears, each naming the current cause and next mover, the operator is tagged, and last night's four silent hours replayed produce a rising sequence instead of one message.

title: The report pile is worked on a schedule, with a bound that converges
description:
Operator-directed at p1, 2026-09-07: the report pile is not being worked and the arithmetic says it never can be. 564 of 1313 filed reports are unhandled; the oldest is from 2026-08-17; they arrive at 20 to 45 a day; at most 10 reach any one conversation, once, and only when somebody talks to the product manager. The pile grows faster than it can drain, so a real defect can sit three weeks with nobody deciding anything about it - which is what happened tonight: a reviewer found a genuine bug (report-5cb3e8c7, the provider-blind account pool), it was filed correctly, posted to Slack, and reached no one who could act on it. The routing is built and correct; throughput is the defect.

TWO SHAPES, both admitted here as one item because they only work together: (1) A RECURRING TASK that works the pile on a schedule, on the same configured-task machinery the development manager's hourly sweep runs on (283), so reports get DECIDED rather than only displayed - each pass handles what it can and records what it decided, per the same batching and already-admitted checks the other loops carry. (2) A DELIVERY BOUND THAT CONVERGES: a persistent position in the pile so a turn resumes where the last one left off rather than re-reading the same worst-first ten, and a larger budget for a turn whose whole job is the pile; either alone may be enough, both may be needed, and the item should measure rather than assume.

Done means the unhandled count falls week over week rather than rising, the oldest unhandled report's age falls, a pass records what it decided, and the pile's size and oldest-age are visible on a surface the operator sees so the convergence is checkable rather than asserted.
notes:

title: The product manager acts on backlog state within her domain
description:
The product-manager half of the operator's 2026-09-07 broad-authority direction, admitted alongside the architect's capability ruling and to be built under whatever capabilities that ruling grants. Today the product manager can admit, order, park, close, retire, attribute and annotate - but a blocked item whose blocking run is terminal, a dependency on work that closed, an attribution orphaned by a goals amendment: each of these is backlog state gone stale, none of them is a decision anyone owes, and every one of them currently waits for the operator's assistant. Scope: the product manager clears stale statuses, retires dead dependencies, and re-attributes orphaned goals within her own domain, on her own authority, without a person invoking a verb.

title: A recorded triage decision carries itself out
description:
Operator-directed at p1, 2026-09-07, admitted as the successor to yoyodyne-ifd.311 - which closed having made a rerun CARRY the development manager's decision, a different thing from FIRING it.

THE CONDITION: 33 items sit decided-and-unfired, some for days, because the only executor is the operator's assistant typing yoyo triage repair. The development manager decides within the hour and then nothing happens. His sweeps have reported this as a standing finding since they began. This is the autonomy goal failing precisely where the machinery is otherwise complete.

THE REQUIREMENT, his words in intent: when the development manager records a repair or rerun, the harness executes it as it executes any other scheduled work - not waiting for a person to run a verb. Execution runs UNDER THE SAME GATES as any other work: the intake hold, the spending pause, the triage budgets, and the preserved-work rules. The run's attribution cites the decision record 311 landed.

THE ALTERNATIVE, named explicitly per his direction if full auto-execution is judged unsafe: execution requires the recorded decision PLUS a clean gate check, and anything refused SURFACES AS A FINDING rather than as silence - a decision that cannot be carried out says so where the sweep reads it, naming which gate refused it and what would clear it. Silence is the one outcome this item forbids in either design.

Done means a decision recorded in the DM's conversation results in the work being dispatched on the next scheduling pass with no person involved; every refusal to execute is visible as a finding with its gate named; the standing 33-item backlog clears without hands; and the interaction with 299 (pre-flight before the budget increment, so a refused carry-out spends nothing) and 309 (the DM's bounded cap crossings) is exercised rather than assumed. The design also respects harness-is-the-only-role-invoker and configuration-never-grants-authority by putting the carry-out in the harness's own pass rather than widening any role's tool posture, and selected-work-passes-intake-and-records-why holds because the actions read the hold before claiming and the fresh run's reason is read from the durable decision. The documentation is reconciled: docs/work.md, docs/conversation.md, the CLI help, the escalation message and the development manager's role text all now describe the carry-out, and I found no surviving claim the change makes false. What blocks approval is one unaddressed interaction: a refusal by a Waiting gate is deliberately unpaced, so the real Outstanding() re-offers that decision on every single pull, and nothing in the change or its tests establishes what the pass then does with it. Fix or demonstrate that, and this is done.
Finding [major] (internal/orchestrator/schedule.go:1172): A carry-out refused by a Waiting gate (spending pause, intake hold, developer capacity) is unpaced by design — TriageCarryOut.Cooling returns false when Waiting — so the real Outstanding() offers the same decision again on the very next pull, for as long as the gate stands. The pass appends a Started entry and increments running for every attempt, and the only thing that can stop the same decision being offered again is occupied[task.WorkItemID], which for a refused attempt has no durable run behind it and comes solely from `mine`. Both possible behaviours are defects: if `mine` retains the item after settleCarryOut's early return, a decision refused under a held intake is never retried by that watching session even after `yoyo release`, which contradicts docs/work.md ("the pass that finds it open carries out the same one"), docs/conversation.md, internal/chat/role.go and the item's core promise; if `mine` does not retain it, the session accumulates a Started entry and writes a superseding TriageCarryOut record on every poll interval for the whole duration of a pause or a full harness, growing schedule.Started without bound. Neither case is tested, and the scheduler double hides it: outstandingUntilCarried in internal/orchestrator/carryout_test.go filters out any task already attempted and its comment asserts "a decision the harness has attempted is not outstanding on the next pull — either it fired and is spent, or a gate stopped it and its pacing has it", which is precisely false for a Waiting gate, so TestAHeldIntakeStillAttemptsTheCarryOutSoTheRefusalIsRecorded and TestAFullHarnessStillAttemptsTheCarryOutSoTheRefusalIsRecorded never exercise the recurrence that actually happens. Add a scheduler-level test that keeps a Waiting-gate refusal outstanding across successive pulls, asserting both that the decision is fired once the gate clears within the same session and that a sustained gate does not accumulate a Started entry or a durable refusal write per pull, and adjust the pass (or the fake) to whatever that reveals.

title: A run that dies before claiming is recorded, and readiness agrees with the claim gate
description:
Operator-directed at p1, 2026-09-07, from one incident with two halves: the scheduler pulled yoyodyne-ifd.285 while it was BLOCKED and the run died at the claim ('issue not claimable: status blocked'), recording nothing - the failure message itself said 'nothing was recorded for anybody to decide'.

(1) THE RACE OR THE DISAGREEMENT: readiness said startable, the claim found it blocked. Either the item changed state between selection and claim - a race the reservation should close by re-reading state under the claim, so the decision to start is made against the state that is then claimed - or the readiness computation and the claim gate disagree about what 'blocked' means, which is the one-read-model invariant one layer below where 277 fixed it (277 made readiness dependency-derived; this is the claim gate agreeing with it). Establish which it is from the run record before fixing, then fix that one.

(2) THE INVISIBLE FAILURE CLASS, which the operator asked about directly: a run that fails BEFORE claiming leaves no docket entry, so it exists in no surface the development manager's sweep reads - every other stoppage class dockets and this one evaporates. That is why nobody could have caught it earlier. Scope: a pre-claim run failure is recorded where the sweep can see it (a docket entry keyed to the run and the item it tried to claim, per 268's create-on-death direction extended below the claim boundary), so the harness's next-mover line means the harness AND someone eventually looks. Done means the 285 shape replayed produces a durable record the sweep surfaces, and the selection-to-claim path either cannot disagree or fails with the disagreement named in that record.

title: A confirmed note write is durable, or the confirmation is false
description:
Operator-directed at p1, 2026-09-07, confirmed independently by him: a tracker note action reported as applied must be readable back on the item. Today at least one write path reports success and persists nothing - two consecutive 'updated yoyodyne-ifd.283: note' confirmations landed no text, verified by reading the item back twice; its notes hold only the admission and goal lines. That makes every note confirmation untrustworthy and silently loses recorded reasoning, which is the class the operator has been burned by twice this week from the other direction (the timed-out write that was actually durable, yoyodyne-ifd.327). Scope: identify the failing path - note versus description versus other fields, and whether item state (blocked, in flight) or note size is implicated; add a READ-BACK ASSERTION AFTER WRITE so a false confirmation becomes an error the caller sees; and audit whether other confirmed-but-lost writes exist in recent history. The 283 shape replayed is the regression case.

CARRIED HERE BECAUSE NOTES ARE UNRELIABLE - the operator's forge-hygiene direction of 2026-09-07, which twice failed to persist as a note on yoyodyne-ifd.283 and belongs in that item's description when someone can edit it: FORGE HYGIENE JOINS THE DM SWEEP'S FINDINGS. The sweep reads the tracker but not the forge today, which is why 30 open pull requests accumulated unnoticed, most superseded by later runs that landed their items. The development manager's hourly sweep reports open pull requests whose items are closed, or whose branches are already contained in the target branch, as findings; the closing machinery is yoyodyne-ifd.69 (p1, with the backlog of 30 as its first-pass acceptance). The operator's division: the sweep does the noticing, 69 does the closing. Batching and already-admitted checks apply - a superseded request is reported once, not once per sweep. Whoever lands this item should put that paragraph into 283's description as part of the work.

description: Carved from yoyodyne-ifd.330 by DM triage of run-f9e67240e251879aa25c93d391463948, citing the architect's merged design (commit 52be6d6, PR #465) for the stream shape. title: Model failover, configurable per agent: a role's turn is served by a permitted alternate
description: Operator-directed at p1, 2026-09-07, sibling of 306 (conversation account failover) - 306 covers accounts, this covers models, and either alone leaves the other hole open. Today at 06:00 fable's capacity window closed while opus had capacity; the product manager, development manager and architect all run on fable, developers and reviewers on opus, so the deciders stopped while the doers were free and the whole queue - held-for-triage items needing DM decisions - stalled behind them until the operator's assistant hand-switched the three management roles to opus (PR 468). The durable fix: when a role's configured model is capacity-exhausted and a permitted alternate has capacity, the turn is served by the alternate; the serving model is recorded per-turn, affinity returns to the named model when its window reopens, and the substitution is reported rather than silent. THE OPERATOR'S REQUIREMENT, shaping it: it must be CONFIGURABLE - enabled per agent, DEFAULT OFF, with the alternate model named in the same per-agent block as the persona binding, the memory setting (308), and the side-thread knob (330); he is willing to try it but may not want it long-term or for every persona. Configuration selects behavior, never authority. Done means an agent with failover enabled and a permitted alternate keeps taking turns through its named model's window, the record says which model served each turn, the substitution reaches the operator per the communication rule, an agent with failover off behaves exactly as today, and this morning's shape replayed leaves the triage queue moving.

title: The architect designs conversation account failover: management keeps thinking through a window
description: Operator design question routed as directed, 2026-09-06: why must a role's conversation pin to one account? The pin's stated basis is provider-session resume, but durable-state-is-provider-independent makes any account able to host any turn by rebuilding from the durable record. Proposed shape, his: a conversation is held on its named account normally, failing over to another active pooled account when the named one's usage window is exhausted, context rebuilt from durable state, and the serving account recorded per-turn - converting a window from 'the deciders stop too' to 'management keeps thinking'. The architect rules: the failover trigger and return, what per-turn account attribution looks like in the record, any invariant interaction (the rebuild is the provider-independence invariant exercised, not weakened), and the cost story. Prerequisite noted: the operator's second account is still unconfigured - this direction is his motivation case for setting it up, so the design should say what configuration it needs. Done means the design is recorded where implementation items can cite it.

title: The tracker's temp files cannot dirty the primary checkout
description: Six reports across two items in one afternoon: bd's atomic-write temp files (.beads/.~issues.jsonl.<digits>) are matched by no .gitignore - the root one lacks the pattern and .beads/.gitignore lists only .beads/proxieddb/ and is bd-generated, so the next bd setup overwrites any edit to it. When the pre-integration cleanliness check on the primary checkout lands inside an export window, it reads the temp files as untracked state the harness does not own and refuses to integrate. Cost so far: run-9b179623 (yoyodyne-ifd.290) and run-90355b9e (yoyodyne-ifd.68.27, discarding approved PR #406) each lost a completed, reviewed round; it is a timing race and recurs unpredictably for any run. Done means either a .~* (or .beads/.~*) entry in the ROOT .gitignore - confirmed against every temp name the exporter actually uses - or the readiness check sweeps or allowlists the exporter's temp pattern before reading the primary checkout; either way, an integration landing mid-export succeeds, with the race as the regression case. The stray files currently sitting in the primary checkout are cleared by the operator's hand and flagged on his checklist this turn.

title: The watchdog and the status head read the usage-pause state
description: Operator-directed at p1, 2026-09-05, from today's 90-minute silence: the watch session waited out a provider usage window from 12:13Z to 13:43Z saying nothing; the stall warning fired with 'nothing accounting for it' when the pause WAS the accounting; on the window rolling, the session recorded 'resumed' and filled all three slots. title: The self-redeploy takeover cannot wedge: deadline, fallback exit, answerable SIGTERM
description: Operator-directed at p1, 2026-09-05, from today's stall: the watch session's restart-into-a-new-build path (230's takeover) logged 'a build was deployed over the one this session was started from, and the session is restarting into it' and then went silent for an hour - alive but choosing nothing - until force-killed; SIGTERM was ignored and SIGKILL required, and a second watch appeared during recovery, so the wedged redeploy apparently spawned its child late and two sessions briefly coexisted. title: The development manager's hourly sweep: find, fix, file, and report
description: Operator-directed, 2026-09-05, ships FIRST of the two recurring-task consumers and runs until its issues are worked out; builds on the architect's recurring-task trigger design admitted alongside. Every hour the harness wakes the development manager to look for unresolved issues - undecided stoppages, dead claims, stuck deliveries, anything held for a person that his recorded authority covers. He fixes what his authority allows, batching broad classes rather than going item-by-item; involves the architect where a ruling is needed; EVERY fix files root-cause work with the product manager; each sweep ends in a durable report the operator reviews at leisure. Binding operator-agreed constraints: findings are checked against work already admitted before filing (the duplicate-admission class 281 guards), and a heavy sweep iterates turns rather than overflowing the action cap. When the system is healthy most sweeps are quick and find nothing; a sweep that keeps finding things is itself a health signal the report states. The operator's assistant runs an interim hourly sweep through the machine-local maintenance job until this ships - explicitly temporary; this item is its durable end. Done means the sweep runs hourly from configuration, its authority boundary is the DM's existing one, its reports are durable, and a week of sweeps shows fixes filed with root-cause work rather than silent repairs.

description: Operator-directed capability, 2026-09-05, the design half, with the architect on the trigger design per his direction. Recurring tasks become configuration in the yaml: a prompt, a cadence, an enablement flag - configuration selects what runs and when, and authority stays the roles' existing recorded authority, never widened by config (this epic's law applied to time-triggered work). description: Operator-directed at p1, 2026-09-04, sibling to 272's dead-claim audit: 41 items held status blocked while every dependency they had was closed - the gates cleared as the week's work landed, nothing flips a blocked status back, and the scheduler trusts the field - so two-thirds of the backlog including two p0 items was invisible and the line sat idle for hours. title: Every run death that preserves work leaves an executable docket entry
description: Operator-directed seam, 2026-09-03, proven three times in two days (242, 209.6, 267): a run that dies before docketing - bootstrap failures, backend kills, publish deaths in early phases - leaves the development manager's recorded rerun decision unexecutable, because yoyo triage rerun requires a docket entry those deaths never create. Each time the exit was the operator's assistant dispatching the item by name, which works but bypasses the recorded-decision path and leaves the DM's recording as a phantom on the ledger - the recorded-versus-executable seam's third face after the note-form override and the phantom repair grant. Done means either every run death that preserves work creates its docket entry at death, or the rerun verb accepts a stopped run by id without one - whichever the implementation finds sound - so the DM's decision is executable however early the death came, with the three named incidents as the regression cases.
notes:
Admitted to the backlog by the product manager in conversation chat-91253e0e070c17b0663651cc48602122, after turn 395.

Reason: Operator-directed with three incidents as evidence: a decision path that needs a person to bypass it three times in two days is exactly the hand-in-the-loop the goal removes.

title: The architect rules the recoverable-versus-terminal boundary for every failure class
description: The design half of the operator's standing rule (2026-09-03): the harness never fails outright on anything that can recover, with Fibonacci backoff capped at 30 minutes. The ruling this item carries: a taxonomy of failure classes per boundary - publish, integrate's remote checks, PR opening, provider invocation, and whatever else fails today on a first refusal - saying which are recoverable (retried), which are judgments on the work (never retried, handed back), and which are ambiguous and how they are disambiguated; how a retry interacts with the promotion lease (a retried publish must not violate one-promotion-per-target-branch), the intake brake, and the run's budgets, so a retry can never double-spend or double-promote; and what exhausting the cap produces - escalation with the failure named, never a silent terminal failure. Done means the ruling is recorded in the governed design documents where the implementing items can cite it, and any follow-on it orders is admitted as its own work.
notes:
Admitted to the backlog by the product manager in conversation chat-91253e0e070c17b0663651cc48602122, after turn 393.

Reason: The rule is safe only with the boundary drawn precisely - retrying a judgment on the work is as wrong as terminating on a connection reset - and that boundary, plus its interaction with leases and budgets, is the architect's to rule.

Reason: The architect's recoverable-versus-terminal ruling now has the two real costs it must price: unbounded provider re-billing, and lease-held waits that starve the queue the moment capacity exceeds one.

Two spend-and-availability findings for this ruling, both from 264's reviewer and developer (run-e83e13a5): (1) past the relaunch budget, a provider death classified as recoverable reissues the whole developer or reviewer invocation for as long as the two-hour window allows - roughly eighteen further full billable provider calls where the previous ceiling was execution.transient_relaunches_before_blocking (default 2); a provider dropping connections mid-response after generating a complete reply bills for each; neither docs/configuration.md nor docs/operations.md mentions it, and nothing bounds it but the weekly budget. The ruling should decide whether the provider boundary gets a narrower window than the forge boundaries, and the guide says so either way. (2) Five boundaries (remote-target re-read, merge, merge confirmation, remote-branch delete, catch-up) hold the target's promotion lease with a two-hour window each, while the promotion queue bounds waiting at fifteen minutes (promotion.go:41) - so above max_concurrent_developers: 1, a forge outage longer than fifteen minutes stops every run reaching integration for that branch, where before 264 the holder failed fast and the queue drained. Per-boundary windows under the lease are the design decision this ruling owns.
Noted by the product manager in conversation chat-91253e0e070c17b0663651cc48602122, after turn 628.

Reason: The boundary ruling is where the cost of waiting is decided; the developer named a cost nobody had weighed.

2026-09-19, from the developer on 264 (2026-09-04): the recovery waits 264 added at the merge and after it are taken while the run holds the target branch's promotion lease, so a forge outage now stalls other runs' promotions into that branch for up to two hours instead of failing them. Harmless at one seat; this project runs two and a third is planned. The recoverable-versus-terminal ruling should bound how long a recoverable wait may hold a shared lease, or say the lease is released and re-taken across the wait.

title: Recoverable failures retry with backoff at every publish and integration boundary
description: Operator standing rule, 2026-09-03: the harness never fails outright on anything that can recover. Any non-terminal failure - a network drop, a connection reset, an API refusal that is not a judgment on the work - gets a retry with Fibonacci backoff capped at 30 minutes between attempts, never treated as terminal while the failure class is recoverable. The concrete case: four GitHub network failures today each killed a run at its final publish or integrate step - completed, sometimes reviewed work recorded as failed over a single connection reset the next attempt would have survived - and the intake brake then held the whole line three times. This item implements the rule at the boundaries that failed: the publish step (which retries nothing today), integrate's remote checks, PR opening, and provider invocation beyond the current relaunch budget, for the clearly-recoverable classes (connection reset, network drop, transport-level refusal). The retry-with-backoff pattern 232 gave tracker reads is the template. Done means a single connection reset at any of those boundaries no longer records completed work as failed, retries are visible in the run record with their intervals, and exhausting the backoff escalates rather than silently failing. The full recoverable-versus-terminal taxonomy is the architect's companion ruling; this item does not wait on it for the classes named here. Note: the operator's machine reroutes GitHub SSH to port 443, which mitigates the local trigger but not the class.
notes:

title: A run survives its own verbosity: output is truncated with a marker, not fatal
description: Operator-directed reliability defect, 2026-09-03: the developer backend kills a run whose process output exceeds 8 MiB - 209.6's soak-machinery run (run-32e3f059) died on it with zero dollars recorded and six hours of claimed-but-dead silence after, and a parity harness that diffs execution traces is exactly the workload that bursts stdout. The DM's rerun guidance (keep traces in files) is the workaround; this is the durable end.

title: A registered run.complete action: workflow definitions can express finishing the work
description: From the developer on run-010dd3ae (yoyodyne-ifd.209.5): the delivery action registry has no door onto (*activeRun).finish - recording the outcome on the work item, closing it, and pricing it - so a workflow definition cannot express the completing step at all, and a definition-driven run would promote a change and never close its item. The coverage test in internal/orchestrator/actions_test.go does not catch this because candidate.integrate claims the completing phase. Done means a registered run.complete action exists and the delivery definition uses it, a definition-driven run closes and prices its item exactly as the hard-coded loop does, and the coverage test is held against the steps a run performs rather than only the phases it occupies, so the next missing step fails the test instead of the soak. This blocks the opt-in parity soak (yoyodyne-ifd.209.6) from running the loop end to end.

title: A refused tracker block is recorded, carried, and shown back to the role that sent it
description:
Operator direction (Mason, 2026-09-01): we shouldn't silently drop anything. The refused-whole semantics of tracker blocks is right and STAYS - what changes is the silence around it. Two gaps, one item:

(1) A refused tracker block becomes a durable recorded event - role, action count, refusal reason - so status and the Slack tier can carry it; today it reaches only the invoking terminal, and an automatic wakeup turn's refusal would reach nobody at all.

(2) The refusing role is shown its own refusal at the start of its next turn, verbatim, so it re-issues the lost actions itself instead of believing they landed - today it learns only if a human tells it.

Proof case, named: on 2026-09-01 the product manager's 12-action block was refused whole (limit 10) and the miss was caught only by the operator's assistant checking the tracker afterward - three admissions and seven report dispositions silently gone until re-issued by hand.

Done means a refused block produces a durable event visible in status history, the role's next turn opens with the verbatim refusal, an automatic wakeup's refusal reaches the same surfaces a human-invoked one does, and the proof case replayed self-corrects on the next turn with no human courier.
notes:
Admitted to the backlog by the product manager in conversation chat-91253e0e070c17b0663651cc48602122, after turn 359.

Reason: The silence-must-find-you principle applied to the roles' own action path: a governed action channel whose failures evaporate teaches roles to believe in work that never landed - and the proof case was this role's own hand. Freeze-aligned reliability; the wakeup-turn case makes it live before automation deepens.

title: A stall watchdog notices that nothing is happening and says so unprompted
description:
Operator-identified observability gap (Mason, 2026-09-01): nothing detects scheduler silence itself. Today's 7.5-hour dead window (06:05-13:35, the watch dead on the since-fixed transient-read crash) was discoverable only by a human noticing - every existing surface answers when asked, and the DM tier fires on recorded stopped-states, but a dead or wedged scheduler records no state at all, which is why this class keeps costing the most calendar time.

Shape, the operator's: when the tracker reports startable developer work and no run has started for a threshold window, that becomes a durable recorded event - surviving into status history - and the Slack direct-message tier carries it to the operator once per stall, never per check. The checker is the maintenance job or the harness's own loop, builder's choice; the recorded-event-then-DM path is the same one the drift notices (241) and stopped-state DMs already use.

Complements, not duplicates: 51's throughput view and 187's named refusals explain what happened when asked; this notices that nothing is happening and says so unprompted. The operator's framing rides the item: the first two bottleneck classes were bugs since fixed - this is the instrument that catches the next class before it costs half a day.

Done means today's window replayed produces a durable stall event within the threshold and exactly one DM, a clearing stall closes its event, per-check re-firing is impossible by the dedup record, and the event shows in status history afterward.
notes:

Reason: The silence-must-find-you principle applied to its last uncovered case - the process whose death silences everything else. Freeze-aligned reliability at the frontier; delivery is a checker plus one event kind through existing machinery.

title: The idle line says what was passed over and names the conversation that moves next
description:
Operator-admitted status defect, 2026-09-01, three times misleading: when the watch is idle on one slot because the only tracker-ready items are conversation-executor items, the standing line says 'nothing among the N ready item(s) is startable that this session has not already tried. Next: the product manager's - nothing is chosen until work that is ready is admitted.' Both halves mislead: (1) it renders while a developer run is in flight on the other slot, so 'nothing is chosen' reads as a stall while the chain is moving; (2) 'Next: the product manager's' points at admission when the real next mover is the conversation the ready items name - today the architect's, for 212, 203, and 162.

The fix, per the certainty contract (139): the line says what the session actually found - how many ready items were passed over and their why-class (conversation-executed, parked) - and names the conversation that is the true next mover; a refusal names its reason, and the named next actor must be the one who can actually act. The in-flight slot renders on the Running line so idle-on-one-slot never reads as system-idle.

Done means today's state replayed renders 'one run in flight; N ready items passed over: conversation-executed (architect: 212, 203, 162)' in substance, the admission-pointer appears only when admission is genuinely the next act, and the three-times-misleading line is unreproducible.
notes:
Admitted to the backlog by the product manager in conversation chat-91253e0e070c17b0663651cc48602122, after turn 342.

Reason: The surface teaching a false fact at the deciding moment, three interventions' worth - and both falsehoods are exactly what the certainty contract's exhaustive-enumeration and whose-move clauses forbid. Freeze-aligned status reliability at the frontier.

title: The watch session retries transient tracker reads and exits only on persistent failure
description: Operator-admitted robustness defect, 2026-09-01 ~05:40Z: the scheduler logged 'nothing was started: the harness could not be read for another pull', then 'scheduling stopped: list in_progress work items: bd list failed with status cancelled and exit code -1', and exited - on a read that succeeds in 0.4s minutes later. Likely cause: store contention with a concurrent reconcile or a settling run's write. The interim maintenance job restarted it within its cadence (three consecutive 'scheduler was not running; started it' entries), so the cost was idle gaps - but a session that dies on one transient read defeats both the just-landed self-redeploy (230's mechanism restarts a session that must otherwise stay alive) and the durable-service direction (139/142). Shape, the operator's: the watch retries tracker reads with backoff and exits only on persistent failure, saying how long it tried. Done means the observed sequence replayed rides through the transient with the retry logged, a genuinely persistent store failure still exits with the duration stated, and the interim job's restart entries stop appearing for this cause.
notes:

Reason: A resident that exits on contention it will meet routinely - reconcile and settling runs write the same store - is unattended operation with a coin-flip lifespan, and every other resilience investment (self-redeploy, the service direction) presumes the session survives. Freeze-aligned reliability at the frontier.

Follow-on to the closed yoyodyne-ifd.193, whose subject is now cleanly proven broken after its close (the note carrying the proof landed on the closed item, where no builder reads it). The evidence, from the DM's critical of 2026-09-01 (report-c9ea12e8): on 224 the escalation was recorded, the operator's one-round scoped override was recorded against the item EXACTLY as the refusal text directs, and the resubmitted decision was refused with the identical message - the guard does not read note-form overrides, and no structural override verb is known to exist. Second occurrence; 192 was first, muddied by a wrong remedy; 224 is unambiguous. Every cap refusal's prescribed remedy is a dead end costing an escalation round-trip plus a fresh-admission workaround (191/192/230 are three uses of the workaround).

The builders' choice, either way ending the lie: ship the override recording the refusal text promises - a structural, operator-attributed verb the guard actually reads - or change the refusal text to name the real path. Acceptance is end to end: the 224 sequence replayed - escalation, operator override, DM resubmission - results in the resubmitted decision recording, proven by test, not by the text asserting it.

Design question in scope, from the same docket: 224's last cap round was spent by a round ending in APPROVAL, before the conflict - the cap exists to stop repair loops and an approval is the opposite of one; whether approving rounds count against the cap is decided here with reasoning recorded.
notes:
Admitted to the backlog by the product manager in conversation chat-91253e0e070c17b0663651cc48602122, after turn 328.

Reason: The override clause of the autonomy goal, still failing after its fix item closed: the operator's decision remains unexecutable by any recorded path, and every occurrence costs a round-trip plus item surgery. Priority 1: third workaround use this week, clean reproduction in hand, and the acceptance is the replay that today fails.

title: A 2-of-2 review stoppage escalates itself to the development manager
description:
Operator direction (Mason, 2026-08-31), starting after he resumes the system (suspension on epic 209 completion per directive-18dfadd17c8e07ad35ae20cb9b25f51e). When a run fails independent review twice - the 2-of-2 review-requires-repair stoppage - it escalates automatically to the development manager, who judges among: resolve it, send it back to the developer for another cycle, or escalate further.

The evidence: tonight this flow ran by hand twice (the runs on 224 and 226, both stopped at 2-of-2 with preserved work) - assistant relayed to the DM's conversation, DM recorded repair grants, assistant fired the triage carry-out verbs. Everything worked; every step between stoppage and recorded decision was a human relay. The automation preserves what governance already requires - ledger-recorded decisions before carry-out, attempt caps, the preserved-work guard - and removes only the relay.

Design and sequencing are the architect's, routed via 210 (link set): whether this lives inside the configurable-workflows triage conversion as a workflow definition, or as its own item ahead of it. Done means a 2-of-2 stoppage reaches the DM's judgment with no human courier, her decision is ledger-recorded before any carry-out exactly as today, the caps and preserved-work guard hold unchanged, and tonight's two cases replayed require zero relays.
notes:

Reason: The autonomy goal's hierarchy doing its own recovery - the DM's judgment reached by machinery instead of couriers - with governance explicitly preserved per the operator's instruction. Child of the workflows epic since its likeliest home is the triage conversion; the architect's placement ruling comes through 210, and execution waits for the post-209 resume by the operator's own sequencing.

Review summary: The mechanism itself is sound and well evidenced. A docketed 2-of-2 stoppage is delivered from the `yoyo work` pull into the development manager's own conversation under the harness's existing lease, spending pause, and session budget; the judgment stays hers and is recorded through the same triage conversation path as a hand-carried stoppage; nothing is carried out by the delivery, so the caps and preserved-work guard are untouched. The durable record is keyed per docket entry, claimed before the turn, bounded to three attempts and paced at fifteen minutes, and gives the attempt back only for failures that provably asked her nothing — and the new tests exercise all of that, including a stand-in replay of the two hand-relayed cases and a session stopping on its budget over deliveries alone. All four declared checks pass. What blocks approval is a documentation contradiction the change itself introduces: docs/conversation.md, docs/work.md, and the `yoyo work` help text all promise that a stoppage the development manager has already decided is never delivered, while alreadyJudged detects only decisions that move a repair-grant or re-run counter, and the code comment beside it says plainly that a decision spending nothing — an escalation to the operator, a re-scope, a wait — leaves the stoppage deliverable. That is exactly the hand-carried case the prose claims to protect. Separately worth knowing, though not blocking: the change decides on its own that deliveries proceed while intake is held, and the work item routes design for this item through 210 with no guidance supplied.
Finding [major] (docs/conversation.md:0): The docs assert a guarantee the code does not provide. docs/conversation.md says "one she has already decided is not delivered at all, whether or not the harness has carried that decision out yet, which is what keeps a stoppage somebody brought her by hand from arriving a second time by machine"; docs/work.md repeats it ("a stoppage she has already decided is not delivered at all") and so does the `yoyo work` help text in internal/cli/schedule.go ("a stoppage she has already decided is passed over whether or not her decision has been carried out yet"). Escalator.alreadyJudged in internal/orchestrator/escalate.go reads only TriageCounters (CommittedRounds vs ReviewRounds, Reruns vs claimed re-runs), and its own comment states that a decision leaving no counter — an escalation to the operator, a re-scope, a wait — means "a stoppage she settled that way is delivered again if the harness ever reaches it". Resolve it one way: either narrow the three documented claims to the decisions the harness can actually see (a repair grant or a re-run recorded against the item), or widen the detection so any recorded triage decision naming the stopped run suppresses the delivery.
Finding [minor] (internal/runstate/escalation.go:0): EscalationStore.Attempt refuses only a record that is Spent (delivered or out of attempts), so two concurrent `yoyo work` sessions can both pass the claim for one stoppage — the second sees attempts=1, increments to 2, and goes on to take a turn. What actually prevents the double delivery is the conversation lease openChat takes, which makes the second attempt fail as unreachable and withdraw. That is adequate today, but the at-most-once guarantee the file's own header claims rests on a lock it does not hold; consider refusing an attempt that is still cooling inside Attempt, or saying in the comment that the conversation lease is what serializes concurrent deliverers.

title: The watch session redeploys itself between runs
description:
Operator feedback (Mason, 2026-08-31): the stale-watch-session problem is still biting - the status warning fired again today with the session 43 harness changes old, and the line says the next move is the operator's; he thought this was fixed. The durable fix: the session redeploys itself.

Why external supervision cannot work, the operator's analysis: the interim maintenance job bounces the watch only when no run is live, because killing the watch cancels its live run - that cancellation has actually happened. With two slots and a deep backlog the scheduler starts the next run the moment one settles, so a 10-minute-cadence external job never lands in an idle window and the session stays stale indefinitely. External supervision at any polling cadence loses this race by construction; only the session itself stands in the gap between runs.

Shape, the development manager's to design: between runs - after a run settles, before the next is claimed - the watch session notices bin/yoyo is newer than its own start and re-executes itself, or exits with a distinct code its supervisor restarts it on. It must never interrupt a live run. The binary-age warning (189's line) then becomes a transient rather than a standing operator chore.

Sequencing note, per the operator: this overlaps the supervision/coordination direction (142) - if the coordination design already absorbs session redeployment, say so here and sequence it there rather than duplicating; the DM checks 142's design before building standalone.

Done means a fix landing on main reaches the resident inside one settle-claim gap with no live run interrupted, the 43-changes-stale case cannot recur as a standing state, and 189's warning is observed transient in practice.
notes:
Admitted to the backlog by the product manager in conversation chat-91253e0e070c17b0663651cc48602122, after turn 321.

Reason: The stale-resident class caused the substituted dispatches, the phantom warnings, and two weeks of misdiagnosis, and the operator has now been handed its chore twice after thinking it fixed - the self-redeploy is the only shape that wins the race his analysis proves external supervision loses. Freeze-aligned reliability at the frontier.

title: Checkpointed workflow execution: an instance runs a compiled graph durably
description: Fourth runtime child of 209. The executor: runs a compiled workflow graph one transition at a time with a durable checkpoint at every state boundary, the instance pinned to its definition digest from creation to terminal state - in-flight work is never silently migrated, per the design. Exercised against test graphs only; the delivery loop is not encoded here. Done means: an instance's durable record carries its digest, current state, and checkpoint history; a process killed at any checkpoint resumes exactly there, tested for every boundary of a fixture graph; a definition change mid-flight is refused for the pinned instance rather than adopted; capability checks are enforced at execution from the registry's declarations, not from the definition; no production workflow runs on it yet; the diff is shown whole to review. title: Strict definition loader and compiler: invalid definitions fail before claiming work
description: Third runtime child of 209. title: Every run and resident pins the harness build it ran, and the records prove deployment
description:
From four reports across 195 and 201, 2026-08-31, the week's largest retrospective finding: the resident scheduler ran a stale binary through the storm. The four substituted repair dispatches (180, 182 on 08-27; 143, 68.22 on 08-30) all happened AFTER 178's refusal merged on 08-27 09:47, and the refusal is test-proven on the dispatch path - so the dispatching process cannot have run main. The phantom invariant warning ran six days (24 runs) from a binary predating its own in-tree fix, stopping only when bin/yoyo was rebuilt 08-30 20:54. watch.jsonl began stamping builds only 08-30 11:15, so the records cannot say which binary did what before then. Most of the week's 'code defects' were deployment defects, undiagnosable as such.

Scope: every run record pins the harness build (commit or digest) alongside backend, model, account alias, and configuration revision - the durable-state invariant's missing field; every resident stamps its build in its own records from process start; and the staleness heartbeat (189, landed) reads these rather than inferring. Done means a substituted-dispatch or phantom-warning incident is answerable from records alone - which build did this - and a fix landing on main while a stale resident runs is visible as the named degraded state 189 defines, with the build gap stated.

title: Configurable workflows: the graph becomes project-owned data, capability stays trusted code
description:
Operator-directed epic, 2026-08-31, from the configurable-workflows design brief (relayed core; the full document routes to the architect via the promotion child). His goal: get as much of the hard-coded logic into configuration files as possible, starting with the workflow graph. The brief's spine: replace hard-coded workflow topology with versioned declarative state-machine definitions, preserving current behavior first; configuration chooses sequence but cannot grant capability - actions, role authority, Git operations, evidence validation, and leases stay in trusted Go; every instance pinned to its definition digest; in-flight work never silently migrated.

SEQUENCE, recorded for the DM's decomposition under this epic once the architect's design lands: (1) behavioral baseline golden tests - the enabling first step, admitted alongside; (2) the architect's promotion of the full brief - precedes implementation; (3) the brief's runtime sequence in its own order: schemas and capability/action registries wrapping existing code, strict loaders and compiler, checkpointed execution, the delivery loop encoded as built-in data, opt-in parity soak with legacy runs resumable, declarative default, project-owned files, then triage and management conversions, agent context, Sentinel, triggers, specialist reuse. The authority workstream interleaves per the brief: inventory, capability registry, default bundles expressing the five roles, capability-based authorization, separation policy - all reaching parity BEFORE configurable role definitions are admitted; that ordering is held as non-negotiable.

TRADE STATED, NOT DECIDED, per the operator's relief-first posture: the coordination slice (142) proceeds bespoke now and converts to this runtime at the management-requests conversion; the cost is one workflow built twice, accepted knowingly, and the conversion is scope this epic owns so it is not forgotten.

title: A repair dispatch invokes the handback path, never a fresh run in its place
description: From the developer's critical on ifd.178's run, 2026-08-24 - the mechanism finding that survives 178's fix: the lost repair rounds were NOT dispatched by yoyo triage repair, whose path re-enters the stopped run via Store.Adopt -> Pipeline.resumeRun and never calls Worktrees.Create; only Pipeline.Run's fresh path (Reserve + Create) produces the observed fresh worktrees with new suffixes off current main. title: Inbound replies are discriminated by intent: questions get answers, not directive receipts
description:
Operator screenshot defect, 2026-08-30, beside the reply-path work; the screenshot is the fixture. He asked in a thread - What does 'in force from now' mean? - and the inbound machinery, having only one category, recorded his question AS a directive, then acknowledged it circularly using the exact phrase he was asking about. Nothing answered him, and the durable directive record now holds a question as if it were an instruction.

The fix shape: inbound operator replies get intent discrimination - a question routes to the product manager and her ANSWER returns to the thread, tagged; only imperative content becomes a directive; anything ambiguous gets asked back, one line. Until the PM-through-Slack conversation (140) lands, the minimum honest behavior ships first: the receipt says 'recorded as a question; an answer follows' rather than declaring a question in force.

General ack-wording rule, the operator's: receipts must not explain a term by restating it - a receipt that answers a question about a phrase by repeating the phrase is the fixture's second defect.

Done means the screenshot replayed produces a question-receipt and a tagged answer rather than a directive; the directive record holds only imperative content; ambiguity asks back in one line; and the miscategorized question from the fixture is corrected in the record.
notes:
Admitted to the backlog by the product manager in conversation chat-91253e0e070c17b0663651cc48602122, after turn 273.

Reason: A directive record that ingests questions as instructions fails the goal at its foundation - enforceability presumes the record contains only things somebody actually directed - and the operator's live experience was a circular non-answer. Priority 2 beside the reply-path work per his placement, with the interim honest receipt explicitly sequenced ahead of the full discrimination.

Goal served: Make user directives durable, discoverable, and enforceable regardless of which agent received them.

title: An operator-decided escalation can clear or raise an item's caps, recorded and attributed
description:
The durable fix from the DM's deadlock ruling, 2026-08-30. The escalation protocol currently ends in decisions nobody can execute: the rounds-cap check refuses the DM's rerun recording regardless of the operator's decision (refused at 5-of-4 and 6-of-4 on the two priority items), the rerun verbs refuse without that ledger record, and the escalation entry satisfies neither - so a cap-exhausted item is permanently unrunnable by any recorded path, and the operator's REBUILD decisions had to be executed by admitting fresh items instead.

Scope: an operator-decided escalation outcome can clear or raise an item's rounds cap through a recorded, attributed override - the ledger accepts it as an operator decision, the verbs honor it, and the override names who decided and when. The caps' purpose is preserved: they stop machines looping, and only an operator's recorded decision crosses them - no agent path, no default. Done means the 143/68.22 deadlock replayed resolves through the recorded override rather than through fresh-item surgery, and the escalation protocol's decisions are executable end to end.

title: An empty-diff round is an environmental refusal: it spends no budget and counts toward no cap
description:
Operator admission, 2026-08-30, extending 187's own definition: an empty-diff round is an environmental refusal - the run delivered nothing because the environment handed it nothing - so it must not spend the item's repair budget or count toward its rounds cap. Tonight it did, three times: the doorbell tests, pooling, and the environmental-refusal item itself each burned a granted round on a clean worktree the stale-binary dispatch handed them.

Scope: a round whose diff is empty and whose run records an environmental cause - handback-missing-change, dirty primary, sandbox spawn failure, stale-binary dispatch - is classified environmental at settle: budget unspent, cap untouched, the cause named in the round's record, and the item stays where it was rather than advancing toward escalation. A genuinely empty delivery with no environmental cause recorded still spends, so laziness cannot hide in the class - which composes with the review pipeline carrying the developer's outcome report (148), the evidence that distinguishes the two.

Done means tonight's three cases replayed spend nothing, an environmentally-refused round is visible as such in the docket and the thread, and no sequence of environmental failures can walk an item to its cap.

title: Parked work is unschedulable: a status the scheduler respects, not a priority it drains to
description:
From Thursday's tail, 2026-08-27: the scheduler drained the queue to priority 4 and ran the PARKED Codex adapter - ifd.6, $34.38, failed - because parked-by-priority is schedulable whenever the queue empties, contradicting the scope decision's off-the-critical-path intent. The product manager's own convention created the gap: priority 4 as parking is a reading the scheduler does not share, and watch mode makes queue-draining routine, so every parked item is one thin day from being paid for.

Scope, the operator's two options, builder decides with reasoning: a parked status the scheduler respects - never selected regardless of queue depth, visibly distinct in listings - or a deliberate floor above 4 that selection never crosses without an explicit operator release. Either way, done means the current parked set (the Codex adapter, the plugin contract, contributor mode, fork publishing, external config) cannot be selected by a drained queue, the parking is visible as parking rather than as low priority, and the ifd.6 case replayed selects nothing.

title: An environmental refusal is a named state the operator hears about, never a tried-memory entry
description:
Operator ask after the third silent-stall incident, 2026-08-27, three fixes as one behavior. The incident: a two-line hand edit sat uncommitted in the primary checkout - correct per the architect's conversation-documents ruling, runs refuse a dirty primary - but the refusal was invisible: the watch session marked every ready item already-tried and idled, the heartbeat said nothing-startable without saying WHY, and the operator diagnosed it by asking his assistant, twice, days apart.

(1) A run start refused for a dirty primary checkout is a NAMED state, not a tried-memory entry: the watch retries it each pass, and the heartbeat says exactly 'runs cannot start: uncommitted changes in the primary checkout (<file>); commit or stash to release' - whose-move the operator's. (2) That state joins the DM tier the moment 68.20 lands: it is a system-stopped state by that item's own definition, so the operator's phone says it, once, with the file named. (3) The tried-memory poisoning generalizes: environmental refusals - dirty checkout, capacity, sandbox failure - must NEVER mark an item tried; only the item's own failures may, or every environmental stall reads as an exhausted queue.

Done means the dirty-primary case replays as a retrying named state with the exact heartbeat line, the DM tier carries it once 68.20 lands, no environmental refusal class writes tried-memory, and the three recorded incidents' silence is structurally impossible.

Clause 3 is generalized correctly and in the only way that can cover classes a readiness read cannot see — declaration at the refusing step plus a probe where nothing declared — and the four new tests replay the incident, the drain case, the undeclared case, and the E2BIG-shaped sandbox case, each of which would fail without the change. docs/work.md, docs/configuration.md, docs/reporting.md are all brought into line, and no delivered invariant is touched (the new gate sits after the intake-hold read, adds no write path, and the heartbeat still projects the shared watch-transition read model rather than deriving anything of its own). Finding [major] (internal/orchestrator/pipeline.go:690): The two ValidateReady wraps repeat the condition inside the error they wrap, and blockedReason then spends almost the whole 100-byte detail budget on that repetition. In Run, describe() yields "the repository is not ready for an isolated run: repository is not ready for an isolated run: <cause>" — 94 bytes before the cause starts, so singleLine(..., maxBlockedDetailBytes) leaves about six bytes of it; the resumeRun wrap ("the repository is not ready to resume a run" + "repository is not ready to resume run <id>: ...") loses the cause entirely. The dirty-checkout case is unaffected because blockedReason matches PrimaryDirtyError first, but every other readiness failure (an unexpected worktree, an unreadable repository) reaches the operator as a doubled generic phrase with the reason cut off, which contradicts what docs/work.md now promises — "the session reports whichever condition it was in that step's words" — and what docs/configuration.md promises about the session saying which condition it is. Resolve it without changing Error(), whose verbatim delegation is deliberate: either drop the duplicated prefix from the condition at these sites, or have describe/blockedReason apply the byte bound to the wrapped cause rather than to the condition plus cause.

Review summary: The finding is resolved, and resolved the way it was asked to be. The marker now goes innermost around the bare cause at every declaring site — `fmt.Errorf("repository is not ready for an isolated run: %w", refusedByEnvironment(...))` rather than the reverse — so `Err` is the cause alone and `Error()` still delegates verbatim, and `describe()` applies `maxBlockedDetailBytes` to that cause rather than to condition-plus-cause. The doubled phrase is gone from every operator-facing path: `blockedReason` renders `runs cannot start: <condition>: <up to 100 bytes of cause>`, which for the Run and resumeRun readiness wraps now reaches the operator with the actual reason attached instead of about six bytes of it, and both forms still fold inside the heartbeat's 200-byte bound with the move that clears the line intact. The dirty-checkout sentence is unchanged and still matched first, so the exact line the item requires is untouched, and the rest of the change is as previously reviewed: the readiness gate is read at every pull before anything is chosen, WatchBlocked is a first-class state distinct from idle and carried verbatim by the heartbeat ahead of idle, environmental refusals (declared or probed, including capacity declines) are remembered only to the next interval and never written as tried-memory or counted toward blocked_runs_before_intake_hold, and docs/work.md, docs/configuration.md and docs/reporting.md say what the code now does. fmtcheck, test, race and vet all pass. No delivered invariant is touched: no new write path, the gate sits after the intake-hold read, and the heartbeat still projects the shared watch-transition read model. Two minor observations accompany the approval; neither blocks.
Finding [minor] (internal/orchestrator/schedule_test.go:0): Nothing in the suite would fail if the marker were moved back outside the wrap or the byte bound put back across condition-plus-cause. The E2BIG test builds the marker directly with a short condition and a 46-byte cause, so it renders identically under the old and new describe(), and the two dirty-checkout tests never reach this branch. A case with a long cause taken through the Run or resumeRun wrap — asserting the cause survives rather than being truncated behind the condition — would lock in exactly what this round fixed, which is otherwise a wrapping order easy to flip back.
Finding [minor] (docs/configuration.md:1707): docs/configuration.md enumerates "a sandbox that will not spawn a shell" among the starts the machine refused, and docs/work.md repeats it, but no production site declares that class: the seven refusedByEnvironment calls are the in-flight read, the two ValidateReady wraps, CurrentBranch, NewRunID, the reservation, and loadInvariants, none of which spawns a shell, and a spawn failure inside the developer attempt is deliberately excluded by refusedByTheMachine's RunID gate. The probe half cannot see it either, since such a failure leaves the checkout clean. The mechanism is right and the E2BIG test proves it works once a site declares; what is not yet true is the enumeration. Either declare it at whichever step actually meets it, or say in the docs that the class is covered when the refusing step marks it rather than listing it as covered today.

title: A handback carries the preserved change, not a clean worktree
description: From the developer on 68.19's repair round, 2026-08-23: the repair was given a fresh clean worktree (base 57e4897) rather than the preserved change it was told to repair, and the developer reconstructed the ten-file change by reading the preserved worktree by hand. If the harness intends a handback to carry the stopped run's branch or worktree, that path is not working - and the next handback may silently start a repair from nothing, which a less careful developer would deliver as an 'empty repair' or a reinvention. Done means a handback to a repair carries the preserved branch or worktree it names, a repair that arrives without its preserved change refuses loudly rather than proceeding from clean, and the 68.19 case replayed hands the repair its ten files.

title: A moved remote target cannot close an item as integrated into a state nothing resolves
description:
From the reviewer on ifd.154's verification run, 2026-08-23 - a live defect on the current publishing path, not the hypothetical team-mode one: when the remote target moves under a run (any human push to main during a run suffices), the local promotion has already happened, ErrRemoteTargetDrift cannot fail the run, the work item closes as integrated, and CatchUpTarget then refuses to reconcile the diverged local target because 'only a person can say which history is right'. An outstanding publication is recorded, and nothing resolves it - a permanent wedge the operator discovers later. Routed only as a Work-discovered bullet in docs/diagnoses/yoyodyne-ifd-154-promotion-precondition.md until now.

Scope, per the report's citations: internal/orchestrator/publish.go's recordPublishFailure path and internal/gitworktree/converge.go:113-121. Done means a target moved under a run cannot produce an item recorded integrated against a divergence nothing owns: either the drift fails the run before the item closes, or the outstanding publication routes to an owner (the docket, or reconcile with 170's forge re-ask) with the divergence named - and the human-push-during-run case replays into a resolvable state.
notes:

Reason: Automatic integration recording success against a state it then refuses to reconcile is the goal failing with a receipt: the item says integrated, the repository says diverged, and nothing owns the difference. title: The system-stopped states DM the operators: the push half of the heartbeat
description:
Operator request from today's brake, 2026-08-23, for the Slack epic. Direct messages to the operators - plural, from the mapping - when the system as a whole waits on a person: the channel heartbeat worked, he read it and asked, but a channel line is something you find when you look, and the all-stopped state is the one condition that deserves to find YOU.

The noise discipline, his shape: a single blocked item stays a channel warning with its status reaction - it has an owner (the DM docket), and DMing every block would teach operators to ignore DMs. The DM tier is reserved for system-waits-on-human states: the brake tripping (nothing new chosen until a human releases), the capacity-blocked state past its wait budget, and plausibly a directive or escalation naming the operator explicitly. Each DM says what stopped, why, whose move it is, and where the full record lives, tagged per the operators mapping; the brake release cancels its own follow-ups.

Mechanics for the builder: the app manifest likely needs the im:write scope - another workspace-approval click, worth bundling with any other pending scope change so the operator approves once.

Done means the three named states produce DMs to mapped operators with the four contents, a single blocked item produces no DM, release cancels follow-ups, and the scope change ships bundled. Pairs with the heartbeat as the push half of one principle: silence must never mean waiting-on-you-without-telling-you, and a stopped line should not depend on the operator checking the channel.
notes:
Admitted to the backlog by the product manager in conversation chat-91253e0e070c17b0663651cc48602122, after turn 221.

Reason: The all-stopped state is the one message whose delivery cannot depend on the reader looking, and today's brake proved the pull half alone leaves the operator finding out by asking. Priority 1 with the frontier; the noise discipline is recorded in the item so the DM tier stays trusted.

Operator refinement, 2026-08-23, generalizing this item from alarm to decision surface - folded into scope. The DM goes to ALL configured operators. The top-line message is brief and says specifically what is being asked, naming the item and the tension - his example: item1234, 'DM messages to operator on item failures', needs your call: a possible conflict with the PM's goal 'don't be too chatty'. IN A THREAD under that DM, the system gives a bit more context and the specific ask as enumerated options - (a) re-write the goal to match the work item, (b) update the work item, (c) something else / need more information. The operator answers IN-LINE: the reply in the DM thread IS the decision, routed through the same directive machinery thread replies already use, and the decision is recorded against WHICH OPTION was chosen, not just free text - the settled receipt says what was decided.

Two shaping constraints from the operator: (1) this is the management-loop protocol's escalation shape - blocked outcome, why the operator, options in nontechnical terms, recommendation - delivered as a DM instead of read from a docket; render that governed format, do not invent a second one. (2) The in-line answer extends reply-steering from sink-opened work-item threads to sink-opened DM threads: the architect's narrowing said sink-opened threads and a DM thread the sink opens qualifies, but the receipt vocabulary and identity check apply there explicitly - stated so the builder does not guess.

Invariants hold as far as the evidence shows: the DM reply directs work only through the existing directive path and explicitly refuses to work the machine, no role is invoked, and the new directs.json goes through the store's existing write helper alongside threads.json and cursors.json. Checks pass and the new tests exercise the new behaviour rather than skirting it. One problem blocks approval: docs/slack/setup.md tells an operator they may delete im:write as a supported opt-out and that "everything else in this document still works", while the code makes a missing im:write fail the whole delivery pass with a permanent refusal and the same document's troubleshooting row says the channel then runs late until the app is reinstalled. Those two claims cannot both be true, and since there is deliberately no switch to turn the escalation tier off, the scope deletion is the only opt-out on offer and it is the one the code punishes.
Finding [major] (docs/slack/setup.md:99): docs/slack/setup.md offers deleting `im:write` as a supported configuration — "An operator who would rather not steer from Slack, and would rather not be messaged, can delete `im:write` and the three `*:history` scopes ... everything else in this document still works" — but the code makes that configuration a permanently degraded sink. Sink.escalate returns the OpenDirect failure to pass(), which fails the whole pass, and the troubleshooting row this change adds for `slack refused conversations.open: missing_scope` says the sink then waits the refusal out for minutes and "the channel runs late until you reinstall". Nothing in HarnessFeed lets the escalation tier be turned off, so an operator who follows this paragraph gets a channel that permanently reports late with no way back except the reinstall the other row tells them to do. Resolve it by making the escalating half treat a missing `im:write` the way it treats having nobody to message — log it once and let the cursor advance, so the channel keeps its pace — or by withdrawing the claim that removing `im:write` leaves everything else working and saying plainly what it costs.
Finding [minor] (internal/slack/escalate.go:231): capacityStoppage takes the age of the block from oldest.UpdatedAt, which is a generic last-written timestamp rather than when the run became parked. If anything rewrites a parked run's state while it waits — a supervisor pass, a reconciliation, a retry that re-records the same usage limit — the two-hour budget restarts and this state never escalates, which is silent failure of exactly the condition the tier exists for. Worth confirming that runstate.State.UpdatedAt is not touched while a run holds UsageLimitResetsAt, or deriving the age from the moment the limit was recorded instead.

title: Each cut writes release notes: key functionality, enhancements, fixes
description:
Operator requirement, 2026-08-23. With each release tagged, a release notes file is produced - what was added since the last tag - organized as key functionality at the top, enhancements below, bug fixes at the bottom, with one exception: a critical bug fix may go up with key functionality. The judgment of key versus enhancement versus fix is the product manager's until the post-v1 release-manager role exists (recorded as post-v1 intent beside the operations role).

Mechanics: the raw material is what landed between the last tag and this one - the closed items with their titles, types, and goals, richer than commit messages; the notes live versioned in the repository (a releases or notes home the cut writes, the file named for the tag it cuts) so the release page and the repository tell one story. Composes with the daily delegation: the release-worthy call produces the tag, the reason in the channel, and the notes file - one act, three outputs.

First exercise and acceptance case: v0.3.0's notes, written retroactively covering v0.2.0 to v0.3.0 - five days of the system building its own scheduler, triage, Slack stack, installer, and security remediation - authored by the product manager's judgment from the generated raw material. Done means the cut produces the notes file from the closed-item material, the sections follow the operator's shape, the v0.3.0 retroactive notes exist in the notes home, and the daily cadence ships notes with every tag thereafter.

title: Verify the promotion precondition the team-mode design leans on
description: Bounded verification commission, the ifd.97 pattern, from the reviewer's warning on ifd.82.2's run, 2026-08-23: the design's cross-machine promotion safety argument rests entirely on an asserted property of the existing promotion path - that before the forge merges, the remote target must already contain the commit the run was written against and carry exactly its content, so a target another machine moved fails closed and replays. That claim is what lets the document downgrade the proposed shared turn record to advisory and what the proposed narrowing of one-promotion-per-target-branch leans on - and nothing in the evidence demonstrates it. Deliverable: a developer run that reads the promotion code and produces findings with citations - the precondition is enforced (where, by what check), or it is not (what actually holds) - plus a test pinning it if it holds. The architect's ruling on the lease-narrowing amendment waits on this evidence; if the precondition is not enforced, the proposal loses its guarantee and the narrowing should not be granted, per the reviewer's own framing.

title: The architect rules on the release push: a second writer of main and the promotion lease
description: EXECUTOR: conversation:architect. From both reviewer warnings on ifd.150's run, 2026-08-23: scripts/cut-release.sh now advances local main by a housekeeping commit and instructs git push --atomic origin main <tag> - previously the cut only created a tag. That introduces a writer of origin/main that takes no promotion lease, alongside the harness path that one-promotion-per-target-branch serializes. The reviewers' own analysis: it looks safe in practice - a concurrent harness promotion makes the operator's atomic push a rejected non-fast-forward rather than a lost update, and the pre-tag HEAD-vs-origin/main gate catches divergence on the next cut - but under the delegated daily cadence the push becomes routine, a rejected push wedges the next cut until someone reconciles by hand, and nobody has decided who runs the push or what they do on rejection. The architect decides whether an operator-run release script advancing the integration branch belongs inside the invariant's scope, and the who-pushes-and-what-on-rejection procedure is recorded with the ruling. Interim mitigation, recorded: under delegation the product manager triggers cuts, and a rejected push means the cut waits with the reason in the channel rather than a hand-reconciliation under time pressure.
