title: Git commands that walk worktree registrations tolerate a concurrent run's half-written registration
description: Developers on 70 (2026-08-19) and 275 (2026-09-04): a git command in one run's worktree fails on another run's half-written registration under .git/worktrees ('failed to read .git/worktrees/<other>/commondir: Undefined error: 0'; 'git worktree list' crossing a registration). gitworktree retries the listing (worktreeListAttempts) which covers the microsecond window in practice, but every other command that walks the registrations - rebase among them - is unprotected, and a loaded machine stretches a registration past three reads 50ms apart. The named fix: a shared read lease that Create can pass into its own verification (it currently holds the exclusive creation lease across Inspect, so readers cannot take it). Done means: creation holds a lease readers can take and every registration-walking command takes it; the intermittent failures in TestSchedulerRunsSeveralEligibleItemsAtOnceInWorktreesOfTheirOwn and TestTwoRunsPromotingIntoOneTargetBranchSerializeAndBothLand no longer reproduce under a concurrent creation loop by test; and the retry on the listing is either removed or kept with a comment saying what residual it covers.

title: The architect scopes all five roles on Codex
description:
Operator-directed, 2026-09-07, routed to the architect for the same treatment she gave multi-provider support: he wants all five roles able to run on Codex, and asked for a way to get there. Codex serves the developer only today, and the reasons are specific rather than general:

(1) THE REVIEWER POSTURE. Codex's read-only sandbox stops writes and network but still lets the agent read the whole machine, while the reviewer posture requires that it read NOTHING outside the evidence it was handed. The descriptor names what would lift the restriction - an adapter that achieves that property - and the operator's read is that this is likely HARNESS-SIDE CONFINEMENT rather than a Codex setting.

(2) THE MANAGEMENT ROLES. Codex enforces no schema on what an agent finally says, and the product manager, development manager and architect need structured output and the tracker action protocol. What that costs, and whether it can be achieved by validation-and-retry above the adapter rather than by the provider, is the question.

THE ASK, in the shape that worked for multi-provider: what each of the two obstacles ACTUALLY COSTS, and whether all five roles is REACHABLE or whether some roles stay on Claude FOR A STATED REASON - a recorded 'no, and here is why' is an acceptable answer and better than an open question. The capability-validation machinery that already refuses role/backend pairs is the enforcement point either way, and yoyodyne-ifd.340's endpoint model is where role eligibility is derived from declarations. Done means the scoping is recorded where implementation items could cite it, with each obstacle costed or explicitly deferred with its reason.
notes:

Reason: Operator-directed scoping; the two obstacles are architecture questions (confinement and output contracts) rather than product ones, and her multi-provider scoping is the proven shape for turning a want into buildable slices.

title: An account names its provider, and a wrong-provider account is refused before a claim
description:
Operator-directed at p2, 2026-09-07, from the reviewer on run-5f8eb416 (yoyodyne-ifd.347): accounts in the pool are not provider-scoped, and the adapter passes an assigned account's directory straight through to the provider - so a developer configured for Codex on a pooling installation would be invoked with CODEX_HOME set to a Claude Code provider home, die unauthenticated AFTER the work item was already claimed, while yoyo doctor still reported the pool healthy. It does not bite this installation today because nothing is pooled and no agent runs on Codex; it bites the moment either changes.

THE FIX SHAPE, the operator's: an account NAMES ITS PROVIDER; an account of the wrong provider is REFUSED BEFORE A RUN CLAIMS ANYTHING, so the failure costs nothing rather than costing a claimed item and an unauthenticated death; and the DIAGNOSIS ASKS EACH ACCOUNT ABOUT ITS OWN PROVIDER rather than assuming one - poolDescriptor in internal/doctor/doctor.go already admits the same bound for the diagnosis half and is where that starts.

Prerequisite in fact for yoyodyne-ifd.306 (account failover): failover across a pool that can hand a Codex run a Claude home fails the moment it is exercised, so this lands first or 306 is built on ground that gives way. Done means an account declares its provider, a mismatch is refused pre-claim with the reason named, doctor reports per-account provider health, and the Codex-developer-with-Claude-home shape is the regression case.

title: A goal has a stable identity, so amending its wording breaks nothing
description:
Exposed today, 2026-09-07: the multi-provider goals amendment silently invalidated every future admission naming the prior wording, and the failure surfaced only when four admissions were refused at intake - the operator learned of it by watching them fail. Attribution matches a goal by its exact prose, so re-wording a goal orphans every item attributed to it and refuses every admission quoting it. This is the third instance: the legibility amendment orphaned four items in September (117.2/117.3/117.4/68, then 117.1/128/68.9), and the 122 parse change silently truncated wrapped statements in August, turning recorded attributions into fragments that no longer resolved.

THE PRODUCT MANAGER'S CALL, made rather than deferred: attribution resolves by STABLE GOAL IDENTITY, not by exact text. An amendment-time re-attribution offer is a patch on a design that treats prose as a key; identity makes the class impossible and reduces amending a goal to editing a sentence rather than renaming a thing. Scope: each goal in the goals documents carries a stable identifier (assigned once, never reused, surviving re-wording); attribution records and resolves that identifier; the goal's prose is what a human reads and what the item displays, not what the match depends on. description: The architect's final slice from her multi-provider scoping (design PR 481), admitted 2026-09-07, sequenced AFTER the endpoint model and the refusal-classification conformance suite: failover across providers rather than within one - the generalization of 331 (model failover within a family) and 306 (account failover within a provider) onto the endpoint model. title: One refusal-classification conformance suite every adapter passes
description: The architect's third slice from her multi-provider scoping (design PR 481), admitted 2026-09-07: a single conformance suite that every provider adapter must pass on refusal classification, with Claude and Codex first. Refusal vocabulary is where adapters diverge invisibly - a provider that says 'capacity' differently, or rejects a model selector before calling its API and emits no terminal event, breaks failover and the recoverable-versus-terminal boundary at once (see 333's unobserved 404 shape and 265's boundary ruling). Done means one suite, run against both existing adapters, asserting that each classifies the same provider conditions the same way - capacity exhaustion, model unavailable, authentication, network, and a refusal that is a judgment on the work rather than an environment failure - and a new adapter cannot be declared complete without passing it.
notes:

Reason: Every failover and retry decision downstream reads a classification; one suite is what keeps two adapters (and later a third) from meaning different things by the same word.

Goal served: Keep roles, policies, and provider selection configurable without making safety invariants optional, and support multiple providers behind one adapter contract.

title: The architect scopes multi-provider support: Codex and Gemini/Antigravity alongside Claude
description: Operator direction, 2026-09-07, routed to the architect for SCOPING - he asked for scoping, not immediate build. He wants Codex and Gemini/Antigravity supported alongside Claude. What exists to build on: the provider-plugin contract is designed and closed (yoyodyne-ifd.32) - a project can declare a provider in configuration, supplying dialect and executable, but only for something speaking a protocol an already-compiled adapter reads; a genuinely different protocol needs an adapter, which is a change to the harness. Codex is in the configuration vocabulary with no adapter (yoyodyne-ifd.6, parked at p4 by the 2026-08-22 V1 scope decision, which this direction reopens). Capability validation already refuses role/backend pairs whose sandbox cannot hold a role's tool posture - that machinery is the model for admitting new providers safely. THE OPERATOR'S SCOPING QUESTIONS, his to the architect rather than the product manager's: (1) what a second and third adapter actually costs - Codex's CLI, Gemini/Antigravity's; (2) which roles each provider may serve under capability validation, with the reviewer's no-tools posture and the developer's worktree-write as the discriminators; (3) how model failover (331) and account pooling (143/306) generalize ACROSS providers rather than within one; (4) what the durable records must carry so evidence stays provider-independent, per the standing invariant; (5) whether the parked Codex item is resumed or superseded by a general adapter workstream. NOTE FOR THE OPERATOR, raised in conversation rather than assumed: building adapters for new providers goes beyond what the recorded goals state - 'provider selection configurable' is satisfied today by choosing among providers the harness has adapters for - so a goals amendment is his to make before implementation items are admitted; this scoping item stands either way. Done means the scoping is recorded where implementation items could cite it, with each of the five questions answered or explicitly deferred with its reason.

title: Runs the harness launches cannot start a Git prune that eats a worktree registration
description: Re-issue after an over-limit block was refused. From the developer and reviewer on run-4c4c3c1f (yoyodyne-ifd.73) and two earlier filings on ifd.71: the auto-maintenance fence covers only Git commands issued through gitworktree.Manager, because the settings are passed per command rather than written to any config. Any other Git command in the same repository - including anything an agent or a run's own build tooling invokes inside a harness-created worktree, which shares the common Git directory - still triggers auto-maintenance, and a prune can judge a registration still being created stale and delete it mid-creation, losing the run ('fatal: could not open .git/worktrees/<id>/locked for writing', reproduced on git 2.50.1 within seconds when a prune races concurrent adds). The product manager's decision, recorded: take the middle path the reviewer names rather than the full fence - the harness controls the environment it launches run and agent processes in, so inject GIT_CONFIG_COUNT/GIT_CONFIG_KEY_n setting gc.auto=0 and maintenance.auto=false into that environment, closing the agent-and-build-tooling path without touching the operator's repository config or disabling object GC for a repository that keeps growing. Done means every process the harness launches carries the fenced environment, a build tool or agent Git command inside a worktree cannot trigger maintenance, the residual (a person running git gc by hand) is documented as the operator's own, and the concurrent-creation shape is the regression case alongside 332's listing tolerance. The full fence - writing the settings into the managed repository's config - stays available to the operator if losses continue.
notes:
Admitted to the backlog by the product manager in conversation chat-91253e0e070c17b0663651cc48602122, after turn 476.

Reason: A lost run from a neighbouring Git command is the same waste 332 attacks from the reading side; the environment injection closes the likely path at no cost to the operator's repository, and the full-fence alternative is put to him rather than taken silently.

title: Reports render tight and honest: no warning without an ask, no post without a point
description: Operator-directed, the implementation half, built against 313's recorded ruling, with his survey as the measured baseline: 2,250 channel posts to date, roughly three-quarters per-event progress narration - report.filed 320 (individual pushes mostly asking nothing), watch.idle 206, watch.started/stopped 267, checks.passed 200, review.approved 140, run.started 138, publication/merge/promotion ~313, backlog.admitted 114 - against under forty posts of the genuinely important-or-actionable kinds (intake.held, watch.braked, usage-limit.exhausted, run.parked, tracker.block-refused, directive.recorded). Scope, his: (1) per-event milestones live in their item's thread or the durable record only - the channel level carries importance and asks; (2) status renderings stop enumerating queues - the four-line contract, no item lists; (3) reports digest rather than push individually, and the filed-report templates plus the personas' report-writing guidance push to one plain sentence of what and one of why it matters; (4) a post that is neither important nor needs action does not post. title: The architect amends the channel rules: severity means actionability, and no action means no post
description: Operator-directed, expanded by him 2026-09-06 into the full COMMUNICATION RULE, drafted by the product manager and delivered through the channel for his review - it binds only after his approval, and governs the recurring-loop reports from their first real posts. title: Stall detection runs without Slack
description: From the reviewer on run-60ff2754 (yoyodyne-ifd.242): stall detection is produced only by the Slack sink's poll loop - internal/slack/feed.go is the sole caller of the reconciliation - so a product with no sink running records no stalls and its yoyo status stall history is permanently empty. Slack reporting is documented throughout as opt-in and 'an observation and never a gate', so the harness's only instrument for noticing that nothing is happening depends on an optional process the operator may never start. title: Only one watch session runs per product: the watch takes a lease
description: From the developer on run-e72d3cf0 (yoyodyne-ifd.288): nothing prevents two 'yoyo work --watch' sessions running against one product at once - the command takes no lease, and a run does not appear in durable state until it reserves, several steps after it starts, so two sessions can choose the same item in that window. This is how two watches briefly coexisted during the 2026-09-05 wedge recovery. The machinery exists and is unused here: runstate.TryLeasePath, which internal/slack/sink.go takes for exactly this only-one-may-run reason. Done means yoyo work --watch takes a product-scoped lease at start and refuses with a plain sentence naming the holder when one is held, the wedge-recovery shape (second watch started while the first is alive) is the regression case, and the lease releases cleanly on every exit path 288 hardens - including the takeover fallback exit. Look at scheduleWork in internal/cli/schedule.go and the occupiedItems/mine bookkeeping in internal/orchestrator/schedule.go.

title: A thread settles its own pausing directive without naming an id
description: Follow-on the 68.26 fix created, from the developer on run-7aeff796: the in-thread acknowledgment was the only place the channel published a directive identifier, and 68.26 rightly removed identifiers from human-read surfaces - so settling a paused directive from Slack now requires reading its id at a terminal first, which is backwards for the thread-first experience the operator directed on 68.23/140. Done means a thread can settle its own single open pausing directive with a bare 'resolve <how>' - no identifier - refusing with a plain sentence when more than one is open (naming them in words, not ids); and the design boundary this requires is decided deliberately: the Slack sink's Directives interface forbids reads today, so either that interface gains a narrow read (this thread's open pausing directives only) or the resolution routes through the role conversation that already reads them - the builder consults the architect's standing routing ruling rather than widening the sink's authority silently.
notes:

title: A non-discharging landing re-parks its item; leave-open requires an explicit marker
description: Follow-on to 209.23, from two reviewer reports on run-19a48e34: an item reopened by an evidence landing returns to the backlog as an ordinary open item - nothing marks it recently diagnosed, the landing run is recorded as succeeded so the blocked-run brake never counts it, and autonomous selection can pick it again immediately: another run, another diagnosis, a full integration each cycle. Product default, decided here: a not-doable-yet landing RE-PARKS the item, with the landing's diagnosis as the parking reason naming what would release it - the existing park machinery already keeps it in order, says why, and blocks selection. Where a developer's landing instead justifies leaving the item open, it must carry an explicit marker selection honors - a cooldown or a dependency on the impediment - never bare openness. Done means the 209.23 reopen path re-parks by default with the reason populated from the landing, the leave-open path requires the marker, and selection replayed against a reopened item picks it zero times until release.
notes:
Admitted to the backlog by the product manager in conversation chat-91253e0e070c17b0663651cc48602122, after turn 417.

Reason: 209.23 made honest landings possible; without this its loop costs a run per diagnosis and the succeeded status hides it from every brake - the park default reuses machinery that already exists rather than inventing a cooldown.

Goal served: Keep roles, policies, and provider selection configurable without making safety invariants optional.

title: A run lands evidence without closing its item: closure follows the discharging outcome only
description: Operator-directed class defect, 2026-09-05, from the 209.14 answer: the run was honest - its landing was a 157-line diagnosis stating in bold that it delivered no conversion and 'the anchor stays open' - and integration closed the item anyway, because closure mechanically follows a run's integration regardless of what the landed content says. The fix, his suggested shape: the run's structured result carries an outcome distinct from complete - 'evidence landed, item not discharged' - the developer has a recorded way to claim it, and reconciliation closes only on the discharging kind; a non-discharging landing leaves the item open or re-parks it. The reviewer should see which outcome is claimed, so a diagnosis is judged as a diagnosis rather than as a missing implementation. Pairs with 209.20: both are 'closure requires the right kind of act, not just an act'. Done means the 209.14 shape replayed - an honest not-doable-yet landing - integrates its evidence and leaves its item undischarged, with the closure path tested for both outcome kinds.

description: The two live-bd cases from 277's run (run-a763e941), left unowned when 278 closed before the note recording them arrived; both are load-bearing for the nine items the stale-status release (277) put back in the scheduler's reach and neither is provable from a sandbox. title: Work is not admitted twice from one source, and a satisfied item is caught before dispatch
description: Two incident families in one week: yoyodyne-ifd.274 duplicated the closed 229 - both admitted by the product manager from the same developer report, the second after the first had landed - and yoyodyne-ifd.241 was decomposed twice into parallel pairs (241.1/241.2, then 241.3/241.4); the second occurrence cost a full run, both repair attempts, and a confident review demanding code already merged at feed.go:447 (2db180b, PR #366). title: A gate that needs a human's recorded act cannot be satisfied by item closure
description: Governance bug from the 209.6/209.7 default flip, operator-directed 2026-09-04: 209.6's done condition reserved an operator-recorded soak completion, but the only enforceable encoding available was an item-closed dependency - so when machinery closed 209.6, the flip's gate read satisfied and 209.7 jumped the operator's step. The tracker cannot represent 'a person must record something before this proceeds'. Done means the workflows runtime's human-terminal machinery (or the directive kinds, whichever the design finds right) carries that shape: a gate declarable on an item or workflow step that is satisfiable only by a recorded human act, that item closure alone can never pass, and that reports itself as waiting-on-a-person on the status surfaces; the 209.6/209.7 jump is the regression case. Until it exists, the working rule for admission: an operator step in a done condition gets its own gating item whose executor marks it beyond machinery's reach, never a clause in a closable item's text.

Review summary: The change delivers the missing gate shape well: `internal/humangate` parses `human-gate:` only from author-written fields and never from prose or the harness-appended notes, `internal/runstate/humanact.go` holds a write-once record that no pipeline path can write (with a repository walk enforcing the single door), `backlog.Order` now refuses readiness for any item carrying an undischarged or unreadable declaration, the scheduler refuses to run without a gate reader, `yoyo status` names the gated item on the needs-a-human line, and the workflow executor refuses a gated state — including refusing when the record is unreadable or the reader is unwired. The 209.6/209.7 jump is reproduced as a regression test that would fail without the change, and the four checks pass. The documentation was reconciled rather than left behind: README, configuration.md (counts and the new hold), operations.md (the new section and the needs-a-human bullet), and work.md all describe the shipped behaviour, including an honest statement of what is not yet surfaced. One real hole remains: a gate name is a permanent, product-global identity, so an act recorded once silently discharges every later declaration of that name, which is the same 'gate reads satisfied with the step untaken' failure this item exists to end. Two minor observations accompany it.
Finding [major] (internal/humangate/humangate.go:210): A recorded act discharges a gate name forever and product-wide, so a name reused by later work is passed with nobody having taken that step. `DischargedGates()` returns bare names from a flat directory, `Pending` drops any declared gate whose name appears there, and `RecordHumanAct` refuses a second act for an already-passed name. So an item declaring a natural, recurring name — `release-signed`, `soak-reviewed` — after one has ever been recorded is immediately Ready, no queue or status surface says anything about it, and the operator cannot even record the new act because the gate is already passed. That is the regression this item exists to end, arriving through the namespace instead of through the tracker. Note the reader already holds the rule that 'one name is one act' inside a single item's text: `Read` marks a name declared twice with two different statements unreadable, precisely because one recorded act would pass both. Apply the same rule across time — bind the act to what it was recorded against (the declaring item, or the statement it attested to) and treat a declaration whose statement does not match the recorded act as still holding — or give the operator a supported way to re-arm a name. Whatever is chosen must also be stated in docs/work.md and docs/operations.md, which currently describe recording as the whole of it and say nothing about a name being spent permanently.
Finding [minor] (internal/cli/gate.go:145): `yoyo gate list` reads work items in `open`, `blocked`, and `in_progress`, while the read model's queue (and therefore the needs-a-human line) covers only the admitted statuses. An item claimed while still carrying an undischarged gate is reported as waiting on a person by `gate list` and by nothing else, so the two operator surfaces can give different answers to the same question. Either share the status set with the read model's backlog or say in docs/operations.md why this listing is deliberately wider.
Finding [minor] (internal/workflow/compile.go:190): The workflow-step half of the gate reports on no status surface: an instance standing at a gated state is visible only in the refusal raised when something tries to step it. This is documented in docs/work.md, docs/operations.md, and the comment on `Graph.Gates`, and no shipped definition declares a gate, so nothing is currently invisible — but the item's done condition asks for waiting-on-a-person reporting on the status surfaces, and this half does not have it yet.

The permanence rule the finding asked to be written down is written down: docs/work.md has "A name is not spent by being recorded once" and docs/operations.md explains why `--for` is required, both giving the release-signed and per-instance reasoning. The two minors are taken: `yoyo gate list` now reads `backlog.AdmittedStatuses()` (with a test that fails if it names its own statuses or reads `in_progress`), and the workflow-step reporting gap is stated honestly in docs/work.md, docs/operations.md, and the `Graph.Gates` comment rather than being papered over. Finding [minor] (docs/work.md:363): The gate is enforced where the harness chooses work (`backlog.Order` via `Pull.queue`) and at a workflow step, but not on the paths that start a named run: `yoyo run <id>` and `yoyo triage rerun` reserve and claim without consulting the recorded act. `yoyo run <id>` is defensible as the same operator-named exemption the intake hold already grants. `yoyo triage rerun` is the weaker case, because docs/configuration.md classifies it as the harness choosing the work (which is why the intake hold applies to it), so an agent's recorded decision plus one command can start an item whose gate is undischarged. In practice the exposure is narrow — a re-run only ever follows a run that already happened, so the gate was normally discharged or the item was operator-named, and a gate added to the item after that run is the only way in. Worth either extending the same check to the re-run claim or saying in docs/work.md that a gate holds selection rather than every route into a run.

Reason: Five reports converge on one mechanism and one pattern; the in-flight item should land the class, not two instances.

Mechanism found and scope widened to a suite sweep, per five reports from 283's and 209.24's runs: (1) OSProcessRunner.Run sets Cmd.Cancel to a process-group kill but never sets Cmd.WaitDelay, so a descendant surviving the kill holds the inherited stdout pipe and blocks Wait() with no backstop - the 5.27s failure is 'sleep 5' running to completion after the SIGKILL missed it; 95 focused attempts did not reproduce. (2) TestStoppingTheSinkStopsIt asserts Run returns in 5s from a cancelled context, but Run takes a file lock, calls Identify, and writes presence before selecting on ctx.Done - 8.87s observed under -race load. (3) gitworktree replay (manager.go:1343) branches only on ProcessSucceeded, so a harness-killed rebase (30s git timeout under load) reads as ErrRebaseConflict, terminal, prescribing a conflict that does not exist. The pattern is suite-wide: fixed wall-clock deadlines asserted under -race at full parallelism. Bill so far: $43.63 preserved work, multiple repair attempts, a triage cycle, one DM misdiagnosis. Fix as one sweep: WaitDelay set, deadlines sized for load or replaced with signal-waits, replay honest about kills.

title: A decided docket entry closes instead of reappearing forever
description: The docket's other lifecycle gap, from the developer on run-6b25f257 (yoyodyne-ifd.102.2) and echoed by the reviewer on ifd.102: an entry is created when work stops and nothing ever removes or closes one - the docket is rebuilt from durable records at every scan, wait/rescope/escalate decisions spend no counter, so an already-decided stoppage reappears and the only guard against deciding it twice is prose telling the DM to read the notes. The DM's context renders the newest 25 entries (or 48KB) and counts the rest, so on a long-lived product handled stoppages crowd the unhandled out of the section that exists to surface them. Done means a triage decision closes its entry in the durable record, a closed entry does not reappear on rebuild, genuinely-open stoppages still show, and the 250 sweep's twelve-phantom incident is the regression case. Companion to the p1 creation-side item: together they make the docket's lifecycle create-on-death, close-on-decision.

title: Escalation record writes survive a cancelled context
description:
Widened from the give-back alone, per the developer on run-a2e987a0: both escalation record writes run under the delivery's own context, and a cancellation at the wrong moment corrupts the record in opposite directions.

(1) The give-back: internal/orchestrator/escalate.go calls e.Records.Withdraw with the delivery's ctx. In a shutdown-flavoured cancellation that ctx is itself cancelled - if Withdraw or the safe-write primitive beneath it honours ctx, the withdraw fails, the fallback branch runs, and the attempt is spent after all. The teardown case (child process group killed, harness alive) is covered and tested; the shutdown case was not verifiable from review evidence (reviewer on run-d33acfbf).

(2) The settle: internal/orchestrator/escalate.go:560 calls Records.Settle with the same ctx. A shutdown cancelling between the development manager's answer arriving and that write landing leaves DeliveredAt unrecorded while the attempt stands, so a later pass puts the same stoppage to her a second time - the harm the at-most-once record exists to prevent. alreadyJudged only covers decisions that spend a counter (repair, re-run); one that spends nothing is re-delivered.

Done means internal/runstate/escalation.go's Withdraw and Settle paths are checked for ctx sensitivity, both writes run under a context that survives the delivery's cancellation, and both directions are tested: a shutdown-cancelled give-back does not spend the attempt, and a shutdown-cancelled settle does not re-deliver an answered stoppage.
notes:
Admitted to the backlog by the product manager in conversation chat-91253e0e070c17b0663651cc48602122, after turn 379.

Reason: 251's fix exists to stop environment deaths spending the operator's attention budget; a give-back that fails exactly when the harness itself is shutting down leaves the largest death-class uncovered.

title: Repair-request channel messages carry a one-line summary of each finding
description: Operator request (Mason, 2026-09-03), from reading 209.5's repair announcement: the channel message says only the count ('one finding, each one specific enough to act on'), so the operator cannot tell a one-word docs fix from a design problem without leaving the channel. title: A refused run-state save fails loudly, never leaving a stale record behind
description: From the developer on ifd.148's run, 2026-08-24: runstate.State.Validate rejecting a field makes Store.Save fail while the run carries on holding the value in memory, reporting correctly to the tracker and operator - and what survives on disk is whichever earlier state validated. In the observed case that was the pre-review snapshot with evidence deliberately cleared, so a run that was reviewed and blocked read back as a run nothing ever judged - caught only because a test happened to load the record. Everything reading run state after the process ends - yoyo status, reconcile, the triage docket, cost attribution - would have believed it. Scope: a rejected save fails its run loudly rather than continuing over a stale record, and the whitelist shape in State.Validate is reviewed - a validation list that rejects every future addition to a recorded vocabulary is the trap that produced this, and either the list opens per the schema-evolution lessons (the sink's tolerant-reader rule) or additions gain a conformance test that fails at build time rather than at save time. Done means a save refusal is a run failure with the field named, the stale-record shape is test-impossible, and the validate-list policy is decided with reasoning recorded.

description: From the developer on ifd.227's run, 2026-09-01: runstate.Ending returns OutcomeSucceeded before it checks the blocker (internal/runstate/summary.go:82), and Reconciler.saveTerminalFailure leaves an already-terminal run's status alone (reconcile.go:819) - so blockContradictedIntegration on an integrated run whose promotion the target no longer carries produces a record reading 'succeeded' on every surface while the item is blocked and the docket says a person owns it. Reachable whenever a succeeded run short of the complete phase has its promotion contradicted. Scope: the outcome precedence checks the blocker before returning succeeded, reconciled with the sweep's deliberate don't-move-terminal-status rule - the two decisions are individually right and jointly wrong, and the fix states which yields. Done means a blocked-with-contradicted-promotion run reads as stopped-with-reason everywhere, the succeeded mask is test-impossible, and the precedence rule is written where both code sites cite it.
notes:
Admitted to the backlog by the product manager in conversation chat-91253e0e070c17b0663651cc48602122, after turn 330.

Reason: A record that says succeeded while a person owns its blocker is the surface teaching a false fact at triage time - the exact class the vocabulary work retired, surviving in the outcome precedence. Two named code sites, one test-shaped fix.

Goal served: The harness's surfaces read clearly: boundaries between topics and speakers are visible, important findings stand out, every distinction survives a terminal that cannot render emphasis, and user-facing language chooses the ordinary, literal word over metaphor, coinage, or term of art.

title: A late-reconciled stoppage still records why it stopped
description: From three reports on ifd.226's run, 2026-09-01, a live defect the sweep surfaced and did not close: Reconciler.saveTerminalFailure (internal/orchestrator/reconcile.go:783) skips writing State.Failure when the run is already terminal, so a stoppage reconciled late ends with a Blocker and an empty failure string - and every surface rendering 'why did this stop' from State.Failure gives an empty answer: the Slack line now states the absence explicitly, but the triage docket entry and yoyo status's reason block read the same field and were not checked. Scope: the reconcile blocker text is written onto State.Failure as well as the item (or the renderers read Blocker), the two unchecked surfaces are verified, and the field-semantics split the same run found is settled in the same pass - notify keyed stoppage on Failure while runstate.Outcome() keys on Blocker, now aligned, but any future reader of Failure inherits the trap: decide whether Failure remains a field stoppage is ever inferred from, and document or refactor accordingly. Done means a late-reconciled stoppage shows its reason on all three surfaces, and the Failure-versus-Blocker rule is written where the next reader finds it.
notes:
Admitted to the backlog by the product manager in conversation chat-91253e0e070c17b0663651cc48602122, after turn 324.

Reason: An empty answer to 'why did this stop' at exactly the surfaces a person triages from is the certainty contract's residual-category sin in field form. One fix, three surfaces, plus the semantics rule that prevents the fourth.

Goal served: The harness's surfaces read clearly: boundaries between topics and speakers are visible, important findings stand out, every distinction survives a terminal that cannot render emphasis, and user-facing language chooses the ordinary, literal word over metaphor, coinage, or term of art.

title: Every Resolved() call site means has-a-disposition, proven by audit
description: From two reviewer warnings on ifd.168's run, 2026-08-24: the change made directive.Resolved() stop implying no-longer-in-force - an operational directive now carries a Resolution while still applying, and InForce() is the liveness test. The two visible readers were migrated (internal/chat/directive.go, internal/cli/directive.go), but neither reviewer could grep the repository: any other call site filtering on Resolved() to decide what still constrains work - prompt or run-context assembly, Slack or dashboard summaries, enforcement beyond Pauses() - would silently drop a standing operator instruction the moment its first item is admitted. Scope: grep .Resolved() across the repository; confirm or migrate each site to mean has-a-disposition rather than has-lapsed; pin the distinction with a test that a carried-out operational directive still reaches whatever assembles the directives a run is judged against. Done means the audit's site list is recorded, every site is confirmed or fixed, and the silent-drop shape is test-impossible.
notes:
Admitted to the backlog by the product manager in conversation chat-91253e0e070c17b0663651cc48602122, after turn 321.

Reason: A semantics change to the word every directive filter turns on, audited only two call sites deep - the silently-retired standing instruction is the directives goal's worst failure and the grep is cheap. Freeze-compatible: enforcement-machinery reliability.

Goal served: Make user directives durable, discoverable, and enforceable regardless of which agent received them.

title: A worktree gets the current tracker export at creation
description:
Second bite of the export-staleness class, 2026-08-31, now with real cost: a run on 209.12 could not locate the 211 golden traces its item required, because the worktree's .beads/issues.jsonl topped out at yoyodyne-ifd.193 - the export is committed only by release cuts (by design, per 150's housekeeping), so between cuts every worktree reads a picture missing the newest items, while CLAUDE.md's 'current as of that commit' wording promises otherwise. The primary checkout's export is fresh (export.auto: true); the committed copy a worktree inherits is what lags.

Scope, per the refined diagnosis from 214's run: the harness copies the primary checkout's current .beads/issues.jsonl into a worktree when it creates one, rather than relying on whatever the base commit carried; CLAUDE.md's wording is corrected in the same change to say exactly what the export's freshness is. Done means a fresh worktree's export contains items admitted up to run start, the 209.12 case replayed finds its item and its named dependencies, and the instruction files' claim matches delivery.
notes:
Admitted to the backlog by the product manager in conversation chat-91253e0e070c17b0663651cc48602122, after turn 318.

Reason: In-run traceability reads this export, and a confidently wrong picture is worse than a stale one - the second incident cost a run its required inputs. The fix was dispositioned vaguely once; an item ends that.

Goal served: Maintain a traceable chain from the product brief through goals, designs, work, code changes, and verification.

description:

title: The harness sets GOCACHE for the runs it makes
description: The decision five reports across four items now ask for, made: developer-run sandboxes refuse the default Go build cache (~/Library/Caches/go-build - writes are granted only to the worktree, .git, and TMPDIR), so a plain make check fails at setup with 'operation not permitted', which reads as a broken toolchain. This breaks the minute-zero probe (184) first - the invariant that requires the probe is the thing the default breaks - and every run pays the rediscovery; exporting GOCACHE (and GOTMPDIR) into TMPDIR makes everything pass. The decision: the harness sets GOCACHE into the writable set for every run it makes - mechanical, not documentation - covering the developer probe and the harness's own check runner if it shares the profile. docs/developing-yoyo.md documents it for humans working outside the harness. Done means a fresh developer run's probe passes on a clean machine with no per-run discovery, the probe's failure message names the redirect for any environment the harness did not make, and the five reports' failure shape is unreproducible.
notes:

title: Stopping yoyo-status -L kills its background pipeline instead of orphaning it
description:
Operator-reported bug, 2026-08-31: running ./bin/yoyo-status -L and stopping with control-c returns the prompt but status lines keep printing. Diagnosed: follow-latest mode backgrounds each tail -F pipeline to switch when a newer run starts, and the only trap cleans temp files - nothing kills the backgrounded pipeline on interrupt, so it orphans and keeps writing to the terminal. Fix shape: trap INT and TERM to kill the current background pipeline (track its pid, or run children in a killable process group) before exiting.

The operator's related question, decided as the item's first step: the status fold (63) landed yoyo status --follow in the binary - the builder checks whether it covers follow-latest, and if it does, the right fix is retiring the script's -L in its favor rather than patching the shell. One fix, not both. Done means control-c on whichever surface survives leaves a quiet terminal, and if -L retires, the script says where the capability went.
notes:
Admitted to the backlog by the product manager in conversation chat-91253e0e070c17b0663651cc48602122, after turn 312.

Reason: A status surface that keeps talking after being told to stop fails the reader at the most literal level, and the check-63-first instruction may make the fix a retirement. Freeze-compatible: status-surface reliability.

Goal served: The harness's surfaces read clearly: boundaries between topics and speakers are visible, important findings stand out, every distinction survives a terminal that cannot render emphasis, and user-facing language chooses the ordinary, literal word over metaphor, coinage, or term of art.

Review summary: The change lands the opt-in parity soak machinery as an observation beside the legacy path: `execution.declarative_delivery` defaults off and is only readable from a project file (no bundle default, no harness default origin), a run created under it records a `workflow_instance_id` and steps the shipped delivery definition through doors whose `Perform` does nothing, and `workflow_divergence` records the first boundary where the run and the definition disagree. All four stated 'Done' conditions are met and evidenced: the opt-in is explicit and off by default (`internal/config/declarative_test.go`); the durable record is distinguishable and diffable — `declarative_test.go` drives eight real delivery paths with the trial on and holds each instance's checkpoint transcript against the same transcript the parity harness measures that trace by; legacy resumability is tested in both directions (`TestALegacyRunInFlightIsNeverMigratedIntoTheTrial` flips the flag on between a paused legacy run and its resume and asserts no instance is ever minted, and the converse test keeps an in-trial run observed after the flag is turned off), which holds because observation is settled from the run's own record and never from the resuming process's configuration; and the soak is left as the operator's post-landing step, as the item names. Delivery behaviour is untouched — the observation returns nothing, cannot fail a run, and drops its own save errors — and `observedDeliveryGraph` compiles the inert graph under the same `deliveryGrant()` and asserts digest equality with the shipped compile, so no configuration key widens authority and no integration decision moves. Documentation is reconciled rather than left stale: the new configuration section describes the flag, the two fields, the known expected divergence and the new-runs-only rule; the baseline document adds both durable fields to its gap list (which the mechanical disclosure check enforces) and amends the 'what the traces are of' paragraph; and the stale 'nothing walks through that door' comments in actions.go, workflow.go and execute.go are corrected. Checks pass: fmtcheck, test, race and vet, with the new tests exercising the new behaviour directly. One minor observation about how the soak is counted is below; it does not hold up the change.
Finding [minor] (internal/orchestrator/declarative.go:380): A run that ends by a route the definition has no outcome for — a review error that is not an operator stop, a `complete` that failed, or a worktree failure before the first developer attempt — is deliberately not observed, so its instance stays standing mid-graph while the run reaches a terminal status and no `workflow_divergence` is written. Since docs/configuration.md states the divergence field is 'the whole measure of the trial' and 'a clean soak is N real items observed with none of these', such a run reads as clean in exactly the way the code comments elsewhere warn against. Leaving the instance where it stands is the right call; consider also recording a divergence (or surfacing instance terminality on the summary) when a run reaches a terminal status with a non-terminal instance, so the soak's headline count cannot silently undercount.

title: Reviews read the cached prefix instead of rewriting it every time
description: From two identical developer findings on ifd.171's run, 2026-08-27, measured across 57 recorded runs on 2026-08-23/24: the harness's short one-shot provider invocations - the reviewer's above all - report cache_read_input_tokens of exactly 0 while each writes 10,000 to 160,000 tokens of fresh cache; roughly 130 of the 256 priced invocations in those windows. Every review pays the cache-write rate for a contract, persona, and invariant prefix identical across reviews that should read at the cached rate. This is why ifd.84's lever measured nothing, and it will defeat any later prompt-caching work the same way. Scope, per the reports: where cache_control breakpoints land in what the harness sends the Claude Code CLI for a review, and whether reviews are spaced beyond the cache TTL; fix so the stable prefix reads cached, verified by the cache-read share the ifd.171 tooling now reports moving off zero for review invocations. Done means review invocations show nonzero cache reads on the stable prefix, the per-review cost drops accordingly, and the measurement that proves it is quoted on this item.
notes:
Admitted to the backlog by the product manager in conversation chat-91253e0e070c17b0663651cc48602122, after turn 289.

Reason: Half the priced invocations are paying write rates for reads - a measured, recurring overspend on every review the loop runs, and the silent defeater of all caching work. Priority 2: real money at known scale, with the verification instrument (171) already shipped.

Goal served: The operator can see what the harness spends on their behalf: provider-reported cost, per work item, per run, and in total.

title: Codex's read-only claim matches what its sandbox prevents, or the descriptor stops claiming it
description: From the developer's warning on ifd.6's run, 2026-08-27: the Codex backend cannot hold the harness's read-only tool posture as defined. internal/backend/registry.go declares Codex holds both postures, and the adapter maps read-only to Codex's read-only sandbox - which stops writes and network but still lets the agent read the machine. The posture's stated purpose is preventing injected evidence from reading unrelated local files and sending them to a provider, and that is exactly what is not prevented. Decision needed, with the safety invariant in view: either the descriptor stops claiming read-only for Codex - capability validation then refuses reviewer-posture Codex assignments honestly - or the adapter achieves the posture's actual property, with sandboxForPosture (internal/backend/codex/backend.go) as the written-down difference. Done means the claim and the enforcement agree, whichever way, and a configuration selecting Codex for a read-only role gets what the posture promises or a refusal naming why. Note: the Codex adapter itself is parked (ifd.6); this item is the safety-claim reconciliation, which should not wait for the adapter's return since the registry's claim is live code.
notes:
Admitted to the backlog by the product manager in conversation chat-91253e0e070c17b0663651cc48602122, after turn 283.

Reason: A posture that claims a safety property it does not enforce is the goal's exact prohibition - the invariant made optional by a descriptor's optimism. Priority 2: the adapter is parked but the claim is in the registry now, and the fix may be one honest line.

Goal served: Keep roles, policies, and provider selection configurable without making safety invariants optional.

description: From four reports across three runs, 2026-08-30: the invariant loader treats docs/decisions/invariants/README.md as a constraint file and reports it unreadable - no frontmatter naming id, title, status, origin, revisions - in every run's delivered context, while docs/configuration.md states README.md in the invariants home is a directory index skipped rather than reported, the README itself says the same, and yoyo invariant create readme is refused. title: The status probe observes leases without acquiring them
description: From the developer's warning on ifd.194's run, 2026-08-31: the four-line status decides whether a persona turn is in flight by taking each conversation's advisory lease and releasing it immediately (internal/readmodel/standing.go, InFlight - the mechanism yoyo agent list already used). A yoyo chat or sink process attempting Hold during that instant is told the conversation is held by another process and refuses. The race pre-existed, but yoyo status and the hourly heartbeat now take these leases far more often, so the window is hit more. Fix shape from the report: a non-acquiring probe - fcntl F_GETLK, or a liveness stamp the holder writes - since flock-based leases cannot be inspected without acquiring. Done means observing in-flight state acquires nothing, a chat Hold cannot be refused by a status probe's instant, and the probe's answer stays truthful under the new frequency.
notes:
Admitted to the backlog by the product manager in conversation chat-91253e0e070c17b0663651cc48602122, after turn 283.

Reason: The status surface must not perturb what it observes - a heartbeat that occasionally locks the operator out of their own conversation is the observer breaking the system to describe it. Priority 2: the window is small but now hit hourly by design. Attributed to the legibility goal in its amended wording, pending the operator's approval of that revision; if the amendment is declined, the prior wording covers it identically.

Goal served: The harness's surfaces read clearly: boundaries between topics and speakers are visible, important findings stand out, every distinction survives a terminal that cannot render emphasis, and user-facing language chooses the ordinary, literal word over metaphor, coinage, or term of art.

Review summary: The change replaces the acquire-and-release probe with a liveness stamp: Hold writes a PID/timestamp stamp under the lock (refusing the hold if it cannot be stamped), Release removes it before dropping the lock, and InFlight reads the stamp and confirms the named process with a null signal, acquiring nothing. That satisfies all three parts of "done": observation takes nothing, a Hold can no longer be refused by a probe's instant, and the answer still tracks reality including the killed-holder case, where the stamp is reconciled against the operating system's own view. The evidence supports it: TestAConversationIsNeverRefusedByAProbe hammers Hold/Release against a spinning observer and would have failed under the old mechanism (flock conflicts across descriptors in one process), and the dead-holder, sibling-isolation, and undecodable-stamp cases are each covered. Failure remains a stated problem rather than a fabricated "in flight", and readmodel stays the single answer for both yoyo status and yoyo agent list, so the shared read model is not forked. Documentation is reconciled where it is visible: docs/operations.md, the readmodel package doc, the Conversations interface doc, and the agent.go comment all now describe an observed rather than taken hold, and the two known blind spots (a reused process identifier reading as held, and a pre-stamp build reading as free) are stated in the code rather than left implicit. Ordering is sound in both directions — the stamp exists only inside the lock's lifetime, so the residual windows are brief false negatives in the status rather than refusals of anybody's conversation. The new writes stay inside the runstate store's own root and follow the temp-create/rename/sync idiom already used in that package; no invariant I was given is contradicted, though the set shown to me is a selection rather than the whole.
Finding [minor] (internal/runstate/conversation_test.go:0): In the exitedProcess helper, GO_TEST_EXITED_PROCESS=1 is set on the child's environment but nothing ever reads it, so the line is inert and misleads a reader into looking for the other half. Also worth a sentence there about the residual flake: once Wait reaps the child the identifier is free for the kernel to hand out again, so on a busy host the returned identifier could belong to a live process by the time InFlight checks it, and the test would report a stale stamp as in flight. Dropping the unused environment line and noting the reuse window would leave the helper saying what it actually relies on.

title: Every provider spend is one durable log line at the moment it is known
description:
Operator direction, 2026-08-23, originally recorded as a reshape of ifd.83 - which turned out already closed, so this item carries the scope live; 83's record holds the phase-split history and the reshape note. His words: if we report them into a log, I'll worry about aggregation.

The deliverable is an append-only cost log, nothing more: every provider spend lands as one durable log line at the moment it is known - runs per phase (develop, review, repair, waits) and management-conversation turns alike. Each line carries: the persona or role; the amount with its known/unknown classification; the account alias and configuration revision; the work item or conversation id; and the timestamp. No aggregation is built - that stays the operator's, and any later read-model query builds on the same lines.

Done means every priced provider invocation in any harness process appends exactly one line with those fields at the moment its cost is known, unknown is classified as unknown rather than zero or omitted, and the log is append-only and durable. Standing role: the evidence prerequisite for model routing, which per-line data satisfies better than pre-built rollups. The phase-attribution properties ifd.172 pins apply to the lines this log writes; the exchange-store spend ifd.175 names is a line source like any other.

Review summary: The change delivers what ifd.182 asks for: a per-product append-only JSONL cost log under the state root, one line per provider invocation written at the moment the invocation returns, carrying role and configured agent, phase, amount with an explicit known/unknown classification, account alias and configuration revision, exactly one subject (run — with the work item where there is one — conversation, exchange, or branch review), backend, requested and resolved model, and timestamp, with no aggregation built on top. Making the meter a provider wrapper rather than a step callers take afterwards is what makes 'exactly one line, including when the invocation failed' a property rather than a convention, and the new CostReported flag correctly separates 'priced at nothing' from 'never priced' rather than collapsing both to zero. Wiring covers the developer's first attempt and repairs, run reviews, branch reviews, conversation turns, and exchange rounds, and each has a test that would fail without the change; the whole-run repair test in internal/orchestrator/spend_test.go is the one that actually pins phase attribution against the run's repair counter rather than asserting it by construction. The store's validation refuses an unattributable line, a corrupt log fails the read rather than silently dropping lines, and docs/reporting.md gains a section that matches the implementation and explicitly leaves the existing yoyo cost prices unchanged. The handed-back repair scope is resolved — make fmtcheck, test, race, and vet all pass. No delivered invariant is violated: the log lives outside the repository beside the other runstate stores, adds no operator surface or private state, introduces no second invoker or promotion path, and it strengthens durable-state-is-provider-independent by pinning every invocation to backend, model, account alias, and configuration revision with the session id as evidence only. The observations below are minor and none of them blocks.
Finding [minor] (docs/reporting.md:188): The new documentation asserts closure — 'every process the harness runs appends to it' — but nothing enforces that a future provider invocation site goes through spend.Metered rather than straight at a backend, and an unmetered site would record nothing and look exactly like a process that spent nothing. This repository already has the enforcement pattern for precisely this shape of claim (docs/reporting.md cites the sweep in internal/execution/terminal_test.go as what keeps the set of terminal writers closed). Consider an equivalent sweep over backend.Run call sites so the claim in the doc has a test behind it; while doing so, confirm no invocation reachable from internal/research or any non-claudecode backend plugin was missed, since only claudecode/parser.go sets CostReported and any other plugin would silently classify every invocation unknown.
Finding [minor] (internal/chat/chat.go:509): Reply.SpendProblem is populated and accumulated across rounds, but no hunk in this change renders it anywhere an operator reads, and no test covers it reaching one. It mirrors ReportProblem, so it is probably carried by the same path — worth confirming the chat surface prints it, because the whole justification for the conversation's RecordFailure exception is that the operator is told what the log did not take, and a field nothing displays makes that silence again.
Finding [minor] (internal/orchestrator/pipeline.go:1830): On the run path Metered has no RecordFailure, so any line the store refuses now fails the developer or reviewer invocation on a path that previously could not fail for bookkeeping reasons. The attribution there comes from persisted run state (a.state.AccountAlias, a.state.ConfigRevision), and the store validates both against accountAliasPattern/configRevisionPattern — so a resumed run whose stored state carries an empty or non-conforming value would fail every invocation rather than recording an unattributable spend. title: The sink politely refuses unknown senders, once per thread
description:
Operator item, 2026-08-23, slotted after multi-account pooling in the order (link follows). When someone NOT in the operators mapping interacts with a sink-opened thread or @mentions the app, the sink replies with a polite refusal naming who to contact - his words: I don't know you. Please reach out to {operator(s)} if you need something - with the names resolved from the configured operators mapping. One rule, his: the reply happens no more than once per thread, so an unknown user cannot make the app chatty by repeated attempts - subsequent unknown-user messages in the same thread are recorded and ignored.

Builder notes from the operator: the identity check already exists - the directive path resolves senders against the operators mapping, and unknown senders are silently ignored today - so this adds a first-refusal reply and a per-thread said-it-already mark, fitting the sink's durable-cursor discipline. Reconcile with the architect's acknowledgment-scope ruling (replies only in sink-opened work-item threads, silence outside): this refusal is the one deliberate exception for unknown senders inside sink-opened threads and for @mentions, and the exception is stated in the design so it does not read as a violation.

Done means an unknown sender gets exactly one refusal per thread naming the mapped operators, repeats are recorded and ignored, known senders are unaffected, and the design states the exception.

Reason: The channel's identity boundary made polite: silence teaches a stranger nothing and repeated refusals teach them the app is a toy - one refusal naming the door is the correct middle. Sequenced after pooling per the operator; the link lands once this id exists.

title: A governed-document defect fails its owner's gate, not every developer's build
description: From the developer's warning on ifd.85's gates, 2026-08-23: the new repository-coupled gates make goals and artifact-chain integrity build-breaking - and if a goal is ever written hard-wrapped, or a design acquires a dangling supports entry, make test goes red for every developer run while no developer can fix it: docs/product, docs/designs, and docs/decisions are refused in their diffs, so the only route is an amendment proposal while every run stays red. The check-that-fights-you failure mode, arriving from the owner side. Scope: a governed-document defect surfaces where its owner acts - the gate's failure names the owning role and the amendment path, and either the red is scoped so developer runs on unrelated work proceed, or the failure routes as an escalation to the owner with the build distinguishing 'your change broke this' from 'a document you cannot touch broke this'. Owners also need to know their edits are build-breaking: the artifact-home READMEs (125.5) state it. Done means an owner-side document defect cannot stall unrelated developer work, the failure names its owner and route, and the gates' enforcement value is kept - the defect still fails loudly somewhere someone can act.
notes:
Admitted to the backlog by the product manager in conversation chat-91253e0e070c17b0663651cc48602122, after turn 230.

Reason: Gates that enforce the chain by stalling everyone on defects only owners can fix convert traceability into a denial of service on the whole loop; the wrapped-goal incident already proved the defect class occurs. Priority 2: not yet fired in anger, but the first occurrence stalls everything at once.

Goal served: Maintain a traceable chain from the product brief through goals, designs, work, code changes, and verification.

title: Reconcile re-asks the forge about a failed run's publication
description: From the developer's warning on ifd.69's run, 2026-08-23: nothing in the harness ever re-asks the forge about the publication of a run that failed without integrating - settleQueuedMerge covers only runs with a queued merge, so such records keep whatever state they held when the run died. Live consequences on this machine: ifd.1.5's PR #46 and ifd.102.4's PR #96 are recorded OPEN and unmerged while the work demonstrably landed through them; that stale record is what stops the orphan sweep closing #44 and #98, and it silently misleads anything reading a publication's state. Scope: reconcile queries the forge for the publication state of failed runs' recorded PRs and updates the record - merged, closed, open - so downstream evidence (the orphan sweep, the docket, status surfaces) reads truth. This is the evidence-widening follow-up the ifd.69 criterion amendment explicitly reserved for the operator's request; the mechanism arriving with named casualties is that request's case made. Done means the two stale records read correctly after a reconcile, orphans #44 and #98 become closeable by the sweep, and a failed run's publication can never again hold its death-moment state forever.
notes:
Admitted to the backlog by the product manager in conversation chat-91253e0e070c17b0663651cc48602122, after turn 227.

Reason: Publication records that freeze at a run's death make the forge's truth and the harness's records diverge permanently, and the divergence is already blocking the orphan sweep on two named PRs. Priority 2 with the publishing hygiene it completes.

title: Every artifact home gets a README: purpose, owner, and the hand-edit policy
description:
Operator request for the installer epic, 2026-08-23. Each artifact home under docs gets a brief README.md stating three things: the directory's purpose, which agent owns it, and whether the operator may edit files by hand - including whether hand edits require informing any agent. Written by yoyo init for new applications; checked and repaired by doctor for existing ones.

Ground facts for the builder: the artifact contract already exempts README.md in any artifact home from governance (the ifd.87 decision - indexes are navigation, not authority), so these files are the sanctioned place for exactly this prose. The homes and owners: product and goals (product manager); designs and decisions (architect); invariants (architect, its own scheme). The hand-edit answer is already governed and the READMEs state it rather than invent one: a non-owner proposes an amendment rather than editing; an operator hand edit lands as an unauthorized revision the artifact system reports rather than refuses; staleness detection catches downstream drift.

Also resolved by this: docs/product/goals/README.md's standing shape warning (it opens with its goals) disappears when it is rewritten to this template - purpose first, pointers after. Done means init writes the READMEs for a new application, doctor reports and repairs missing or divergent ones on existing applications, each states the three things from the governed facts above, and the goals README warning no longer fires.

title: The architect states whether repository confinement binds operator-invoked shell tooling
description: EXECUTOR: conversation:architect. From the reviewer's warning on ifd.156, 2026-08-23: it is unclear whether the repository-writes-are-physically-confined invariant binds operator-invoked shell tooling. scripts/release-notes.sh writes docs/releases/<tag>.md with mkdir -p and cp outside the shared safe-write primitive, guarding with a check-then-use symlink test - the exact pattern the invariant's own rationale names as insufficient - and the Makefile and cut-release.sh already perform direct repository-scoped writes into dist/. The reviewer did not treat it as a violation because the invariant was established (ifd.136) against the harness's Go writers of agent output. The architect states the boundary in docs/decisions/invariants: either the invariant reaches shell tooling - making the release scripts non-conforming, with remediation items to follow - or it deliberately does not, with the reasoning recorded. Done means the boundary is stated where the invariant lives, not inferred per-review.
notes:
Admitted to the backlog by the product manager in conversation chat-91253e0e070c17b0663651cc48602122, after turn 224.

Reason: An invariant whose scope each reviewer infers independently will be enforced inconsistently and eroded politely; the boundary is the architect's to state, one conversation, recorded where the invariant lives. Marked conversation-executed - field set, per my twice-learned lesson.

Goal served: Keep roles, policies, and provider selection configurable without making safety invariants optional.
Architect ruling, 2026-08-31: confinement binds harness-owned writers only - code paths the harness invokes as itself; operator-invoked tooling in bin/ and scripts/ is the operator acting, same trust position as their editor, and a boundary against them would be unenforceable. Two bounds: the test is who invokes it, not where it lives - a script the harness invokes is a harness-owned writer wherever it sits and passes through the safe-write primitive or does not ship; and the confinement design's deferred structural check is scoped to harness Go code. One sentence folds into the confinement design's contract section at her next transcription batch: the contract binds harness-owned writers, meaning code paths the harness invokes as itself; operator-invoked tooling is the operator acting.

title: The declared checks cover what the repository is made of, not only Go
description: From the developer's warning on ifd.156, 2026-08-23: the four declared checks (make fmtcheck, test, race, vet) cover Go only, so a change made entirely of shell, Markdown, Makefile, or workflow YAML passes every gate a run applies with nothing having exercised it - ifd.156 was exactly that shape, and its two proving suites (scripts/cut-release-test.sh, scripts/release-notes-test.sh) run only in CI after integration. Scope: the shell suites join make check or the declared checks list directly, and the checks list is audited against the repository's actual composition - shell, markdown (ifd.159's checker), YAML - so a run's gates exercise what a run can change. Composes with the admission practice recorded on the root the same day: done-means evidence belongs in declared checks, and this is the checks side of that bargain. Done means a shell-only change cannot pass a run unexercised, the two release suites run pre-integration, and the checks list names each content class the repository carries or records why not.
notes:
Admitted to the backlog by the product manager in conversation chat-91253e0e070c17b0663651cc48602122, after turn 221.

Reason: A gate that exercises none of what a change contains delegates the whole verdict to a reviewer reading, which is the expensive judgment checks exist to spare; the release scripts the daily cadence runs are the sharpest current case. Priority 2 beside the markdown checker; together they close the non-Go gate gap.

title: A duplicate provider terminal result relaunches like any transient death
description: From the development manager's warning, 2026-08-23: run-e2b8d016 (ifd.117.1) failed mid-development with 'parse Claude Code stream: second provider terminal result received after terminal result' - a duplicate terminal from the provider treated as a run-fatal parse error, throwing away a near-complete change. The work was recovered by triage rerun from the preserved branch, at triage-grant price. The parser should treat a duplicate terminal result as the transient-relaunch class - the self-retry machinery already relaunches provider deaths within a durable budget - rather than as fatal. Done means a duplicate terminal result relaunches under the existing attempt budget with the anomaly recorded, the e2b8d016 case replayed completes without triage, and genuinely malformed streams still fail with the parse error named.
notes:
Admitted to the backlog by the product manager in conversation chat-91253e0e070c17b0663651cc48602122, after turn 221.

Reason: Provider-dialect drift killing runs is the verdict-drift lesson in the stream parser: another process's output evolving is a relaunch condition, not a fatality. Priority 2: the triage rerun contains the damage today, at a price the self-retry class exists to avoid.

Review summary: The change does what the work item asked. The parser no longer treats a second terminal `result` envelope as a fatal parse error; it emits the whole duplicate envelope as an anomaly event (`"anomaly":"duplicate_terminal_result"`) so the drifted dialect is diagnosable, and `Result()` reports the invocation as a `backend.TransientFailure` — the existing self-retry class — while leaving the decided terminal's session, model, cost, and final text intact so the guarded invariant that a duplicate cannot replace the first terminal still holds. Deciding in `Result()` rather than at the moment the duplicate arrives is the right seam given that a usage limit is re-reported as it changes, and the exclusivity with the two wait-answered refusals (`UsageLimit`, `ServerOverload`) is tested in both directions, including the case where the limit lifts after the duplicate. The e2b8d016 stream is replayed as a test that would fail without the change, and the two removed `second provider terminal result` cases in TestRunRejectsMalformedOrIncompleteStream leave the genuinely-unreadable cases still asserting the named parse error. README.md, docs/configuration.md, and docs/operations.md are all updated in the same place the transient-relaunch class is described, so no document in front of me still asserts that a duplicate terminal fails the run. None of the six supplied invariants is touched: no filesystem writes, no role invoking another, no promotion lease, no surface state, and the anomaly is recorded in the run's own event log rather than left in the provider session. Checks (fmtcheck, test, race, vet) all pass, and the new tests exercise the new behavior rather than merely compiling past it. One minor observation below about an interaction the change does not discuss.
Finding [minor] (internal/backend/claudecode/parser.go:670): The relaunch exclusion covers only UsageLimit and ServerOverload, so a stream whose first terminal is a 4xx `api_error` followed by a duplicate now sets TransientFailure and relaunches, where docs/operations.md and README.md still say a 4xx `api_error` "fails the run exactly as it always did". This is defensible under the change's own thesis (neither ending can be trusted to be the invocation's verdict) and is bounded by the attempt budget, but it is untested and undiscussed, and it means a permanently-refused request can now burn the run's whole relaunch budget before failing. Worth either a test pinning the intended answer for that combination or a sentence in the comment on Result() saying the 4xx refusal is deliberately not excluded.

title: Decomposition from a failed run records the parent's landing as a dependency
description: From the developer's warning on ifd.100.1's run, 2026-08-23: child items carved from a failed run's deferral are based on main while the parent's change is unmerged, leaving them with no substrate - 100.1 assumes internal/artifact/write.go and internal/chat/document.go, which exist only on the failed run's branch (PR #174, open, repair budget spent), and nothing in the carved item records that prerequisite, so it reads as ready. Scope: when the development manager decomposes follow-on work from a failed or deferred run, the children carry a dependency on the parent's change landing - by whatever vehicle: the preserved branch cherry-picked, the PR revived, or the substrate rebuilt - and an item assuming files that exist only on an unmerged branch is never tracker-ready. Done means the 100.1 case replayed produces a child gated on its substrate, and the DM's decomposition practice records the rule. Separate question routed with this item for the DM and operator: what becomes of PR #174 itself, whose review assessed the mechanism favourably before the budget ran out - revival may be cheaper than rebuilding.
notes:

Reason: An item that reads ready while its substrate sits on an unmerged branch is the selection-soundness family again, upstream of the scheduler: the queue lied about readiness at decomposition time. Priority 2 - 100.1 is already gated by the DM's link and 155 makes such links bind, so the acute case is contained; this fixes the practice that created it.

The human's routine interface is the product manager: they state intent, approve the brief and goals, and answer questions the product manager escalates. Directing the architect, development manager, developer, or reviewer individually is available for inspection, recovery, and override, but is not part of the normal loop.

title: Reports reach the product manager's rhythm without a human courier
description:
The moral of the 2026-08-23 relay, made structural: agent reports reach triage today only when a human reads the channel and carries one to the product manager - the operator noticed this seam by reading a report and asking what becomes of them. The product manager cannot read the report stream at all: its evidence is the specifications, Beads state, and the shipped-surface documentation; the report store is outside it, so a standing rhythm of reading reports is impossible rather than neglected.

The shape: recent unhandled reports surface in the product manager's briefing or through a bounded read action, the way the queue surfaces through survey - severity-ordered, with enough identity to act on (reporter, item, run). The one-service read model (139) may be the natural carrier; the builder decides the vehicle. Done means a report filed by any role is visible to the product manager's next conversation without anyone carrying it, acted-on reports are distinguishable from unseen ones, and the courier seam is closed.

title: A cheap, safe daily release: one verb wrapping tag, build, checksums, gated on the walkthrough

Done means cutting a release is one invocation from a green walkthrough to a tagged build with checksums, a red walkthrough refuses the cut with the failure named, and the daily cadence costs minutes, not ceremony. description:
Operator request, 2026-08-22: emoji reactions on a thread's opening message reflect the item's current status - working, completed, and by extension blocked and in-review - so the channel reads as a status board without opening a single thread. title: Threads narrate handoffs and name whose move is next
description: Operator request, 2026-08-22, from reading his work-item threads. The handoff class of event has no representation: tonight's brief-promotion item was selected, mis-run, triaged, rerouted to the architect's conversation, and worked to completion there, and its thread would have shown none of that journey. The shape: when an item is handed off to a role's conversation, the thread says so; when that role starts the work, that too; and generally, when a thread goes quiet, its last message names what happens next and whose move it is - a thread's silence should never leave the reader guessing who holds the ball. This matters more as the executor-marker work (144) makes conversation-executed items a first-class kind whose transitions are exactly these events. Done means handoff and pickup events post to the item's thread, a thread that goes quiet ends on a whose-move message, and the brief-promotion journey replayed reads complete in its thread.
