title: A thread never opens on a bare id: tracker actions carry titles, the sink resolves the rest
description:
Bug from the operator's screenshot, 2026-08-22, beside the titles-not-ids item (68.15): the thread the sink opened for the parked Codex adapter says only 'yoyodyne-ifd.6' - no title. Mechanism verified in code: openThread deliberately names topics with titles (its own comment: an identifier alone is a name somebody has to resolve), and titles reach topics from the event that first mentions the item - admissions carry created.Title, run crossings carry the work item title. But this item predates Slack, so its first-ever mention was Friday's reprioritization, and reprioritize events carry no title; WithTitle of the empty string leaves the topic bare and the header falls back to the naked id. Every old item whose first channel appearance is a priority change, a link, or a note opens the same way - the reconciliation's parking moves make this a live class.

Fix shape, two halves that also serve 68.15: every tracker-action record carries the item title the way admissions already do; and the sink resolves a missing title from the tracker before opening a thread rather than posting the bare id. Done means a thread opened by any event kind carries the item's title, the Codex-adapter case replayed opens readable, and no event kind can produce a bare-id thread.

Review decision: repair
Review summary: The pooling mechanism itself is sound and well evidenced: aliases resolve to per-account provider homes through one rule (config.AccountConfigDirectory) that the harness, doctor, and bin/yoyo-account all read the same way; the rotation cursor and weekly-budget spend are derived from the run records rather than a second ledger; a run chooses its account once before the item is claimed and every later invocation (repair attempts, the review) reads the alias back off the record; and a single-account project is left byte-for-byte unchanged. Those parts have tests at the config, runstate, claudecode, cli, and orchestrator layers that would fail without the change, and fmtcheck/test/race/vet all pass. Two things block approval. First, docs/configuration.md — amended by this change — still asserts that an agent whose entry names an `account` runs under that one and nothing chooses at run time, but under a pool Pipeline.chooseAccount consults only the rotation and both the developer and reviewer invocations read the run-level alias, so a per-agent `account` is silently ignored for runs and only governs conversations. Second, the ~118 lines of new doctor account checking — which is the acceptance criterion's own verification path ("its output leaves doctor able to verify each configured alias authenticates") — has no test at all, including the non-obvious Pooled() gate that suppresses it entirely for a single-account project. Two minor observations accompany these.
Finding [major] (docs/configuration.md:2722): docs/configuration.md now claims, under "Pooling work across several accounts": "**Which roles run where is still yours.** An agent whose entry names an `account` runs under that one and nothing chooses at run time; the pool is what serves the agents that name none." That is false for runs. Pipeline.chooseAccount (internal/orchestrator/pipeline.go) asks only the AccountChooser, which rotates the active half without any agent input, and activeRun.account() serves both the developer attempts and the review from the run-level alias. Config.AgentAccountAlias — whose own doc comment says it answers for conversations — is consulted only by chat.go and exchange.go. So an operator who pins `agents.developer.account: work` under a pool gets runs served by whatever the rotation chose, with no error and no diagnostic. Resolve it in one of two ways: either honour the developer agent's configured account when a fresh run chooses (and say explicitly what happens when the reviewer agent names a different one, given the run-level affinity the design relies on), or amend this bullet to state that under a pool a per-agent `account` governs that agent's conversations only and runs are served by the rotation.
Finding [major] (internal/doctor/doctor.go:619): The new account diagnosis in internal/doctor has no test. checkAccounts/checkAccount add five distinct outcomes (state root unresolvable, endpoint unresolvable, claude absent, alias not authenticated, alias authenticated) plus a gate — `if !resolved.Config.Pooled() { return nil }` — that silently suppresses the whole check for a single-account project, and every other new file in this change ships with a paired test. This is the path the work item names as the operator's verification ("its output leaves doctor able to verify each configured alias authenticates"), so the passing check results do not currently support the claim that it works. Add a doctor test over a pooled configuration with a fake runner where one alias reports loggedIn and another does not, asserting the `account:<alias>` findings, their statuses, and that the remedy for the unauthenticated alias is the login for that alias's own provider home.
Finding [minor] (internal/config/accounts.go:130): Config.Endpoint under a pool returns AccountConfigDirectory(stateRoot, alias), which yields "" for every alias when stateRoot is empty. A Pipeline built with a pooled config and no StateRoot would therefore invoke every account against the machine's single provider home while recording distinct aliases on each run — exactly the silent misattribution internal/backend/claudecode/account_test.go was written to prevent. No production caller does this today (run.go passes parts.stateRoot), but consider refusing an empty state root under a pool rather than degrading to the machine home.
Finding [minor] (bin/yoyo-account:1): bin/yoyo-account is added with mode 100644, so `./bin/yoyo-account` fails with permission denied even though the script's own usage header advertises `yoyo-account --alias personal` and `yoyo-account --list`. The README works around it with `bash bin/yoyo-account`. Either add the executable bit (bin/yoyo-status is the precedent) or make the help text show the `bash` form. While there: the usage header documents --alias, --list, and --check but omits --pool, which the argument parser accepts.

title: Human-facing Slack messages speak in titles and plain sentences, not ids
description:
Operator feedback, 2026-08-20, from reading the channel; his example was the priority-change message for the dropped-merge re-arm. Three faults, near verbatim: opaque ids (yoyodyne-ifd.102.7, bare 133) should carry human-friendly names in human-facing messages; the copy could be more concise; the trailing conversation id is not useful to him at all. His explicit boundary: ids and slugs are fine in agent-to-agent communication - they leave human-facing surfaces only.

The shape: the sink's rendering layer resolves work item ids to their titles when speaking to the channel ('the dropped-merge re-arm' rather than yoyodyne-ifd.102.7); leans on thread structure for identity - one thread per work item already names the subject (the 118 headers), so messages inside it need not repeat the id; drops conversation ids from rendered messages entirely, the durable records keeping them for anyone tracing; and tightens copy generally - reasoning that justifies a decision in the tracker is one sentence in the channel, with the record holding the whole. That last clause applies to tracker-originated prose such as reprioritization reasons, whose full text stays in the record.

Done means channel messages name work in words a human reads without resolving anything, no conversation id renders, thread-interior messages carry no repeated item id, and a decision message is a sentence pointing at a record, verified against the operator's quoted example replayed.

title: A dropped queued merge is a durable event, said at warning, and counted by the heartbeat
description:
From the operator's question about today's silently dropped merges, 2026-08-20: four terminal runs' queued merges were refused when origin moved and waited hours unannounced, because the failure has no existence in the reporting language - the merge lifecycle records only queued and completed crossings, both notes; the outstanding-publication state is inferred at read time by status and reconcile rather than recorded when the drop happens, so there is no durable event for the sink to say; and the recovery verb was never built (102.7, promoted alongside, is that verb's self-heal).

Scope, riding the machinery 68.10 and 68.12 built: a queued merge that is refused or dropped is recorded as a durable event at the moment it happens, and the sink says it at warning severity with channel broadcast. Plus the resurface path, folded in here because 68.11 closed before it could carry the note: the idle heartbeat's summary includes outstanding publications - N promotions awaiting the forge - so even a missed event reappears on the next quiet tick.

Done means a drop is recorded when it happens rather than inferred when someone asks, the channel says it at warning with broadcast, the heartbeat counts outstanding promotions in its quiet summary, and today's four-silent-hours case replayed produces an announcement at drop time and a count until resolution.

title: A triage carry-out refused for capacity waits or hands off, never fails
description:
Fourth face of the triage carry-out seam, 2026-08-20, beside yoyodyne-ifd.134. Carrying out the DM's recorded rerun for yoyodyne-ifd.68.13 - item reopened first, per the trap 131 fixed - the launch was refused with 'reserve developer run: developer capacity is full: 2 active runs, limit 2', and because the watch session's binary predates 131's fix, that refusal likely spent the carry-out budget as well. The shape: a triage carry-out that meets full capacity waits for a slot or hands the item to the scheduler - the DM's authorization does not expire because two developers happened to be busy at that second. Done means a capacity-refused carry-out queues or hands off with the state said plainly, the authorization survives until executed or explicitly withdrawn, and no budget is spent by a capacity refusal (131's rule, extended to this refusal class).

Placement fact rather than urgency: the item was reopened first, so the scheduler selects 68.13 from the open pool anyway - the recovery arrives, only the ceremony failed. That workaround-by-reopening becoming the de facto recovery path is itself evidence for 134's one-source-of-truth scope: the ceremony and the pool must agree about what is authorized, or the ceremony atrophies into decoration.
notes:
Admitted to the backlog by the product manager in conversation chat-91253e0e070c17b0663651cc48602122, after turn 181.

Reason: A recorded triage authorization that fails on transient capacity makes the DM's decision weaker than an ordinary scheduler poll - the hierarchy's recovery role losing to timing. Priority 2 beside ifd.134 per the operator's placement, with the reopen-workaround evidence cross-recorded there in spirit; not urgent because the open pool delivers the recovery anyway, which is exactly why the ceremony must not quietly become decoration.

Goal served: Run development nearly autonomously. The human's routine interface is the product manager: they state intent, approve the brief and goals, and answer questions the product manager escalates. Directing the architect, development manager, developer, or reviewer individually is available for inspection, recovery, and override, but is not part of the normal loop.

title: Slack speaker names carry the product: 'Development Manager (yoyodyne)'
description:
Operator request, 2026-08-20, verbatim intent: speaker names include the product - 'Development Manager (yoyodyne)' - because an operator with more than one product in development will get confused about which harness is talking. Near-term teeth: a second product (context-conductor) already exists in the state directory, the installer epic's secret-namespacing assumes several harnesses coexisting, and if two products ever share a channel the speaker name is the only disambiguator the message carries.

Governance boundary, recorded: the who-speaks rule - avatars may change pictures but never names or attribution - is not excepted here. This is a refinement of the name's rendered form, applied uniformly by the voice layer to every speaker including the harness, with the product id taken from config, never authored per message. Done means every posted speaker name carries its product suffix uniformly, the id comes from config, attribution is untouched, and two harnesses in one channel are distinguishable at a glance.

title: A triage rerun refused pre-flight spends no budget: pre-flight before the counter
description:
Bug admission requested by the development manager, 2026-08-20, exercised for the first time an hour ago and worked around by hand. The sequence on yoyodyne-ifd.125.1: her recorded re-run's first carry-out was refused because the item's status was blocked - the standing 102.5 seam - and the second was refused by the once-only guard, whose own message stated the contradiction: already re-run, and no fresh run was recorded for it. So any triage rerun of a blocked item burns its once-per-stoppage budget on the refusal unless someone remembers to reopen first - a remembered step of the kind being eliminated everywhere else.

Her fix shape, recorded on 102.5 and 102.2 for the builders: run the pre-flight checks - status, terminal record, hold - before the counter increment, so only a launch that actually records a run spends the budget; increment-before-act crash safety stays for everything past pre-flight. Done means a rerun refused at pre-flight leaves the budget unspent and says why it was refused, a rerun that passes pre-flight spends the budget exactly as today, and the 125.1 sequence replayed launches on the first unrefused attempt.

title: Warning and critical thread replies also broadcast to the channel
description:
Operator request, 2026-08-20, from reading the channel. Run lifecycle messages live as thread replies, which the main channel view hides by design - right for routine notes, but a warning or an error can sit unseen inside a thread while the channel looks quiet. The rule: severity note stays thread-only; severity warning and critical use Slack's also-send-to-channel functionality - the reply_broadcast flag on chat.postMessage - so they appear in the main channel view as well as inside their work item's thread. The severity model already in the envelope does all the work; no new judgment anywhere.

Pairs with 68.10: an out-of-tokens park at warning that nobody sees inside a thread would repeat the ten-silent-hours lesson at a different layer. Done means note replies stay thread-only, warning and critical replies broadcast, and the channel view shows exactly the messages whose severity says someone should see them without opening threads.

title: Design the one-pane-of-glass architecture: supervision tree, ownership, brake escalation
description:
First child of yoyodyne-ifd.130, the architect's design, per the operator's explicit ask that this be reviewed with her rather than shaped by the product manager alone. Three questions the design answers: the supervision tree - how yoyo chat spawns and supervises the scheduling loop and the Slack sink, and what happens to each when the chat exits; what the chat owns versus what survives it - which residents die with the pane and which persist, and how a returning chat reattaches to what survived; and the brake's escalate-into-conversation flow - how an automatic intake hold becomes a decision the product manager raises in the chat with triage and a recommendation attached, answered in conversation, while the terminal-side release (ifd.129) remains the path that works with no chat open.

Also in scope, the recorded collision with the installer epic: 125.3's start-on-login sink service and this epic's chat-supervised sink are two answers to the same residency question - the design says how they compose or which owns which case, before 125.3 builds the service. And the conversation-lease seam: the operator's console and the operator's assistant must both be able to reach the product manager; the single-holder lock stays correct for provider sessions.

Done means the design is recorded in the architect's home, the implementation children of ifd.130 can each cite the section they build, and the 125.3 residency question has one answer.

title: One pane of glass: yoyo chat is the entry point and the PM manages the rest
description:
Operator direction, 2026-08-20, his words: start up yoyo with the chat and have the PM manage the rest. The chat is the one entry point; it spawns and supervises the resident subprocesses - the scheduling loop, and the Slack sink whenever Slack is configured and available - so nothing else must be remembered, started, or left running. The operator watches the backlog alongside the PM conversation: a live queue view with the release and run verbs present. Holds never wait on a remembered command: the brake surfaces in the chat as a decision the product manager raises with triage and a recommendation attached, answered in conversation, rather than parking silently behind a command that does not exist at the terminal.

The seam this resolves structurally: the operator's open chat window held the conversation lease, so the harness could not relay to the product manager until his console closed - the single-holder lock is correct for provider sessions, but the operator's console and the operator's assistant must both be able to reach the product manager, and today they cannot.

First child is the architect's design, per the operator's explicit ask: the supervision tree, what the chat owns versus what survives it, and the brake's escalate-into-conversation flow. Implementation children follow from her design. Beside the installer epic (noted there): both serve the same first-hour-of-use story - install smoothly, then one command from there on.

Second, the README now promises reachability that the code does not deliver on the one path the item names: openChat still takes the conversation with the refusing Claim, so a harness relay via `yoyo chat --message` hard-fails with ErrConversationHeld whenever the product manager is mid-turn, and a turn may run to the 15-minute timeout. I checked the change against both supplied invariants (one-promotion-per-target-branch, selected-work-passes-intake-and-records-why) and found nothing that touches either; that is the selected pair only, not the whole set, and no invariant file is created, amended or retired here. The item names no protected-path grant and the change edits no granted path.
Finding [major] (internal/chat/chat.go:1573): The change delivers only the conversation-lease seam and none of the work item's named deliverables: chat spawning and supervising the resident subprocesses (the scheduling loop, and the Slack sink when Slack is configured and available), the live queue view with the release and run verbs present, and the brake surfacing in the chat as a decision the product manager raises with triage and a recommendation attached. The item also states that the first child is the architect's design and that implementation children follow from it; this change is implementation with no design behind it and creates no such children. Approving as-is would close ifd.130 with most of its subject undone. Either attach this delivery to a child item scoped to the conversation-hold seam and leave ifd.130 open behind the design child the operator asked for, or complete the remaining deliverables in this change.
Finding [major] (internal/cli/chat.go:370): The README asserts that `yoyo chat --message` in another terminal, anything else the harness runs, and a second `yoyo chat` left open beside the first "all reach the same product manager without you closing anything", and that "what they take turns over is the turn itself". That is not what the code does at the moment of opening: openChat calls store.Claim, which delegates to the refusing Hold and returns ErrConversationHeld when a turn is in flight. So the harness relay — the exact case the work item names as the seam being closed — still fails outright rather than waiting, for as long as the product manager's turn runs, which may be the full 15-minute defaultTurnTimeout. Either have the opening claim wait the way ConversationHold.Retake already does (at least for the single-message path, which is what the harness and the operator's assistant use), or correct the README so it states that opening is refused while a turn is in flight and only the already-open conversation takes turns.
Finding [minor] (internal/chat/chat.go:497): Session.adopt now discards and rebuilds s.proposals from the durable record via restoredProposal on every prompt of an interactive conversation, but no test covers a proposal raised in an interactive turn being approved at the following prompt. The existing chat tests construct options without a Hold, so they never reach reload at all, and none of the new tests in reachable_test.go exercise the propose-then-approve flow across a put-down. A test that raises a proposal, lets the prompt put the conversation down and take it back, then approves it, would pin the one shared behaviour this change routes through a new path.

title: yoyo-status -c groups the cost report by day with daily totals
description:
Operator request, 2026-08-20. yoyo-status -c groups the cost report by day in the local timezone. At the end of each day's group it gives that day's total spend; the current day's group totals at the end of the list. Done means runs and conversations appear under their local-timezone day, each completed day closes with its total, the current day totals at the list's end, and the existing per-run lines within a group keep their shape.

Relation: ifd.63 folds yoyo-status into the yoyo CLI behind a status verb, and the recorded format decision on ifd.51 makes -c's output shape the reference rendering for the Go verb family. This grouping is therefore part of the reference shape once built: the fold inherits it rather than re-deciding it, and yoyo cost's convergence on the -c shape (also recorded on ifd.51) picks up the same day grouping.

metadata.yoyodyne_goal_recorded: A newcomer can go from the documented install to a working first run on their own repository using the readme alone.

title: The installer: a smooth path from nothing to a working, verified, self-repairing setup
description:
Operator-approved epic, 2026-08-20. The new-user run is rougher than it should be; smooth the full path. Four layered children, discussed and agreed:

(1) A thin bootstrap script - the only part outside the binary, because its job is fetching the binary: platform detection, release download or go install, PATH placement with the shell-profile line named, and the two hard prerequisites (bd, claude) checked and installed-or-named.

(2) yoyo setup - interactive, idempotent, resumable, wrapping what exists (bd init, yoyo init with check proposals and the Dolt remote) and offering the optional tier: the Slack walk (manifest, tokens into the keychain per the documented recipe, config section) and a start-on-login service for the sink - launchd agent on macOS running the keychain-launcher wrapper, systemd user unit on Linux - so the sink survives reboots without a terminal.

(3) yoyo doctor - the verb the design's CLI table has promised since Milestone 0: the forever-after verifier. Binary versions against records (it would have caught the 2026-08-20 stale-sink outage), PATH, bd reachable, config valid, checks runnable, Slack config versus tokens versus sink actually running, service loaded, forge auth - every finding carrying its remedy as a runnable command.

(4) The skill - doctor --json emits findings-with-remedies structured for any agent to act on, plus a short shipped prompt document so a newcomer's own Claude session walks them through setup and repair - for this audience, possibly the truest installer UX.

Ordering: doctor first, since it defines correct before setup automates reaching it; the skill consumes doctor's output; the bootstrap is independent. The adoption walkthrough script becomes the CI proof of the whole path.

Done means a newcomer on a clean machine runs the bootstrap, then yoyo setup, and ends with a verified working installation the walkthrough proves in CI; yoyo doctor thereafter names anything broken and the command that fixes it.
notes:
Admitted to the backlog by the product manager in conversation chat-91253e0e070c17b0663651cc48602122, after turn 139.

Reason: Operator-approved. The adoption goal's first minute, smoothed end to end and kept verified forever after - doctor is the goal's enforcement outliving the install, and the walkthrough-in-CI keeps the whole path proven rather than asserted. Priority 2 with the adoption and docs work; children follow once this id exists.

Goal served: A newcomer can go from the documented install to a working first run on their own repository using the readme alone.
Noted by the product manager in conversation chat-91253e0e070c17b0663651cc48602122, after turn 143.

Reason: A contract three components must agree on belongs on the item all three descend from, so it is decided once rather than converged on by accident.

Operator requirement, 2026-08-20, spanning three children: Slack secrets are namespaced per harness instance. The naming scheme - a per-project key, likely derived from project identity or config path - is one contract shared by setup (writes the secrets, 125.3), the sink launcher (reads them), and doctor (verifies the instance's own secret exists and the sink runs against it, 125.1); the skill inherits it through doctor's remedies. Decide the scheme once, in one place, before the writing and reading halves are built separately. Consistency note: several instances, each one product with its own tokens, sits inside the v1 non-goals - this is not multiple products per instance.
Noted by the product manager in conversation chat-91253e0e070c17b0663651cc48602122, after turn 145.

Reason: Recording the operator's stated definition of done in a form a test can enforce, with the bounded reading - yoyo's own config surface, enumerated - stated explicitly so the bar is finite and checkable rather than aspirational.

ACCEPTANCE CRITERION, operator's definition of done 2026-08-20, verbatim intent: there is no configuration or configuration change that the doctor/installer cannot correctly handle, leading to a running yoyo harness. Testable form, recorded by the product manager: (1) the configuration surface is enumerated, and that enumeration is the test matrix - every reachable state of yoyo's own config surface, including states produced by editing config on an already-working install, is in it; (2) every state in the matrix either passes doctor clean or yields a finding whose remedy, followed, leads to a running harness - remedies are tested to work, not merely to print; (3) no dead ends: doctor never reports a state it cannot route the user out of, and a state outside the matrix it encounters anyway is named plainly rather than mishandled; (4) no config change silently strands the sink, the scheduler, or the Slack tier - edits that break a running install surface in doctor with a working remedy; (5) the adoption walkthrough in CI is the floor, not the proof - it covers the happy path, and the matrix covers the rest. The universal bar is over yoyo's own configuration surface; arbitrary machine states outside it get honest naming, not guaranteed repair.
Noted by the product manager in conversation chat-91253e0e070c17b0663651cc48602122, after turn 160.

Reason: Two epics now answer 'who keeps the sink running' differently; recording the collision where both builders will read it, with the architect's design named as the decider.

Cross-note, 2026-08-20: the one-pane-of-glass epic admitted today (yoyo chat as sole entry point, chat spawns and supervises the scheduling loop and Slack sink) serves the same first-hour-of-use story as this epic: the installer gets a newcomer to a working harness, the unified surface makes running it one command. The setup child's start-on-login sink service and the unified surface's chat-supervised sink are two answers to the same residency question - the architect's supervision-tree design for the unified epic should say how they compose or which one owns which case, before 125.3 builds the service.
Noted by the product manager in conversation chat-91253e0e070c17b0663651cc48602122, after turn 163.

Reason: Closing the collision this note opened, so the two epics no longer carry two answers to one question.

Residency collision resolved by operator decision, 2026-08-20: the one-pane epic (ifd.130) owns sink residency; 125.3 drops its start-on-login service tier and keeps the keychain recipes. Longer term, per the direction recorded on 130.1, launchd returns as supervisor of the whole PM service rather than of individual pieces - so the installer's story ends at a working verified harness, and keeping it running belongs to the supervised surface.
Noted by the product manager in conversation chat-91253e0e070c17b0663651cc48602122, after turn 620.

Reason: Two small newcomer-path gaps with no child of their own; recorded on the epic so the next child carries them.

2026-09-19, from the developer on 75 (2026-08-23), for this epic's remaining scope: yoyo setup writes the configuration by calling initializeProject directly, so it bypasses the gitignore warning that yoyo init prints - the newcomer path is the one still silent - and yoyo doctor has no finding for it either (internal/cli/setup.go and internal/doctor/doctor.go). Also from 125.3's developer: doctor's remedy for a configuration that exists but does not load is yoyo init, which refuses when config.yaml exists and with --force deletes the edits that broke it; distinguishing 'no configuration' from 'a configuration that does not load' lets the second case offer the editor instead. Both belong to whichever child next touches setup and doctor.

title: Docs architecture: a readable README, focused documents, one link map
description:
Operator directive, 2026-08-19. The README is 149KB and the adoption goal is failed by a document nobody can read alone: reduce it to a brief value proposition with the testimonials, the quick start for end users, and links out to focused documents, with everything else split into smaller focused documentation. Pairs with ifd.117 (the 118KB configuration guide split) as one effort with one structure decision.

Role split, confirmed by the product manager: the product manager owns what the README is for and drafts the new opening structure, with the operator's approval on the result; developers execute the split across runs with reconciled docs as definition of done; reviewers enforce truth; the architect has a voice on anchor stability and cross-link structure, and the structure child states the moved-anchor policy up front rather than each run discovering it. A technical-writer persona was considered and deferred: review already enforces writing quality adversarially, and a new role is a harness change worth making only if documentation structure still lacks an owner after this restructure.

Ordering, per the product manager: the structure decision spans both documents so the link map lands once; the adoption walkthrough's asserted claims must stay true through the split, and that test gates the merges, not review alone.

Done means a newcomer can read the README start to finish, reach a working first run from its quick start, and find everything else one link away; no anchor cited by an item or design dangles.

title: Configurable persona avatars for Slack reporting
description:
Operator request, 2026-08-19. Each persona's avatar is a fixed emoji in the voice table - gear for the harness, clipboard for the product manager, compass for the development manager - code, not config. Add a per-role override in the slack config section accepting either an emoji shortcode (including workspace custom emoji, which cost no new permissions) or an image URL (Slack's icon_url, under the customization scope the manifest already declares; the sink currently sends only icon_emoji, so a few lines there).

Boundary, explicit: names and attribution are NOT configurable - the who-speaks rule stays architect-governed. This is the picture beside the name, which the design itself calls strict decoration.

Sits beside yoyodyne-ifd.118: a builder touching identity rendering could sensibly take both. Done means a per-role avatar override validates and renders in new messages, both shortcode and URL forms work, an absent override keeps the shipped default, and nothing about speaker attribution moved into configuration.

title: Slack thread headers carry the item's title, not just its slug
description: Operator request from live use: threads open as bare slugs (yoyodyne-ifd.68.5), unreadable in a channel meant for humans — the header should carry the item's title and ideally its one-line reason for existing. Design constraint the builder inherits: the sink reads durable records only and never queries the tracker (decision 1 of slack-reporting-design), so the title must ride the durable record into the envelope — the run record and docket entry should carry the item title alongside the id (they know it at claim time), and the header renders 'yoyodyne-ifd.68.5 — Slack run-started messages speak as the role that actually selected the run'. Falls under the legibility goal (boundaries between topics need names humans read) and the Slack epic; existing threads stay as they are, new ones open readable.
notes:

Reason: A thread header carrying the item's title instead of a slug is the boundaries-visible clause for the humans following threads: the topic named in words a reader knows, not an identifier they must resolve. Operator request from live use of the shipped surface.

Goal served: The harness's surfaces read clearly: boundaries between topics and speakers are visible, important findings stand out, and every distinction survives a terminal that cannot render emphasis.

title: Conversation milestones reach Slack: admissions, attributions, and decisions thread like run events
description: Found by the operator on first sink start: a run event posted, but nothing about the conversation that had just admitted ifd.113 — PM and DM conversation activity is not in the outbound vocabulary, so the backlog changing (the factory's steering wheel moving) is invisible in the channel built for visibility. Extend the reportable set with conversation-produced tracker milestones: an item admitted (with its goal), an attribution, a priority change, a decomposition, a decision on a proposal — each speaking as the persona that acted, per the who-speaks rule, threading to the work-item topic where one exists and the product topic where not. The design says a new producer adds kinds without the sink, threading, or inbound half changing — this is that clause exercised. Conversations already persist durable event streams the notifier can select from, same shape as runs. Relates to 68.5 (voice) and ifd.99's echo (which covers ask exchanges; this covers the conversations that exist today).

title: Slack run-started messages speak as the role that actually selected the run
description:
The shipped voice templates attribute every run-started message to the development manager, but the architect's who-speaks revision (recorded on slack-reporting-design) requires the speaker to follow the run's recorded selector - and today every run is operator-named, so every production thread misattributes run-started to a persona that made no selection. The fix reads the selection reason the run record already carries.

Sequencing per the architect, recorded as a dependency: land with or before yoyodyne-ifd.102.6, which introduces the first genuinely DM-selected runs and records the triage decision as the selection reason - the exact field the corrected logic reads - so the distinction ships the day it first has two cases to distinguish.

Done means run-started messages name the operator when the operator selected and the development manager when its triage did, matching the recorded selector, with the templates' misattribution gone.

title: DM re-run action: a fresh run against changed ground
description: A triage action that starts a fresh run of a named item on the DM's decision, for the case where the ground moved under a correct change (the 68.3 pattern). Done means: the run consults the intake hold and does not start under one — the DM naming an item is not the operator's exemption; the run's durable state records the selection reason as the DM's triage decision with its reasoning, satisfying selected-work-passes-intake-and-records-why; guidance the DM recorded in the item's notes (what the preserved branch holds, what to cherry-pick) reaches the developer's context; the action is refused past one re-run per triage entry.
notes:
Architect constraints: (a) refused unless the prior run is terminally recorded — blocker standing, nothing resumable — so two live runs of one item cannot exist; checked, not assumed from docket filtering; (b) the action records the preserved branch and worktree's disposition — kept until the fresh run integrates, then retired explicitly — or triage accumulates orphan worktrees nobody discovers. Structural note to state in the child so nobody fixes it: DM guidance travels in notes, notes are excluded from grants, so a re-run can never acquire artifact-home access through triage guidance — correct by construction and deliberate.

Re-recorded 2026-08-19 after the operator's agent clobbered the creation notes with a replace-style update: the goal below is the one the development manager supplied at decomposition, restored.

Goal served: Run development nearly autonomously. The human's routine interface is the product manager: they state intent, approve the brief and goals, and answer questions the product manager escalates. Directing the architect, development manager, developer, or reviewer individually is available for inspection, recovery, and override, but is not part of the normal loop.

title: Bounded repair-continue on a blocked run
description: A triage action that re-enters a blocked run's repair loop on the preserved branch and developer session, with the reviewer's findings intact and unedited, under an explicit grant of further repair attempts. Done means: the run continues the same change rather than starting over; the grant size comes from configuration; the action is refused once the per-item grant counter or the rounds cap says the budget is spent; it consults the intake hold before spending on a provider and records the DM's triage reasoning durably on the run and the item; the triage decision is recorded on the work item.
notes:
Architect constraints: (a) re-entry passes the existing worktree HEAD-state ownership check — anything touched since the blocker (including an operator mid-surgery) refuses and escalates; one more door onto the existing gate, not a new mechanism; (b) the durable blocker is superseded at the moment of re-entry, or the record lies to status, reconcile, and the docket. Authority decision (architect's boundary-preserving recommendation, adopted): the DM never narrows a PM-admitted item's criteria — the split child is DM-created as always, and the parent's narrowing is a triage note plus a proposal to the PM (an ask once ifd.99 lands). The ifd.70 path builds that shape.

title: Durable per-item triage counters
description: Durable counters per work item, in run/tracker state rather than in any conversation: repair grants given, re-runs caused, merge re-arms made, and total review rounds across all runs of the item. Done means: each counter increments durably before the action it counts takes effect, so a crash cannot double-grant; the counters survive process restarts and are readable wherever the item's record is read; the triage actions consult them and are refused past their caps; a second triage pass on an item is visible from its record alone.
notes:
Architect constraints: (a) one durable home, per-machine today — record the team-mode limit (two collaborators hold full budgets per item) so ifd.82.2's designer finds it stated; (b) a round is a reviewer verdict produced by a developer attempt, across all runs of the item, EXCLUDING integration-replay re-reviews of an unchanged diff on moved ground — counting those punishes losing a race; (c) increment-before-act stands, and a grant truncates to the rounds remaining under the cap with the truncation recorded — at defaults (2 repair attempts = 3 rounds spent, cap 4) an untruncated grant of 2 is unspendable and an overshooting one makes the cap decorative.

title: yoyo init configures the Dolt remote when a git remote exists
description: Operator decision, 2026-08-19, from the manual-seams audit. Beads syncs via a Dolt remote on the git remote and nothing configures it: every bd invocation has printed the warning all week, and an unconfigured tracker remote is recorded gap 1 of team mode - the tracker silently diverging per machine. yoyo init configures the Dolt remote when a git remote exists. Done means a fresh init against a repository with a remote produces a tracker that syncs, the warning is gone, and team mode's first gap is closed at install time rather than discovered at first divergence.
notes:

Docs get one line each on repo-size accounting (tracker history counts against the repository) and forge tolerance of custom refs (GitHub fine; others worth a caveat).

title: A typed artifact-write action for owning roles, closing the copy-paste seam
description:
Operator decision, 2026-08-19, surfaced while examining how the team-mode scope document reached disk. Today a drafted document - the scope doc, the operations goals - crosses from chat to repository by hand: fenced markdown, an approval in prose, then a human or an operator's agent transcribing path, frontmatter, commit, and pull request. That transcription is where this week's only governance error lived: the drafted content was correct, and the agent placing it invented an ungoverned state the store refused.

The proposal flow shows the right shape and documents should feel identical: the owning role emits a typed create-or-revise-artifact action with kind and content; the chat renders it for the operator's y; the harness performs the write through the existing Authorize gate under that role, generates the contract-required frontmatter, records the operator's approval in the approvals block, and opens the pull request. An illegal kind or wrong home is refused at the action layer before anything touches disk.

The same machinery serves the architect's design transcriptions, script-extracted by hand today for exactly this error class. The architect designs the action's shape: it extends the authority boundary its first session ratified.

Also traces to adoption: a newcomer with only the readme and chat hits the copy-paste seam immediately - the operator's agent has been papering over it invisibly all week. Adoption attribution appended separately.
notes:

title: An inter-role ask channel: durable, visible, judgment-only exchanges
description:
Operator decision, 2026-08-19, adopting the product manager's recommendation. Roles can ask each other questions through the harness - the product manager asking the architect for a cost estimate or a design-intent clarification is the motivating case. Three properties are load-bearing: every exchange is durable and visible, preserving the no-side-conversations property the traceability goal implies; the channel is judgment-only - both conversations are toolless, so an ask moves opinion, never evidence, and verification stays commissioned as developer work (the ifd.97 pattern); and the channel is decisionless - no authority moves through an ask, and decisions still land as amendments, proposals, and directives. The refusal it retires: a one-question exchange currently costs either an operator relay or a full work-item cycle.

The architect designs it.

Operator addition: when the Slack epic lands, inter-role ask exchanges are echoed to Slack so operators can follow the conversation and redirect if needed. Dependency shape: the echo is a consumer of yoyodyne-ifd.68.2's notifier, not a blocker of the channel itself - the channel ships without Slack and gains the echo when the notifier exists.
notes:
Operator requirement, 2026-08-19: the channel is explicitly bidirectional, and both directions are first-class in the design with these canonical exchanges recorded as its motivating examples — PM asks architect: 'what does this goal cost, and what am I missing?' (feeding cost and feasibility into backlog ordering before admission); architect asks PM: 'what would the user be impacted by — if we sacrifice some performance, is that an unacceptable trade-off from the user's standpoint?' (feeding user impact into design decisions before they are made, rather than as findings after). The judgment-only, decisionless, durable-and-visible properties apply identically in both directions, as does the Slack echo once 68.2's notifier exists. Second operator requirement, same date: a configurable hard limit on rounds per exchange thread — default 10, validated at least 1, durable with the exchange so a process death cannot reset it (the repair-budget pattern). Hitting the cap is not a silent cutoff: the exchange closes as unresolved-after-N-rounds and escalates to the operator as a question or report, converting the pathological two-judgment-models-deferring-forever loop into a rare legible operator question. Per-exchange cost is reported beside the rounds so the operator sees what a conversation spent (ties to the cost goal).

title: Gate developer diffs on protected paths, deterministically, before review
description:
Operator decision, 2026-08-19. Protected paths - .yoyodyne/**, docs/product/**, docs/designs/**, docs/decisions/** - are default-deny for a developer's diff: refused before review like a failing check and handed back inside the existing repair loop, unless the work item explicitly grants the path, so every exception is declared in reviewed item text rather than discovered as surprise. The refusal names the grant mechanism, so a developer that genuinely needs a path raises it instead of sneaking it.

Rationale for the record: closes the design's one admitted gap - an agent with an editor in its worktree - deterministically. Today that class costs an Opus review cycle to catch; ifd.70's scope-creep refusal burned two repairs and $18 reaching a conclusion this gate reaches free. It is the checks-expansion lever in its purest form: a class of reviewer finding retired into a gate.

The grant mechanism must cover the legitimate precedents: ifd.1.9's item required moving the design document; ifd.4's touched the built-in bundle. A CODEOWNERS forge layer was considered and rejected - it only has value if the operator personally reviews, which he declines.

The architect may want a voice in the grant field's shape, which borders the fixed-roles decision recorded in its first session; consult before settling it.

title: Shadow-review experiment: Sonnet re-reviews branches Opus already judged
description: Data-gathering that lets model tiering (the efficiency lever deliberately scheduled last) graduate from prediction to measurement, at zero risk because shadow reviews gate nothing. Method: yoyo review is a replayable pure function over a branch and base; re-run it with a Sonnet-configured reviewer against historical branch states whose Opus verdicts are recorded ground truth, and diff the findings. Ready-made benchmark with graded difficulty: ifd.1.9's six review rounds — findings split between local/mechanical catches (missing CLI test, missing colon, stale comment) a smaller model plausibly makes, and accumulated-shape catches (a flag set from both read loops, a layout claim contradicted by the branch's own test, an approvals entry whose reason claimed a revision its index did not name, JSON/text divergence between commands) that are the reviewer's real value. Deliverable: miss-rate and false-positive comparison per finding class, and a per-review cost comparison — which also needs ifd.83's phase costs to price what tiering would save. Operator-requested 2026-08-18. Related: ai-output/2026-08-18-token-efficiency-levers.md lever 1.

title: Surface failed runs and their reasons through a yoyo verb
description: The write side of failure persistence is solid: a terminal run's record keeps status, the phase it died in, and the failure message coherently (23 such records on disk, from full review verdicts to 'primary checkout is not ready for integration'), with separated companions — check_failure, publish_failure, cleanup_failure, completion_recording_failure — so bookkeeping failures cannot masquerade as run failures, and the same reason lands in the work item's notes. The read side is weaker: no yoyo verb lists failed runs with their reasons — today the operator goes through bd show per item, yoyo-status, or the raw run JSON. Add the surface, most naturally in the yoyo status verb ifd.63 builds (recent runs, terminal status, phase, first line of the failure, cost), with --json for scripts. Related: ifd.83's per-phase cost breakdown reads the same records, and granularity varies by class — provider-side deaths persist thin reasons like 'developer reported failure: api_error', worth enriching while in there. Operator-requested 2026-08-18.

title: Expand declared checks to retire recurring reviewer findings
description: Lever 2 of the token-efficiency brainstorm (ai-output/2026-08-18-token-efficiency-levers.md): every mechanical defect a deterministic check catches is attention the reviewer does not spend, and the candidates come from our own report stream — (a) a goals-file lint enforcing one physical line per goal statement (the 0n1 class); (b) a documentation link checker for the reference problems the artifact layer already warns about; (c) the dispatcher-coverage test suggested by ifd.70's reviewer is deliberately NOT here — it is ifd.81's second half, referenced to avoid duplication. Detecting negative impact: (1) false positives — the run records keep every check's pass/fail per verify pass; a bad check is one that fails often while the diffs fixing it are trivial appeasement churn, versus a good check's signature of rare failures with real causes; (2) runtime drag — checks run on every verify pass including each repair, so wall-clock per check (recorded, timeouts configurable per ifd.56) multiplies; an expensive check needs to earn it; (3) reviewer complacency — invisible in check data, visible in the escaped-defect rate: bugs filed in beads against already-merged work, the backstop metric for any quality-affecting change; (4) the findings channel itself — developers report checks that fight them, as this week's reports demonstrated. Operator-approved 2026-08-18.

title: Team mode: collaborators each run yoyo against one shared repository
description:
Operator decision, 2026-08-18. Collaborators download yoyo and run it against the shared repository. The git/forge layer already survives multiple committers - namespaced run branches, branch protection, drift replay with fresh verdicts - and the supported answer today is one harness plus friends as ordinary committers. What breaks when each person runs their own harness is the coordination layer, single-operator throughout. Five recorded gaps bound the scope: (1) the tracker diverges per machine - Beads syncs via a Dolt remote on the git remote, nothing configures it, every bd call warns; (2) no distributed claim - two machines can claim one item in the sync window and one loses after paying for development and review; (3) the one-promotion-per-target-branch lease is machine-scoped flock, so across machines the invariant silently narrows and the forge is the only backstop; (4) report stores, run state, product-manager conversations, and the pause switch are per-machine - findings and control do not travel; (5) operator identity is recorded without proof, the forgeability gap already a design precondition on ifd.25, multiplied across humans whose intent can conflict.

Scope questions this epic answers: what team mode promises, who counts as an operator, whether one-harness-many-committers is the supported v1 answer. Sequencing decided by the operator: the product manager's scoping document first; the architecture pass waits for the architect role ifd.4 creates, with the explicit constraint that operator identity is designed once, jointly for ifd.25's precondition and this epic, not twice.

RECONCILIATION PENDING: the team goal this epic names is drafted but not yet in v1-goals.md, and v1-non-goals.md still records multiple human users as a v1 non-goal - both need the operator's pen. title: Document the contributor workflow the harness already supports: local-only .yoyodyne via .git/info/exclude and --config
description: A contributor to a repository they do not own may not want to commit tool-specific configuration. title: Warn when .yoyodyne is gitignored, in init and config validate
description: A newcomer who reflexively gitignores tool config gets no error and eventual drift: the launch checkout keeps working from disk, but clones and collaborators get an unconfigured project, and dev worktrees (which check out tracked files only) silently lack the directory. yoyo init and yoyo config validate should check whether .yoyodyne is matched by the repository's ignore rules (git check-ignore) and say plainly what committing it means: the project stops being self-describing for every other machine. title: Fold yoyo-status into the yoyo CLI behind a status verb
description:
bin/yoyo-status is the operator's daily observability driver - it follows run and conversation event streams live and reports per-run cost - but the install does not install it, so it exists only for someone working from a checkout. The brief's bar is someone who has never seen the internals pointing Yoyodyne at their own repository; for them this surface is absent. Decided by the operator 2026-08-18: fold its functionality into the existing yoyo command behind a status verb rather than packaging the script separately.

Done means: yoyo status covers what bin/yoyo-status does today - following runs and conversations live, listing recent ones, per-run cost - and ships with the install; the operator's preferred output shape (bin/yoyo-status -c's, recorded on yoyodyne-ifd.51) is the reference rendering; what becomes of the shell script (retired or kept as a thin wrapper) is the implementer's call, stated with reasoning; documentation reconciles, including the design document's yoyo status entry, which this finally builds.

Relation: yoyodyne-ifd.51's shipped-work ledger becomes a section of this verb per the updated decision note on that item, and its per-item cost data stays in the one Go join yoyodyne-ifd.41 built. This supersedes the product manager's earlier stay-separate surface decision on ifd.51, revised on its merits: that decision protected the operator's daily workflow and avoided a naming collision, and the install gap defeats the first while absorption removes the second.

Finding [major] (internal/cli/statusstream.go:0): An empty answer under `--kind` states something false. `describeNoStreams` is worded for the unnarrowed query, so `yoyo status --list --kind reviews` on a machine with fifty runs and no branch reviews prints "no runs, conversations, or branch reviews are recorded under <path>" and exits 0, and `--spend --kind reviews` does the same instead of ever reaching the window message. This is exactly the misreading the section's own prose says this surface cannot afford — the operator is told their state directory is empty when it is not. Make the empty message name the kinds actually queried (all three when none was narrowed to), and check `reportSpend`'s `report.Streams == 0` branch with it so a narrowed spend query with no matching streams still distinguishes "none of this kind recorded" from "nothing spent in the window".
Finding [minor] (internal/cli/statusstream_test.go:0): `--latest` has no test of the behavior it names. The only occurrence in the suite is the refusal case asserting it needs `--follow`; nothing exercises `followOne` finding a later stream, draining the one it is leaving, and continuing on the successor — which is the one non-obvious invariant in the follow path and the one the comment there specifically claims ("nothing is dropped between the two"). A test that appends to a first stream, creates a second, and asserts both the pre-switch tail and the successor's events arrive would fail without that drain.
Finding [minor] (internal/cli/status.go:0): Two options are silently ignored outside their half of the verb, against the rule stated a few lines above them ("An option that belongs to the other half of the verb is refused rather than ignored"): `--lines` is accepted and dropped in the recorded-run mode, and `--limit` is accepted and dropped under `--follow`/`--events` (`streamOptions.limit` is never read by `followStreams`). Both have non-zero defaults, so detecting that they were actually given needs `flags.Visit`; refuse them there the way `--raw`, `--all`, and `--kind` are refused.

title: Show the recently shipped work with its price and its wall clock
description:
The operator wants one call that answers what shipped lately and what it took: yoyo status listing the n most recently shipped work items, each with its provider-reported cost and the wall-clock time from claim to promotion.

Cost attribution already exists: ifd.41 records provider-reported cost per item across every run made for it, and yoyo cost reports it. What is missing is the time dimension and the ledger view -- most-recent-first, bounded, glanceable.

yoyo status is also the verb the design document has always listed for the CLI and never built; the conversation's /status covers in-flight work. This item may introduce the command with shipped work as its first section, or extend yoyo cost -- implementer's call, stated with reasoning, but the operator asked for it as yoyo status.
design:
Wall clock is two honest numbers, not one. Elapsed from first claim to promotion includes usage-limit pauses, which on 2026-08-17 were hours of the night; the pause seconds are already durable per run (usage_limit_paused_seconds). Report elapsed and paused side by side so a four-hour item that spent three parked reads as what it was. Sum across every run the item took, including failed and discarded attempts, consistent with ifd.41's accounting: the honest time includes rework.

Timestamps come from what is already recorded -- the tracker's started/closed times and the runs' started/completed times -- rather than new bookkeeping. An item whose runs predate some of the recording reports what it can and marks the rest unknown, never zero, per ifd.41's rule.

Output is a table: item, title, cost, elapsed, paused, runs, most recent first, default n around ten, machine-readable with --json like everything else.
acceptance_criteria: One command lists the n most recently shipped items with provider-reported cost, elapsed wall clock, and paused time, most recent first; totals across the listing are shown; unknowns are stated as unknown rather than zero; --json works; the choice of verb (yoyo status or an extension of yoyo cost) is recorded with its reasoning; the conversation's /status is unchanged.

title: Mark downstream artifacts and work stale when an upstream artifact changes
description:
When a goal changes, the designs that serve it and the work that traces to it may no longer be right, and nothing says so. Today a goal can be amended while work built on the old wording continues to completion, and the divergence is found by a person or not at all. Propagate staleness downstream when an artifact changes.

DONE: amending an artifact marks the artifacts and open work items downstream of it as stale; staleness is visible to the operator and names what changed upstream; staleness is recorded durably rather than held in a running process.

CONSTRAINT: stale is not cancelled. Marking work stale must not stop or discard it - a change to a goal's wording is frequently not a change to what the work should do, and a system that discards work on every edit teaches operators not to edit. What happens to stale work is a decision for the operator or the owning role, and this item surfaces the condition rather than acting on it.

title: Pause the work a directive affects when the directive is ambiguous or changes an artifact
description:
ifd.1's acceptance criteria require that the harness pauses affected work for ambiguous or artifact-changing directives. Today a directive that changes what an in-flight item should do does not reach that item; work continues against the intent it was given. Reconcile a new directive against work already in flight and pause what it affects.

DONE: a directive that changes a governed artifact, or that is ambiguous enough to need the operator, pauses the work items it affects rather than only being recorded; the pause names the directive and what is unresolved; work resumes when the ambiguity is answered or the artifact change is decided; a directive reaches the work it affects regardless of which agent received it.

CONSTRAINT: pause, do not cancel, and settle what a paused run leaves behind exactly as stopping already does rather than abandoning it. The failure to design against is a directive that is durably recorded and reaches nothing, which is the state today - recording a directive is not enforcing one.

title: Let a role propose a change to an artifact it does not own
description:
Once ownership is enforced, a role that needs an upstream artifact changed has no way to say so. The escalation path is already described: a developer proposes an upstream change, the architect evaluates it and owns the design amendment, and only an unworkable goal reaches the product manager. Build the mechanism that carries a proposed change from a non-owner to the owner and the operator.

DONE: a role can propose a change to an artifact it does not own; the proposal reaches the artifact's owner and the operator with what is proposed and why; the owner or the operator decides, and only that decision writes; a proposal is durable rather than lost when the run that raised it ends.

CONSTRAINT: reuse the proposal and decision path yoyodyne-ifd.24 already built for work items rather than building a second one. A proposal is never a deferred edit - nothing an unapproved proposal contains reaches the artifact. Do not let a proposal mechanism become a way for a downstream role to change upstream intent slowly.

Decomposition belongs to the development manager; this shape should be re-derived or ratified when the role runs. Do not start before the ownership enforcement child lands.

title: Let a conversation turn wait out a usage limit the way a run does
description:
A run that hits a provider usage limit records the reset time, pauses, and resumes; a conversation turn that hits one simply fails. Observed 2026-08-17: turn 13 of the product-manager conversation performed seven tracker reads, delivered its reply preamble, and then died with 'You've hit your session limit, resets 8:30pm' when the continuation invocation was refused -- the ifd.1 decomposition it was about to create never happened, and the operator asking 'did we stop?' is what surfaced it.

The machinery exists: the rate-limit envelope is parsed, the reset time is known, and runs already wait bounded intervals against a budget. Conversations bypass all of it.
design: Reuse the run behavior rather than inventing a second one: on an exhausted limit with a reset time inside the in-process bound, wait and reissue the turn; past the bound or with no reset time, follow the same rules runs follow. The turn's partial work is already durable -- tracker actions applied before the failure stay applied, which is correct and should be stated: a reissued turn continues a session that already holds them. Interactive mode should show the wait through the activity display rather than sitting silent, and --message mode should wait the same way since an unattended caller is exactly who cannot retry by hand.
acceptance_criteria: A conversation turn that hits a waitable usage limit waits and completes rather than failing; the wait is visible in interactive mode and bounded by the same configuration runs use; tracker actions applied before the pause are not repeated after it; an unwaitable limit fails with the reset information stated; a test replays the limit-then-reset sequence against a fake backend.
notes:
Fresh evidence 2026-08-18: a chat --message turn failed outright with 'product manager reported failure: api_error' where a run would have waited and retried. The turn was retried by hand and the operator's agent lost nothing, but the asymmetry the bead describes is now demonstrated on the PM's own conversation, not just predicted.

title: Put a price tag on every completed work item
description:
When the operator asks what is done, each completed item should come back with what it cost. The evidence already exists and is already attributed: every provider invocation ends in a run.completed event carrying the provider-reported usage and total_cost_usd, and every run records the work item it served. Nothing joins them, so cost today is answerable per run (yoyo-status -c) but not per item, and not from inside a conversation at all.

The join matters because it changes what the number means. An item's honest price includes every run it took: failed attempts, discarded first tries, and repair attempts, developer and reviewer invocations both. yoyodyne-ifd.2.7 cost roughly twenty-eight dollars across a rejected attempt and a successful one; a per-run view shows two numbers and a per-item view shows the truth.
design:
Record the cost durably on the item when a run for it completes, aggregating across all of its runs, so the tracker carries the price and everything that reads the tracker -- the product manager's briefing, /show, bd itself -- sees it without a second data source. Use the provider-reported cost, never an estimate from a price table that can drift.

Surface it where the operator actually asks. The question 'what is done' is asked in the conversation, so completed items in /status carry their price, and /show breaks it down by run: attempt, outcome, cost. yoyo-status may grow a by-item grouping, but the conversation is the primary surface.

Backfill what already happened: the durable run state and event streams for past runs still exist under the state directory, so closed items can be priced retroactively rather than starting the ledger today.

Scope honestly: runs only. Conversation turns also cost money and are recorded, but attributing a conversation that discussed five items is a judgement call this item should not attempt; note the gap rather than solving it. A run whose events are gone prices as unknown, stated as unknown rather than zero -- a zero that means 'no record' would corrupt every total it touches.
acceptance_criteria: A completed work item carries the total provider-reported cost of every run made for it, including failed and repair attempts and reviewer invocations; asking what is done in the conversation shows each item's price; /show breaks the cost down by run with outcomes; existing closed items are backfilled from recorded run state; a run with no surviving record prices as unknown, never zero; costs are provider-reported, not estimated.
notes:
From the operator, 2026-08-17: 'lets us get the token cost for each completed item so that when I ask what's done they come back with a price tag.' Related: yoyo-status -c already prices runs (and excludes conversations, a known gap recorded on ifd.23); this item is the per-item join and the conversational surface.
Noted by the product manager in conversation chat-91253e0e070c17b0663651cc48602122, after turn 11.

Reason: Recording the attribution the audit found missing, now that the operator has supplied the goal. The tracker's goal field cannot be rewritten, so the note carries it.

Goal attribution: this item was admitted before work items carried one, and the backlog audit found it traced to no v1 goal. The operator has approved a new v1 goal covering it: 'The operator can see what the harness spends on their behalf: provider-reported cost, per work item, per run, and in total.' That is the goal this work serves, and the acceptance criteria here already match it - provider-reported rather than estimated, aggregated per item across every run including failed and repair attempts, unknown stated as unknown rather than zero.

title: Stream the reply and surface run milestones while the operator watches
description:
A turn's reply appears all at once when it completes; until then the spinner from ifd.28 says something is happening but not what is being said. And a background run started with /work is silent between prompts -- its milestones exist in the event stream but are reported only when the operator next asks.

Three parts. First, stream the product manager's reply as the provider generates it, replacing the spinner with prose forming. Second, when this conversation started a run, print one-line milestone notices as it crosses phases: checks passed, review approve, pull request queued, merged. Third, small comforts: a terminal bell and title update when a background run finishes, and per-turn cost in the status line, since the operator watches spend.
design:
Streaming is the invasive part and belongs behind the backend boundary: the Claude Code adapter already parses assistant events incrementally, so the text exists before the terminal result -- what changes is that the console shows it as it arrives rather than holding it. The recorded reply must be byte-identical to the non-streamed one, redaction must run on every fragment before it is shown, and a stream that dies mid-reply must not leave a half-reply looking whole: say plainly that it was cut off.

Milestones reuse the notices channel that already carries harness activity into the conversation, printed above the input region ifd.22 built, so they never corrupt what the operator is typing. Keep them to phase transitions -- an event log scrolling by is exactly what the activity display was designed not to be.

Bell and title are terminal escapes behind the same capability checks as colour; cost comes from the usage the provider already reports per turn. All of it degrades to nothing when output is not a terminal.
acceptance_criteria: The reply appears as it is generated and the recorded conversation is byte-identical to the non-streamed form; redaction applies to every fragment before display; an interrupted stream is reported as interrupted; a run started from the conversation reports phase transitions as they happen without corrupting input; a finished background run rings the bell and updates the title where the terminal supports it; per-turn cost appears in the status line; NO_COLOR, TERM=dumb, non-terminal output, and --json see none of it.
notes:
From the operator, 2026-08-16. Ranked below the trust and proposal items by the operator's agent because streaming is the only piece that reaches into the backend; the milestones and comforts could land separately if streaming proves heavy.

title: Settle the architect and development-manager artifact homes
description:
Open design question raised by the operator on 2026-08-16, deliberately not settled: if the product manager works from specifications in docs/specs (yoyodyne-ifd.20), the architect and the development manager plausibly want the same treatment -- the architect for architectural invariants, possibly as ADRs in a directory, and the development manager for design documents. Both artifact kinds support the product manager's goals.

This is filed as a question rather than a feature because it reassigns ownership in a way the current design document contradicts, and getting that wrong is expensive to unwind.
design:
RESOLVED by the operator, 2026-08-16. The architect keeps designs and additionally owns decision records and invariants; the development manager decomposes those designs into work without owning a document of its own.

Artifact ownership after this decision:
- product manager: docs/product/ -- the brief and the goals derived from it
- architect: docs/designs/ -- designs and specifications, unchanged from what the design document already states; and a decision home for ADRs and the invariants extracted from them
- development manager: no document; it converts approved designs into Beads work with dependencies and acceptance criteria

This is deliberately the smallest change from what is written and shipped: the artifact ownership table gains a row rather than moving one, and the architect and development-manager personas need no rewrite. The alternative considered and rejected was moving designs to the development manager, which would have been a cleaner separation between system-wide constraints and how one body of work is structured, but would have rewritten the ownership table, the intent graph, and both personas for a role that does not exist yet.

ADRs and invariants remain complementary rather than alternatives, as recorded before: an ADR is the durable record of a decision, with a status that can become superseded, and an invariant is the live constraint extracted from it. Using either as the other fails predictably -- edit ADRs to stay current and the decision history rots; bury live constraints in historical prose and nothing can tell what currently holds. The architect owns both, and yoyodyne-ifd.17 is what makes an invariant reach a developer, which is the only thing that makes it constrain anything.
acceptance_criteria: The artifact ownership table and intent graph in docs/v1-harness-design.md record the decision above, adding the architect's decision and invariant home without moving designs; the architect and development-manager personas remain consistent with it; the relationship between decision records and invariants is stated rather than implied.
notes:
From the operator, 2026-08-16, phrased tentatively: 'possibly we should have a similar set up for the architect ... and the dev manager ... both of those artifacts should support the PMs goals.' Recorded as an open question rather than a decision. Relates to ifd.17 (architect owns invariants), ifd.20 (product manager specifications), and ifd.1 (artifact governance).

title: Add restart reconciliation for interrupted runs
description:
Milestone 1 calls for restart reconciliation and duplicate-run prevention. Duplicate-run prevention exists (ExistingRunError), but nothing reconciles an interrupted run. The code repeatedly documents a reconciler that does not exist: internal/orchestrator/pipeline.go describes leaving 'a succeeded run in the cleaning_up phase with worktree_removed still false, which is a resumable instruction rather than a lost run', and internal/gitworktree/manager.go documents CleanupIntegrated as resumable specifically so a reconciler can finish it.

This matters beyond tidiness: the durable-evidence invariants tightened during PR #3 review were all defensive against a reconciler reading state back, and that consumer still does not exist, so none of them are exercised.
design:
Compare durable run state against observed reality at startup, as the Recovery and Idempotency section describes: the recorded phase, the worktree registration, the branch, whether the recorded source commit is contained in the target, and provider session state where queryable. Then resume cleanup, mark an external outcome, or raise a durable blocker. Never start a second developer for an item because a process handle was lost. Cleanup over already-absent artifacts must remain a safe no-op.

CONSTRAINT FROM A FAILED FIRST ATTEMPT (run-b0414b72946f17eb3eb95acd5287b67f, preserved for reference only at branch yoyodyne/yoyodyne-ifd-2-8/b0414b72, commit ee5b231). That attempt produced working reconciliation code and was discarded because make test failed on TestPipelineResumesTheRepairLoopAtTheRecordedAttempt.

Build on the resume path that already exists rather than introducing a second one. yoyodyne-ifd.2.7 restructured the run onto activeRun and added resumption that continues the repair loop at the recorded attempt, deliberately so an interrupted attempt still counts and a restart cannot buy a fresh repair budget. Its tests encode that contract. Reconciliation must extend that path and keep those tests passing; if a test must change, the change has to be justified as a corrected contract rather than adjusted to fit new code. Run the full suite, not only new tests: the failure here was a pre-existing test in internal/orchestrator, not one this work would add.
acceptance_criteria: An interrupted run in each non-terminal phase is reconciled to a correct terminal state or an explicit blocker; a run interrupted between integration and cleanup completes its cleanup without re-running the developer; reconciliation is idempotent and safe to run repeatedly; a run whose artifacts are already gone reconciles without error; tests cover interruption at each phase boundary.

title: Verify language agnosticism with a non-Go fixture project
description:
Support for projects in languages other than Go is now a recorded goal and a design invariant (docs/v1-harness-design.md: the harness assumes no language, build system, or test framework, and verification is whatever commands the project declares). Nothing verifies it. Every fixture and every check example in the repository is Go, so the claim currently rests on the observation that internal/checks/runner.go shells out to /bin/sh -c and reads an exit code.

Add a fixture project whose configured checks are not Go commands and drive it through the harness end to end, so a future change that quietly introduces a Go assumption -- in context assembly, worktree handling, diff summarization, or check execution -- fails a test rather than surfacing when someone points Yoyodyne at a TypeScript or Python repository.
design: The harness's only contact with a toolchain is running declared commands and reading exit codes, so this needs a fixture whose checks are not Go commands, not a second language integration and not a dependency on a language runtime being installed in CI. Prefer checks that are plain shell (a script in the fixture that exits 0 or 1) over commands requiring node, python, or a JVM, so the test verifies the harness's language independence rather than the CI image's contents. Cover both a passing and a failing check, since the failing path is what gates integration.
acceptance_criteria: A fixture project with non-Go checks runs through the harness end to end; a failing non-Go check stops the run before review and integration exactly as a failing Go check does; the test requires no language runtime beyond a POSIX shell; the language-agnostic invariant in docs/v1-harness-design.md is cited by the test so the link between claim and verification is discoverable.
