title: Add branch-scope review over an accumulated change
description: The independent reviewer sees exactly one work item's worktree diff (review.Request carries a single gitworktree.ChangeDiff), so it structurally cannot see defects that only appear across accumulated beads. PR #3 demonstrated this concretely: three of its five findings were cross-cutting durable-evidence invariants in internal/runstate and internal/gitworktree, each individually consistent within the bead that introduced it and only visible against the combined shape of the branch. Those were found by an external reviewer, not by the harness. Give the harness a review scope that covers an accumulated change against a base, so that class of finding is caught by the loop rather than by whoever happens to open the pull request.
design: Reuse the existing reviewer contract, structured verdict, and independence evidence; vary the change under review rather than the review protocol. The diff is a branch against a recorded base commit rather than one worktree, so the existing DiffLimits truncation and redaction paths need to hold over a much larger change, and the reviewer must be told that findings may span commits. Decide explicitly whether a branch-scope repair verdict blocks anything or is advisory, since the per-bead work it covers is already integrated by the time this runs.
acceptance_criteria: The harness can run an independent structured review over a branch against a base commit and record the verdict with the same session and model evidence as a per-item review; diff limits and redaction hold over a multi-commit change; the outcome of a repair verdict at this scope is defined and enforced; tests cover a multi-commit review with a fake backend.
notes:
Raised 2026-08-15 from PR #3 review. The operator asked that the harness reviewer take over review work; this bead is what makes that true at the pull-request scope rather than only per work item.

title: Let the product manager propose Beads work items
description: Give the product-manager conversation a governed way to turn discussed intent into proposed Beads work items. The product manager emits structured proposals; the operator approves before anything is created. Research is advisory and must never silently become an approved goal, design, or work item.
design: Keep proposal separate from authority. The product manager returns a structured proposal (title, description, rationale, parent, dependencies) rather than calling bd directly, and the harness creates items only after explicit operator approval, consistent with the default 'goals: human' approval in builtin:v1. Record the conversation turn the proposal came from so a created item traces back to the intent that produced it.
acceptance_criteria: The product manager can propose one or more Beads work items from a conversation; nothing is created without explicit operator approval; a rejected proposal is recorded rather than silently dropped; created items record the originating conversation; tests cover approval, rejection, and the refusal to create without approval.

title: Let the product manager research and evaluate operator ideas
description: Give the product-manager role a governed workflow for considering ideas proposed by the operator. The product manager can clarify the idea, gather relevant evidence from configured capabilities such as web search, compare the evidence and proposal against the product brief, goals, directives, and known constraints, and recommend adoption, rejection, deferral, or an experiment. Research is advisory: it must not silently turn an idea into an approved goal, design, or implementation directive.
design: Keep research capabilities separate from product-manager authority. Evidence sources and tools are configurable and permissioned. Preserve source URLs or identifiers, retrieval time, material claims, uncertainty, counterevidence, and the reasoning behind the recommendation. Treat retrieved content as untrusted evidence rather than instructions. Store the evaluation durably and route any proposed brief, goal, or design change through the existing artifact-governance and approval workflow. Bound research by configurable privacy, cost, time, and source policies, and report when adequate evidence cannot be obtained.
acceptance_criteria: The operator can present an idea conversationally; the product manager asks necessary clarifying questions, uses configured research tools when evidence would help, cites discoverable sources, distinguishes facts from inference and uncertainty, evaluates alignment with the current brief and goals, and produces a durable recommendation. The evaluation can propose follow-up work or governed artifact changes, but no canonical brief, goal, design, directive, or implementation work is changed or created as approved work without the applicable policy and approval path.

title: The run record names its stop class, so a run that could not write its completion record still says why it stopped
description: Developers on 90 and 173 (2026-08-19 and 08-24): completion_recording_failure is set only on the returned orchestrator Outcome and written into the item's note, with nothing on the run record, so a run whose artifacts were removed and whose completion record could not be written keeps no durable reason and yoyo status cannot report that class; more generally the durable run record has no field naming which gate stopped a run, and the structured fields that look like discriminators (path_refusal, check_failure, review findings) can all be present on a run the provider killed. Done means: each blockOn* and fail site in the pipeline records a stop class on the run state (checks, review, publish, cleanup, completion recording, provider death, environmental, cancelled), the read model and yoyo status render it as the first word of the reason, the classes are pinned by the durable-vocabulary conformance test, and the delivery-pipeline baseline traces each one.

title: Every yoyo verb runs from inside a harness-managed worktree
description: Two developer reports on 70 (2026-08-19), unresolved since: every yoyo verb built on buildComponents - cost, directive, pause, resume, reconcile, run, review, chat - fails with 'repository and worktree roots must not contain one another' when run from inside a harness-managed worktree, because the worktree's own .yoyodyne config resolves the repository to a directory beneath the configured worktree root. yoyo reports avoids it by building only the config and state root. It bites exactly where recovery and inspection happen (inside a preserved worktree after a failed run) and for any agent smoke-testing the binary it just built (92's developer hit it the same week). Done means: a verb run from inside a worktree resolves the repository to the primary checkout the worktree belongs to, or refuses with a sentence naming the primary checkout to run it from; a test drives one verb from a created worktree; and docs/operations.md's recovery section says where verbs are run from. title: A withdrawn thread-recorded directive is answered in its thread
description: Developer on 215, 2026-08-31: a directive recorded from a Slack thread and later withdrawn keeps its under-consideration mark forever, because the sink announces settlements from Resolved() and a withdrawal deliberately is not one. title: The verdict contract gains an out-of-scope disposition distinct from minor
description: From the developer on run-1991b13f (yoyodyne-ifd.279, landed): half the cap-reform direction is not implemented as stated. The reviewer's verdict contract has severities blocker, major and minor only - no out-of-scope disposition - so 'a single trivial or out-of-scope finding does not spend the budget' was implemented as 'a single minor finding does', and a reviewer that wants to say 'right, but out of scope' still has to say 'minor'. Consequence: a review budget now depends on model-generated severity labels, and a real defect labelled minor is a free round as well as a small-looking one, where before the mislabelling affected only what the developer was told. Done means the verdict contract carries a disposition for a finding that is trivial or outside the item's scope, distinct from minor; the budget rule reads that disposition rather than the severity label; the reviewer persona's severity guidance says plainly that minor is a severity and out-of-scope is a disposition; and the durable vocabulary test (internal/orchestrator/durablevocabulary_test.go) pins the addition in both internal/review and internal/runstate.
notes:
Admitted to the backlog by the product manager in conversation chat-91253e0e070c17b0663651cc48602122, after turn 511.

Reason: The operator's rule named two cases and the landing carries one; folding out-of-scope into minor makes a severity label load-bearing for spend, which the report identifies as the new hazard.

description:

FIRST SHIPMENT, the highest-value narrow slice, before the broader scan: reconciling her own decisions against the governed documents. Nine amendments decided in her 2026-08-24 sitting were never recorded or never landed and surfaced weeks later as undecided (386bbb56, e89e6794, 8ed7833e, 609574f1, fd5f20be, eac618f5, d59b87fc, 0249369e, 6e9f6b10 - carried on yoyodyne-ifd.280 with the reconciliation ask). description: From the developer on run-e83e13a5 (yoyodyne-ifd.264): internal/orchestrator/declarative.go:119 beginDeliveryTrial returns silently when deliveryTrialOver or executor.Start fails, so the run records no workflow_instance_id and looks exactly like a run on the legacy path - and 'go test -update-baseline' then freezes that as the trace. description: From the developer on run-965fe2b9 (yoyodyne-ifd.268), deferred twice and still unowned: runstate.State.Failure is unbounded in State.Validate(), unlike Blocker, Summary, Changes and every other recorded reason, and it is written from cause.Error(), which can fold a provider's whole output into it. title: A rerun carries the decision the development manager recorded, not words handed to a flag
description:
From the development manager (chat-419cedb4, first exercised rerun, yoyodyne-ifd.125.1) and raised to p1 by the operator on 2026-09-07 with its scope widened to the condition it actually fixes.

THE ORIGINAL DEFECT: yoyo triage rerun takes the DM's reasoning as a --reason flag and records it as the run's selection reason attributed to the development manager - nothing checks those words against the decision the DM actually recorded, because triage decisions live only as prose in item notes. A run started by hand can therefore carry a development-manager attribution nobody in that role wrote, weakening exactly what selected-work-passes-intake-and-records-why exists for. Fix: triage decisions are written as durable, machine-readable records where the DM's conversation records them (carryOutTriage); the rerun verb READS the recorded decision rather than accepting words; a rerun with no recorded decision is refused naming the missing record; the attribution on the run cites the decision record.

THE CONDITION IT MUST ACTUALLY END, operator-directed: recording a decision is SUFFICIENT TO CAUSE THE RERUN. Thirty-three items stand 'held for a person' today not because anyone owes a decision but because decisions the DM recorded days ago have never been carried out - his sweeps have reported this as a standing finding since they began, and the operator has asked that hands stop being the answer. So a recorded decision is dispatched by the next scheduling pass without a person invoking a verb: the machine-readable record is the enabling half, auto-carry-out is what empties the queue. Done means a DM decision recorded in conversation results in the rerun happening on its own, the run's attribution cites that record, a decision that cannot be carried out says why in a durable place the sweep reads, and the standing 33-item finding clears without hands.

Coordinate with what already landed in these counters: 299 (pre-flight before the budget increment, so a refused carry-out spends nothing) and 309 (the DM's bounded cap crossings) both touch this path.

Reason: An attribution anybody can type is not an attribution; the chain invariant this weakens is the goal's own sentence, and the triage store the fix needs now exists where it did not in August.

title: A refused rerun spends nothing: pre-flight precedes the budget increment
description: From the development manager (chat-419cedb4, first exercised rerun, yoyodyne-ifd.125.1): a triage rerun refused pre-flight for blocked item status recorded no run but consumed the once-per-stoppage budget; the second attempt was then refused by the guard whose own message stated the contradiction ('already re-run, and no fresh run was recorded for it'). Any rerun of a blocked item therefore burns its budget on the refusal unless the item is reopened first - a remembered step, worked around by hand. The DM's fix shape, preserving increment-before-act crash safety: pre-flight checks (status, terminal record, hold) run BEFORE the counter increment, so only a launch that actually records a run spends the budget, and re-entry supersedes the standing blocker as 102.5's constraints specify. Done means a rerun refused pre-flight leaves the budget untouched and says so, a rerun that launches spends exactly once, and the 125.1 contradiction shape is the regression case - checked against whatever the 279 cap-reform pass has already changed in these counters.

title: Secrets probes require the variables, not the file
description: Two reports, one defect in two places: doctor's checkSlackSecrets (internal/doctor/slack.go) stats ~/.config/yoyo/<product>/slack.env and checks its mode but never looks for the two export names, so an empty or placeholder file passes and the sink then refuses to start with 'SLACK_BOT_TOKEN is not set' over a diagnosis saying the secrets are stored; and setup's ensureSlackSecrets (internal/cli/setup.go:782) reports 'secrets are already stored' from the file's existence alone, so an operator who runs setup after doctor is told the step is done over a sink that will not start. Done means both probes require SLACK_BOT_TOKEN and SLACK_APP_TOKEN to be present and non-empty in the file, the two surfaces agree with each other, and the empty-file case is tested on both. The tokens' values are never printed - only their presence is checked.

title: The tracker export cannot be smuggled into a run's committed change
description: From the developer on run-c7bc7bc9 (yoyodyne-ifd.223): the refreshed .beads/issues.jsonl is kept out of a run's change only by Git's skip-worktree bit in the worktree's index under .git/worktrees/<id>/index - and a developer sandbox grants writes to .git, so an agent running 'git update-index --no-skip-worktree' (or rewriting the index any other way) turns the export into a modification the harness then commits, promotes, and conflicts other runs against. Creation proves the worktree clean but nothing re-checks, and .beads is not a protected path so the diff gate would not stop it. Done means the change-path gate refuses the export (or .beads/ wholesale) in a run's diff regardless of index state, or the skip-worktree protection is re-verified at submission with a violation failing loudly - either way, the smuggling path is closed and tested.

title: An agent whose amendment proposal was refused learns so before claiming it landed
description: Follow-on to the closed yoyodyne-ifd.246, whose shipped scope was tracker-block refusals; this owns the amendment case my note on that closed item could not. From the developer on run-6ff896ba (yoyodyne-ifd.121): a developer's amendment block naming a document outside the artifact homes was refused, the refusal reached the operator but never the agent, and the agent then wrote into a checked-in document that it had 'raised an amendment against this document' - a false claim durable in prose, which yoyo amendment list disproved and the reviewer could not verify either way. The problem is that the two operator-facing documents this change rewrote now assert that guarantee unconditionally, when the carry-back only fires if the same role is invoked again on the same run. That is the most common run shape failing the claim, and it is exactly the fact the contract text states plainly, so the docs need the same qualification. The implementation only puts the refusal in front of the agent if that role is invoked again on the same run (carriedAmendmentRefusals is prepended in develop, and the refusal is not discoverable before the reply that carried it), so on a run whose developer is invoked once and succeeds the agent is never told. The contract text you added to internal/amendment/amendment.go states this correctly ("if it invokes you again ... and if it does not, the refusal is on the run for the operator and you never hear it"). Qualify the claim here the same way: the refusal reaches the agent on its next invocation if there is one, and otherwise reaches the operator alone, with the contract's prohibition on claiming a proposal was raised being what covers that case.
Finding [major] (docs/reporting.md:490): docs/reporting.md opens the new paragraph with "That naming reaches the agent as well as you." and then describes the carry-back without stating that it depends on the proposing role being invoked again. As written, an operator reading this would conclude every refused proposal is reported back to its author, which is false for any run whose developer is invoked once. State the condition explicitly and say what covers the uncovered case (the contract's rule that nothing an agent writes may claim a proposal was raised), so the document matches the guarantee the code actually makes.

title: An oversized file in a change is shown as omitted, never silently absent from review
description: From the developer on 121.3's run, 2026-08-20, a general mechanism outliving the tranche that found it: an untracked file exceeding the 64 KiB per-file ceiling (gitworktree.DefaultMaxDiffFileBytes) is dropped from the reviewer's patch ENTIRELY - manager.go:778 gates on size, manager.go:586 records it omitted - with only a Truncated flag, unlike the 256 KiB total which clips to whole lines. A reviewer sees no trace of a file the change delivers; the same silent truncation refused PR #129 and re-scoped the docs epic. Fix: an omitted file appears in the rendered evidence BY NAME with its size and the bound - 'delivered but too large to show' - so the reviewer judges a named absence rather than not knowing; composes with 148's evidence-completeness family. Done means a change adding an over-bound file produces review evidence naming it as omitted, the silent-drop shape is test-impossible, and the two historical refusals' mechanism cannot recur unnamed.
notes:
Admitted to the backlog by the product manager in conversation chat-91253e0e070c17b0663651cc48602122, after turn 356.

Reason: A reviewer who cannot tell a missing file from an oversized one judges blind on exactly the deliveries most likely to matter; naming the omission is cheap and the mechanism already cost two refusals.

title: The doctor's slack-secrets probe reads the variables, not just the file

Scope: a lease or equivalent spans account choice through reservation, simultaneous starts are serialized or assigned distinct accounts, and a test drives two concurrent reservations asserting distinct accounts when the pool has them. title: Every priced terminal in a run's log attributes to its phase
description: Carried out of a note that landed on the closed ifd.92: from the reviewer's warning on ifd.83, 2026-08-23. The phase-split instrumentation assumes a run's log contains priced terminals only from the developer's attempts and exactly one per review.started; any other provider invocation - a shadow reviewer that does not announce itself, a summarizer, a reviewer retried without re-announcing - silently lands in the repair bucket, inflating repair on exactly the runs being measured. The shadow experiment (92) has since closed, so if its invocations do not emit review.started the pollution is in live data. Scope: audit internal/execution for every path that can emit run.completed or run.failed into a run's log; every such invocation announces its phase (its own review.started or equivalent); the phase split's assumption becomes an enforced property rather than a hope; and if the shadow review polluted recorded phase data, the affected runs are named. The safety property still holds there — such an invocation carries an unrecognised or empty role and lands in Unattributed — but that is the role mechanism doing the work, not the sweep. Finding [minor] (internal/execution/event.go:171): Event.Validate now accepts any schema version in [MinReadableEventSchemaVersion, EventSchemaVersion], and it gates writes as well as reads — appendLegacyCostEvents in price_test.go relies on exactly that to append a schema-1 terminal through store.AppendEvent. title: A conversation lease survives an interrupted close: Release tolerates EINTR
description: From the developer's warning on ifd.45's run, 2026-08-23, a once-seen flake with a strong mechanism hypothesis: TestAConversationLeaseThatCannotBeAskedIsReportedAsAProblem failed under load with 'already held by another process' on a lease nothing could contend for. Best hypothesis, from the report: conversationInUse (internal/cli/agent.go:360) discards the error from lease.Release(), which is file.Close(); macOS close(2) is interruptible, Go does not retry EINTR, and async-preemption SIGURG makes EINTR likelier under load - so a failed Close leaves the flock held and every later question about that conversation answers 'held by another process', the exact wrong answer the function exists to avoid. The same silent leak would affect a long-lived yoyo chat process, not only tests. Scope, per the report: whether Release should tolerate EINTR, and whether conversationInUse should report a release it could not take rather than discarding it. Done means an interrupted close cannot silently hold the lease, the discard path reports instead, and the flake's mechanism is either fixed or refuted with citations.

Reason: A silently leaked conversation lease locks the operator's own interface out of a conversation until a process restart - low frequency, high confusion when it fires, with a mechanism hypothesis good enough to act on. Review summary: The change addresses all three clauses of the work item's done condition. Lease.Release now drops the flock explicitly with an EINTR-retrying unlockStateFile before closing, so an interrupted close can no longer leave the lock held — the retry is safe precisely because the descriptor is still open and still this process's, which is the property an interrupted close lacks; closeLockError then tolerates EINTR on the close itself, and the residual failure mode is a leaked descriptor rather than an invisible lock. conversationInUse reports the release it could not take instead of discarding it, and Hold now labels the lease so that report names the conversation. Blast radius is the shared Lease.Release, used by the promotion and sink leases as well: unlocking before closing preserves the crash semantics one-promotion-per-target-branch depends on (the OS still drops the advisory lock when the holder dies) and keeps acquisition and release inside the store, so no agent gains contact with the lease; I checked the change against each invariant supplied to me and found none violated. No protected path is touched and the work item names no grant. The doc comments on Release and conversationInUse were updated with the behaviour, and no document visible to me is left asserting the old close-only release. Evidence supports the fix: TestUnlockingALeaseFileFreesItWithoutClosingIt proves the lock is free while the first descriptor is deliberately still open, and TestAnInterruptedCloseIsNotAFailureToRelease covers both the bare errno and the fs.PathError wrapper callers actually receive. Two minor test-coverage observations follow; neither is a defect in the change.
Finding [minor] (internal/cli/agent.go:357): The new report path — returning the Release error as a problem instead of discarding it — has no test behind it, because conversationInUse takes a concrete *runstate.ConversationStore with no seam to fail a release through. The four lines are correct by inspection, but the one clause of the work item most likely to regress silently is the one nothing would catch. If a seam becomes cheap later (for instance a releaser interface at this call site), a test that a failed release surfaces as a problem rather than a false 'not in use' would be worth adding.
Finding [minor] (internal/cli/agent_test.go:419): TestAskingWhetherAConversationIsInUseDoesNotKeepIt passes against the pre-change code as well: the old `_ = lease.Release()` still closed the file, and closing was what dropped the flock, so repeated asks and the subsequent Hold all succeeded before this change too. It documents the intended property but does not guard the fix; the discriminating coverage is in lock_unix_test.go.
Finding [minor] (internal/runstate/lock_unix.go:62): The comment on closeLockError asserts that on every platform the file builds for, the descriptor is deallocated even when close reports EINTR. That holds on Linux and the BSDs but POSIX leaves it unspecified, and the claim carries no citation while the work item asked for the mechanism to be fixed or refuted with citations. It is not load-bearing — because the unlock precedes the close, a hypothetically surviving descriptor would still hold no lock, which the comment itself notes — so a reference (POSIX close(2) rationale, or the Go decision not to retry close) would settle it rather than change it.

title: Repository-coupled goal tests must not fail legitimate states
description: ifd.1.9's reviewer observed (beside the verdict) that the new tests in internal/goal/goal_test.go bind make test to the live contents of docs/product: TestEveryGoalYoyodyneRecordsNamesABriefGoalTheBriefStates fails if any goal in force lacks a Supports trailer or names a brief claim the brief does not state, and configuredStore fails if a configured home directory does not exist — while the item's own constraint says a goals document legitimately stating no goals is a correct report, not a defect. Decide the boundary: which repository states are contract violations the suite should refuse, and which are legitimate states the suite must tolerate (an intentionally empty goals set; a home not yet created on a fresh project). The wrong boundary makes editing product intent break the build.

title: Design distributed coordination for team mode
description:
Second child of yoyodyne-ifd.82, the architecture pass: waits for the architect role that yoyodyne-ifd.4 creates - a dependency link records this - and designs against the approved scoping document. Covers the five recorded gaps: Dolt-remote tracker sync, distributed claim so two machines cannot both pay for one item, a promotion lease that holds across machines rather than narrowing to machine-scoped flock with the forge as backstop, travel for reports, run state, conversations, and the pause switch, and operator identity.

EXPLICIT CONSTRAINT from the operator: operator identity is designed once, jointly for ifd.25's recorded design precondition (approval identity is forgeable - 'by: operator' with nothing distinguishing the operator from an agent with shell access) and for this epic's multi-human case. Not twice.

Attribution caveat: the team goal named here awaits the operator's pen in v1-goals.md; accepted while goal validation is down, verify when ifd.1.9 seeds the store.
notes:
Operator-endorsed design sketch for the shared tracker, recorded 2026-08-18 so the architect starts here rather than re-deriving. The mechanism exists and is wired to nothing: Beads is an embedded Dolt database — git-for-data, full replica per machine, remotes, cell-level merge — and the designed sync path stores tracker data under refs/dolt/data on the same git remote the repository already uses. The team already shares one authority, the forge remote; the tracker rides it. No new server, honoring the amended no-hosted-control-plane non-goal. What must be built is discipline, not infrastructure: (1) wiring — nothing configures the Dolt remote today, every bd call warns about it; team setup or yoyo init configures it once per machine; (2) sync at the natural moments — pull before claim, push after every tracker write, sync at session close; between syncs you work on a replica, which is also the offline story for free; (3) claims become conflict-detected rather than lock-protected — two machines claiming one item in the sync window is a same-cell edit Dolt detects; deterministic resolution (earlier claim timestamp wins, loser releases and re-picks), worst case one duplicated run's bounded visible cost, with forge branch protection the backstop that the race can never corrupt code; this is the scoping draft's no-two-machines-paying promise enforced optimistically; (4) most merges are trivial — tracker activity is overwhelmingly disjoint rows and appended notes, cell-level merge handles different-field edits to one item, genuine same-field conflicts surface with a resolution step and will be rare. Alternatives lose: a central tracker server is the hosted control plane written out of scope; forge issues abandon the beads model; single-writer RPC makes one laptop a worse-availability control plane. Replica-plus-merge matches how the code half already works. Open questions for this design: the .beads/issues.jsonl export's role under multiple writers (probably stop committing it, or one machine owns the export); sync frequency and cost (pull-per-claim is just git, cheap); and whether yoyo pause propagates through the shared tracker — which would answer the scoping draft's 'team-wide pause is a design question' nearly for free, since a pause flag in shared state travels with every sync.

Operator scenario to design for, 2026-08-19 (raised while configuring Slack): two collaborators, shared config, therefore a shared inbound allow-list — can one direct work on the other's machine by replying in threads the other's sink owns? The answer must split by kind, per the scoping document's own line: directives are product intent and must bind regardless of which machine received them (the directives goal verbatim — which requires directives to move from per-machine state into the shared coordination store this design owns), while machine controls (pause, stop, intake hold) remain each collaborator's own and stay unreachable from Slack, as the architect already decided for /stop. The wrinkle to resolve: with two sinks in one channel (the recorded two-threads-per-item limit), which machine acts on a reply is currently an accident of thread ownership — the design should make a reply record into the shared store so every harness enforces it, rather than routing authority by whoever's sink opened the thread.

title: One voice for the product manager, and one table for what --message refuses
description: Two minor findings from ifd.70's approving review, recorded rather than bolted onto an approved branch: (1) the branch introduced 'she/her' for the product manager in README.md and internal/chat/steer.go while the surrounding prose it also edited says 'it' (printChatHeader) — pick one voice for the role across docs and comments; (2) needsConversation in steer.go is an allow-by-default deny-list that parses the command name itself instead of sharing the dispatcher's parsing, so a command added to the dispatcher later is silently permitted in --message mode and a name separated by something other than a space slips past the refusal — derive the refusal from the dispatcher's table, or add a test that fails when a dispatchable command has no decision recorded.

title: Record the output-emphasis discipline once, where every surface inherits it
description: The rules exist as precedent in shipped code - ANSI only when output is a terminal, suppressed under NO_COLOR and TERM=dumb, absent from --json, every distinction survives stripping - and each new surface re-argues them from scratch (the goals listing, the status banner, the conversation rules were each argued separately). Record the discipline once as a contract new surfaces inherit rather than rediscover; where it lives (documentation, an architect invariant, or both) is the implementer's call, stated with reasoning. Done means a new output surface can cite one recorded rule instead of re-deriving it, and the rule names the legibility goal it serves.
notes:
Admitted to the backlog by the product manager in conversation chat-91253e0e070c17b0663651cc48602122, after turn 55.

Reason: Second gap the legibility goal exposes: the goal demands one discipline and today it is per-item precedent. Priority 3 because the shipped theme code already embodies the rules; this records them.

Goal served: The harness's surfaces read clearly: boundaries between topics and speakers are visible, important findings stand out, and every distinction survives a terminal that cannot render emphasis.

title: Design a portable agent configuration system
description:
TODO recorded by the operator, 2026-08-16, when choosing explicit project configuration for now: 'we will want those later ... the design for a more portable agent configuration system remains a TODO.'

The machinery exists and works. A versioned bundle ships inside the executable, a project inherits it by name with extends, three layers resolve with later ones winning, checks are replaced wholesale rather than concatenated, a persona override replaces rather than merges, and version is deliberately not inheritable. What is missing is not capability but a considered answer to what portability should mean once there is more than one project and more than one person.

ifd.35 makes the explicit file the shape a project is shipped with, precisely because the operator is changing agent properties often at this stage and wants an edit's effect obvious. Inheritance is retained rather than removed, so this is deferred rather than discarded.
design:
The question worth answering is what a project should own and what it should receive. An explicit configuration is clear and never improves; an inherited one improves and hides where its values came from. Both are right at different points in a project's life, and the interesting design is the transition between them rather than a choice of one.

Things that will need deciding when this is picked up: whether a project can inherit selectively rather than wholesale, so it owns the agent properties it edits often and inherits the rest; how an operator sees which values are inherited without running a command, given that config show --origins already answers this only when asked; how a bundle improvement reaches a project that has materialized its defaults, which is the specific thing ifd.35 trades away; and whether bundles are ever supplied by anyone other than the executable, which is where this meets ifd.32 and its plugin contract.

Do not start this by writing code. The resolution machinery is already built and tested; what is absent is the decision about when a project should use it.
acceptance_criteria: A recorded design states what a project owns versus inherits, how an operator can see which is which without asking, how a project moves between explicit and inherited configuration in both directions, and how an improvement to shared defaults reaches a project that has materialized them; the design is traceable to a goal; no code is written before that design is agreed.
notes:
Deferred deliberately, not abandoned. The inheritance implementation from ifd.4.2, its tightening in ifd.9, and ifd.4.3 all remain live; ifd.35 changes the default shape a project is shipped with rather than removing what the harness can express.
Attributed to a goal by the product manager in conversation chat-91253e0e070c17b0663651cc48602122, after turn 26.

Reason: Portable agent configuration is the configurability half of this goal made deliberate: what a project owns versus inherits, how an operator sees which is which, and how shared defaults reach a project - all decisions about how configuration works without loosening what must hold. Deferred by explicit operator decision, which affects its order, not its goal.

Goal served: Keep roles, policies, and provider selection configurable without making safety invariants optional.

title: Teach yoyo-status about conversations
description:
bin/yoyo-status follows and reports runs from the runs/ directory. Conversations are recorded separately under conversations/, with their own event streams, so the one tool an operator would reach for to answer 'is this alive' does not look where a chat lives.

Found 2026-08-16 alongside yoyodyne-ifd.22: when an interactive conversation appeared to hang, neither the terminal nor yoyo-status could say what was happening, and the answer had to be read out of the raw JSONL by hand.
design: Follow and report conversations the same way runs are followed, and let the default do the obvious thing rather than making the operator name which kind of thing they mean. Cost reporting already sums usage from run.completed events; conversation turns carry the same evidence, so chat spend is currently invisible in the total and should not be.
acceptance_criteria: yoyo-status can follow a conversation's event stream and list recent conversations with their status; cost reporting includes conversation turns so the reported total is the real total; selecting a run or a conversation by id or prefix works for both; the existing run behavior is unchanged.
notes:
Filed 2026-08-16. Note for whoever takes this: the reported spend figures in this session excluded chat entirely, so the totals quoted while building were low.
Noted by the product manager in conversation chat-91253e0e070c17b0663651cc48602122, after turn 11.

Reason: Recording the attribution the audit found missing. This item serves two goals rather than one, and saying so prevents half of it being read as unattributed scope later.

Goal attribution: this item was admitted before work items carried one, and it spans two goals. Its cost-reporting half - including conversation turns so the reported total is the real total - serves the new v1 goal 'The operator can see what the harness spends on their behalf: provider-reported cost, per work item, per run, and in total.' Its conversation-observability half - following a conversation's event stream, listing recent conversations with their status, answering 'is this alive' - serves 'Run development nearly autonomously', where the operator's routine interface is the product manager and a conversation that cannot be observed is a broken interface. Both halves are wanted; neither is scope to drop.

title: Observe reality before settling a run that already recorded an integration
description:
Minor finding accepted from the independent review of yoyodyne-ifd.2.8 (run run-28db324904cf8b781757bf63c83b55d2). When durable run state already carries an Integration, settle goes straight to completeIntegrated without calling Observe, so the one comparison the design guidance asks for -- durable state against observed reality -- is skipped on exactly the path where the run claims the most. A recorded integration is trusted rather than verified.

Not exploitable through the current pipeline, which writes the integration only after Integrate returns, but reconciliation exists precisely to handle state written by a process that died, so trusting the record is the wrong default in this component.
design: Have settle observe before acting on a recorded integration, and reconcile the two rather than assuming they agree: confirm the recorded source commit is contained in the recorded target before treating the run as integrated. CleanupIntegrated already performs that containment proof, so the check exists and the question is only whether reconciliation reaches it through Observe. Decide what a disagreement means -- a recorded integration whose commit is absent from the target is a durable blocker, not something to complete.
acceptance_criteria: settle observes reality before completing a run that carries recorded integration evidence; a recorded integration whose commit is not contained in its target becomes a blocker rather than being completed; existing reconciliation behavior is otherwise unchanged and its tests still pass.

title: Role names and identifiers are validated the same way everywhere: config, backend role support, directive record, and report and amendment item ids
description: Three developer reports (95, 97, 68.3; 2026-08-19): (1) domain.Backend.SupportsRole returns true for every role on claude-code, so a project config naming a role outside the five validates cleanly (internal/config/config.go is the only role check) and fails at the first provider invocation; (2) yoyo directive record --received-by accepts any identifier-shaped string as a role, so a typo records a directive attributed to a role that does not exist; (3) report.Report.Validate and amendment.Proposal.Validate do not constrain WorkItemID, so a value with a colon or whitespace enters both durable logs and the Slack sink cannot key a thread on it. Done means: one role validator (domain.AgentRole.Valid) is used by config validation, backend support, and the directive record; WorkItemID is held to the identifier pattern in both Validate methods; each rejection is a test; and a hand-edited config naming a bad role fails at load with the role named.

title: Make provider integration a plugin contract users can extend
description:
Everything the harness knows about rate limits, retries, and when to try again is Claude Code's dialect, sitting in internal/backend/claudecode. The parser knows the rate_limit_event envelope, the field names status, resetsAt, rateLimitType, isUsingOverage, and overageStatus, that resetsAt is Unix seconds, that api_retry is the provider's own transient retry, and now that a rejection with no reset time means poll in thirty minutes. None of that is general, and all of it is load-bearing.

Codex is already a planned backend (yoyodyne-ifd.6), and the operator wants users to be able to reach further than that: to write a plugin for whatever harness or API they use, including an OpenAI-compatible one, without changing Yoyodyne.

The existing AgentBackend interface and its Capabilities call are the right instinct but the wrong altitude for this: they abstract starting and resuming a run, not the operational dialect of a provider -- how it says it is throttled, how it says it is exhausted, how to tell those apart, and when to come back.
design:
What the harness needs from a provider is a small set of answers, and the contract should be those answers rather than a way to reach in and parse. Given a provider event: is this an ordinary retry the provider is handling itself, a limit that will lift, or a refusal that will not; and if it will lift, when. The two hard cases are the ones already learned and should be named in the contract rather than rediscovered by each plugin: a limit that names no reset time is unknown rather than fatal and needs a default recheck interval, and a report that names a reset time in the past is malformed and must not be trusted.

Decide how a plugin is delivered, because Go makes this a real choice rather than a detail. Compile-time registration is simple and forces users to fork or vendor. A subprocess speaking a documented protocol keeps them independent and adds a boundary to defend, which matters because the thing on the other side is untrusted. A declarative adapter -- patterns and field mappings in configuration -- covers the common case of an API that differs only in spelling, and covers nothing else. The choice should be made explicitly with its trade stated, not arrived at.

Whatever is chosen, the plugin describes and never decides. It reports what a provider said; the harness decides whether to wait, how long, and against which budget, because those decisions are what the operator's usage_limit settings and the run's safety properties depend on. A plugin that could decide to keep waiting could spend an account.

Keep the capability model honest as it grows. Codex is already documented as not matching every Claude Code feature, and an unsupported role or policy combination fails validation before work is assigned; that must hold for a plugin nobody here has seen.
acceptance_criteria: Rate-limit, retry, and reset-time interpretation lives behind a documented provider contract rather than in the Claude Code adapter; the Claude Code behavior is one implementation of that contract with no special casing above it; a second provider can be added without changing harness code, and the delivery mechanism for a user-supplied one is documented with its trade-offs stated; a plugin reports what a provider said and never decides whether or how long to wait; the unknown-reset and past-reset cases are part of the contract rather than per-plugin behavior; capability validation refuses an unsupported role or policy combination for a plugin as it does for a built-in backend.
